runs.prompt: Jim, an Australian expat in Jerusalem, is considering buying property and is interested in the Australian dollar against the Israeli Shekel and the Australian dollar against the US dollar. He wants to know how to assess the overall liquidity of currency pairs, find standardized measures of volatility, identify support points in rate pairs, and understand the primary geopolitical and macroeconomic factors influencing any given currency pair.

entries.script:
Corn: Buying a flat is stressful enough without the deposit developing a foreign policy. Jim, an Australian expat in Jerusalem, wants to understand the Australian dollar against the Israeli shekel and the American dollar before buying property.

Herman: And he’s asking exactly the right underlying questions: How liquid are these currency pairs? How do you compare volatility? Can you identify support levels? And which economic and geopolitical forces actually move the exchange rate?

Corn: Welcome to My Weird Prompts. I’m Corn, and that’s my brother, Herman Poppleberry. Today: how to buy a home without accidentally taking a second job as a currency speculator.

Herman: There’s an important distinction right at the start. Jim’s eventual obligation is probably in shekels. His savings might be in Australian dollars. The Australian dollar against the US dollar matters, but it isn’t his final scorecard.

Corn: The seller does not accept excellent performance against America.

Herman: Exactly. If his Australian dollars rise against the US dollar, but the shekel rises even more against the US dollar, his Australian dollars still buy fewer shekels. He can be right about Australia and still find the apartment more expensive.

Corn: So let’s settle one thing immediately: which pair should he watch?

Herman: Australian dollars against shekels for the actual purchase. Australian dollars against US dollars, and US dollars against shekels, to understand why the purchase rate is moving. Those two legs are the diagnostic tools.

Corn: And let’s not pretend we have a live dealer screen. We’re going to use hypothetical exchange rates, not quote today’s market or announce that a particular price is support.

Herman: Good. Suppose one Australian dollar buys sixty-five US cents, and one US dollar buys three point seven shekels. Multiply those numbers. One Australian dollar buys two point four zero five shekels, before spreads and fees.

Corn: That multiplication is the spine of this episode. Australian dollars into US dollars, then dollars into shekels. Even if Jim’s transfer company gives him one Australian dollar to shekel quote, those underlying markets help explain it.

Herman: And the quote direction matters. With Australian dollars against US dollars, a rising number means the Australian dollar strengthens. With US dollars against shekels, a rising number means the shekel weakens. Write the units beside every chart: shekels per Australian dollar, for instance.

Corn: A surprisingly effective defence against confidently trading backwards.

Herman: Now let’s put a property behind the arithmetic. Imagine Jim needs three million shekels. At two point four shekels per Australian dollar, that requires one point two five million Australian dollars. At two point three, it requires about one point three zero four million.

Corn: More than fifty-four thousand Australian dollars extra. Same apartment. Same kitchen tap.

Herman: And that is why his first spreadsheet should show the Australian dollar cost of the actual shekel payments at several exchange rates. Not just a chart with a hopeful upward arrow. Include taxes, legal fees, transfer costs, and whatever payment timetable the contract actually establishes.

Corn: I’d go further. Before studying support levels, ask: how far can the rate move against me before I can’t complete? That’s a much more useful number than somebody’s price target.

Herman: Agreed. Though knowing the market structure helps him choose how to execute. Let’s take liquidity first. People often equate it with trading volume, but liquidity really means being able to transact a given amount promptly, at a competitive price, without moving that price much.

Corn: A market can be busy and still give you a terrible quote for your particular trade.

Herman: Yes. There are several dimensions. Tightness is the bid-ask spread. Depth is how much can trade near the current price. Immediacy is how quickly you can execute. Resilience is how quickly pricing recovers after a large order or shock.

Corn: Which of those can Jim actually observe without installing a trading desk next to the kettle?

Herman: Spreads and executable quotes are the practical starting point. Ask several providers, at almost the same time, how many shekels will arrive for the exact Australian dollar amount, with the same settlement date. That’s much more informative than comparing their advertised transfer fees.

Corn: Zero fee. Generous exchange-rate imagination.

Herman: Right. A provider can charge through the exchange rate. Suppose the indicative midpoint is two point four shekels per Australian dollar. One provider delivers two point three nine five, another two point three seven. On a million Australian dollars, the difference is twenty-five thousand shekels.

Corn: That’s not rounding. That’s furniture.

Herman: Compare the all-in outcome, including receiving-bank charges where applicable. Also ask how long the quote is valid, whether it is executable for the full amount, and whether the amount arriving is guaranteed or only estimated.

Corn: And what about the grand, overall liquidity ranking? Jim asked about currency pairs, not just which app has the nicest button.

Herman: The Bank for International Settlements publishes the Triennial Central Bank Survey of foreign-exchange turnover. That’s the standard starting point for global turnover by currency, instrument, and major pair. Central banks also publish regional surveys. Check the survey date rather than treating an old table as current.

Corn: Does it give us a clean answer on these two pairs?

Herman: A clear relative answer. Australian dollars against US dollars is a major, heavily traded pair. Australian dollars against shekels is a much less actively traded cross. But global foreign exchange is decentralized, so there isn’t one exchange tape showing every transaction or one universal liquidity score.

Corn: And turnover in a currency isn’t turnover in every pair containing it.

Herman: Exactly. Also, distinguish spot from swaps and other instruments. A giant headline turnover number that includes foreign-exchange swaps does not tell Jim the spread he’ll pay on a spot conversion for a flat.

Corn: This feels like a recurring financial trick: the impressive number is technically answering a different question.

Herman: It happens. His direct cross may be priced synthetically through the US dollar. The final quote can reflect spreads and risk in both legs, plus the provider’s margin. But he shouldn’t assume that personally making two transfers through dollars will be cheaper.

Corn: Two opportunities to pay a spread. An ambitious savings strategy.

Herman: It could occasionally work out better, but compare executable end-to-end quotes. Otherwise there are extra fees, settlement timing, and the possibility the second exchange rate changes while money is moving.

Corn: What would make you suspicious that a provider’s quote is poor because of liquidity rather than just a large markup?

Herman: Compare across providers and trade sizes. If spreads widen sharply for larger amounts, that suggests limited accessible depth, although provider limits can contribute. If everybody widens during a shock, that’s market stress. If one provider stays expensive while others are competitive, that’s probably their pricing or business model.

Corn: So Jim can run a modest little experiment: same time, same amount, same destination, several quotes. Then repeat at another normal business time.

Herman: Yes. Australian dollar against US dollar trading is active across major sessions, but the shekel leg has its own activity patterns, local holidays, and banking constraints. Ask when the provider sees the best executable liquidity for this particular cross. Avoid assuming a weekend app quote represents normal market conditions.

Corn: Now volatility. Liquidity tells us how expensive the doorway is. Volatility tells us how much the floor moves.

Herman: Nicely put. The standard historical measure is the standard deviation of returns. Take a consistent series of daily exchange rates, calculate daily percentage returns, or logarithmic returns, then measure their standard deviation over a specified window.

Corn: Specified is doing work there.

Herman: A lot. Twenty trading days describes something different from a year. To compare pairs, use the same sampling frequency, observation time, return definition, and lookback period. Raw changes in exchange-rate points are not a fair comparison between differently scaled quotes.

Corn: A move of point zero one means nothing until you know what it’s a fraction of.

Herman: Exactly. Daily volatility is commonly annualized by multiplying by the square root of roughly two hundred fifty-two trading days. If daily return volatility is half a percent, that’s roughly eight percent annualized.

Corn: And eight percent annualized does not mean the currency will be eight percent higher next year.

Herman: Nor does it mean it will stay within eight percent. It describes variability under that calculation. It isn’t a direction forecast, a maximum loss, or a promise that the statistical assumptions will survive the next emergency cabinet meeting.

Corn: How does Jim translate it into his three-month property timeline?

Herman: Under a simple square-root-of-time approximation, eight percent annualized volatility corresponds to about four percent over three months. That gives scale, not a reliable boundary. Currency returns can have fat tails, volatility clusters, and jumps. Weekends and political events are particularly uncooperative with neat distributions.

Corn: The contract deadline, meanwhile, remains punctual.

Herman: I would show Jim rolling one-month and three-month realized volatility, plus a longer history and actual worst moves over relevant payment horizons. Add stress scenarios rather than trusting one average to describe both quiet markets and crises.

Corn: Can he use average true range? It appears on practically every charting platform.

Herman: Yes, as a supplementary measure. Average true range measures the typical range of price movement, including gaps from the previous close. Express it as a percentage of price to make comparisons more meaningful. But it isn’t the same statistic as return volatility, and different chart feeds may produce different daily ranges.

Corn: Especially for a thin cross where the chart looks precise but the executable quote is somewhere else.

Herman: Exactly. Use a reputable data source, consistent timestamps, and watch for stale prices. A cross constructed from two live legs can be more informative than a stale direct quote, although it still isn’t a promise of the price Jim can transact.

Corn: Historical volatility tells us what happened. What tells us what the market expects?

Herman: Options-implied volatility. It’s inferred from option prices, typically quoted on an annualized basis for a specified maturity. One-month and three-month implied volatility can show how expensive protection against future moves has become.

Corn: Expensive protection is not necessarily an accurate prophecy.

Herman: Correct. Implied volatility incorporates risk pricing and demand for insurance, not just an unbiased forecast. And comparable, publicly accessible options data are much easier to find for Australian dollars against US dollars than for the Australian dollar-shekel cross.

Corn: Could he just add the volatility of the two dollar legs?

Herman: No. Their correlation matters. For the cross, the logarithmic return is the sum of the returns on Australian dollars against US dollars and US dollars against shekels. Its variance includes both individual variances plus a covariance term.

Corn: In ordinary language: sometimes the legs cancel, sometimes they gang up.

Herman: Precisely. During a global shock, the Australian dollar might fall against the US dollar while the shekel also falls against the dollar. Those effects partially offset in the Australian dollar-shekel cross. But a strong shekel alongside a weak Australian dollar compounds Jim’s problem.

Corn: Which is why measuring his actual cross beats guessing from two scary headlines. Now, support. This is where someone draws a horizontal line and briefly becomes a prophet.

Herman: I’m more sympathetic to chart levels than you are. Support is an area where buying has previously been strong enough to interrupt a decline. In shekels per Australian dollar, it’s a lower zone where the Australian dollar has previously found buyers.

Corn: Previously. That word is the entire warranty.

Herman: True. But repeated reactions can reveal positioning, orders, and attention. For Jim, I’d begin with a daily chart covering perhaps a year or two, then look at weekly history. Mark meaningful swing lows and zones with several distinct reactions, not every tiny wiggle.

Corn: I’ll concede that visible history is useful. I object when a line gets treated like a load-bearing wall.

Herman: So do I. It’s a zone, not a force field. Round numbers can attract orders. Moving averages, like a two-hundred-day average, can provide context. Neither creates guaranteed support. A level tested repeatedly might attract buying, or it might eventually fail as buyers are exhausted.

Corn: You’ve just described both possible outcomes.

Herman: Fair criticism. That’s why a useful analysis specifies what would count as failure. For example: the market moves decisively through the zone and stays below it, rather than briefly touching it. That doesn’t establish a universal trading rule; it makes the interpretation less slippery.

Corn: I’d still tell Jim not to build his completion plan around that distinction. He needs shekels, not vindication from a candlestick.

Herman: Agreed. Also, if he’s waiting for a better conversion rate, he’s hoping for a higher shekels-per-Australian-dollar price. That means resistance above the market may matter as much as support below it.

Corn: Good correction. “Where could it bounce?” and “Where should I convert?” are not the same question.

Herman: And direct cross support may be less widely watched than levels in the two dollar legs. It can still be economically meaningful, but don’t assume enormous pools of orders sit at a line just because a charting package lets you draw it.

Corn: So my verdict: use support to organize scenarios, not to authorize an unaffordable gamble.

Herman: Mine too, though I’d let it inform the timing of a discretionary portion. Not the money that must be available to complete.

Corn: Let’s get to the forces moving these things. If Jim opens the news tomorrow, how does he distinguish a relevant story from fifty people shouting “uncertainty”?

Herman: Start with expected interest-rate differences. For Australian dollars against US dollars, compare the expected paths of the Reserve Bank of Australia and the Federal Reserve. Inflation, employment, wages, and growth matter because they change those expectations.

Corn: Not simply “Australian rates went up, therefore Australian dollar goes up.”

Herman: Right. If everyone expected a larger increase, a smaller increase can weaken the currency. Markets trade the surprise relative to what was priced, and the implications for future policy. A rate decision’s accompanying guidance can matter more than the announced rate.

Corn: What’s your second Australian-dollar driver?

Herman: China and commodity demand, particularly the implications for Australian export income and the terms of trade. Iron ore is an important example. Chinese construction weakness can hurt demand expectations. But “China bad, Australian dollar down” is still too crude.

Corn: Because the rest of the world inconveniently keeps happening.

Herman: And because prices may already reflect the bad news. Supply disruptions, fiscal stimulus, and changes in other export prices can complicate the story. The Australian dollar also often behaves like a risk-sensitive currency, weakening when investors retreat from risk.

Corn: While the US dollar can benefit from demand for dollar funding and liquid assets. Though not every American problem automatically strengthens America’s currency.

Herman: Exactly. The source of the shock matters. Watch US yields, Federal Reserve expectations, and broad dollar performance. If the Australian dollar falls alongside many currencies against the dollar, the story may be predominantly American or global, not uniquely Australian.

Corn: Now the shekel. In Jerusalem, geopolitical risk isn’t an abstract newsletter category.

Herman: Security developments can affect the shekel through risk premiums, capital flows, investment confidence, fiscal spending, tourism, and expected growth. Escalation, de-escalation, and the credibility of any durable settlement can all change pricing.

Corn: And a currency can strengthen on an awful headline if the market expected something worse.

Herman: Yes. That sounds cold, but it’s necessary to understand market reactions. Prices respond to changes in expectations, not a moral score for the news. Watch the actual exchange rate, bond yields, and credible reporting rather than assuming the headline dictates direction.

Corn: What belongs beside security on Jim’s Israel dashboard?

Herman: Bank of Israel policy, inflation, growth, fiscal deficits, government financing needs, and confidence in institutions. Sovereign credit-rating changes and outlooks can matter, especially when they confirm a broader reassessment of risk. Technology-sector investment and foreign capital flows also matter for Israel.

Corn: There’s a less obvious mechanism you were excited about before we started. Something involving pensions and American shares.

Herman: Israeli institutional investors hold substantial foreign assets. Their currency hedging can link global equity moves to shekel flows. When foreign equity holdings rise in value, an institution maintaining a target hedge may sell more foreign currency and buy shekels.

Corn: The shekel can move because a pension manager’s spreadsheet got larger.

Herman: Sometimes, yes. If foreign equities fall, hedge adjustments can work the other way. But the effect depends on hedge ratios, actual exposures, and decisions by institutions. It’s a mechanism, not a guaranteed daily relationship.

Corn: And central-bank intervention?

Herman: Important. The Bank of Israel has intervened in foreign exchange, including announcing a dollar-selling program during the shock in October twenty twenty-three. That historical example shows why foreign reserves and official policy announcements belong in the analysis. It does not establish a permanent exchange-rate floor.

Corn: Even the central bank has not signed Jim’s purchase contract.

Herman: Nor does a large reserve stock tell you exactly when intervention will happen. For any pair, ask the same questions: Is the exchange rate floating or managed? Are capital flows restricted? Who needs to buy or sell this currency, and under what conditions?

Corn: Let’s give Jim a workable routine. Not twenty screens. He presumably also has to inspect plumbing.

Herman: One page. At the top: shekel amounts and payment dates, available Australian dollars, and the exchange rate that would exhaust his budget cushion. Then current executable all-in quotes from two or three credible providers.

Corn: Below that, a chart of shekels per Australian dollar, with a few relevant zones. Beside it, the two dollar legs, so he can see which side is moving.

Herman: Then consistent realized-volatility measures and a calendar of Australian, US, and Israeli central-bank decisions and major data releases. Add a short note on the dominant current driver. “US rates repricing” is more useful than collecting every geopolitical headline.

Corn: What about practical execution? This is where perfectly good financial analysis meets a bank asking for a document on Friday afternoon.

Herman: Start onboarding early. Confirm transfer limits, source-of-funds requirements, beneficiary details, settlement dates, and local banking holidays. Verify payment instructions through an independently trusted channel. A large transfer delayed by compliance checks can matter more than a beautifully timed conversion.

Corn: Liquidity includes whether the money can actually reach the seller.

Herman: Strictly speaking that’s also operational and settlement risk, but for Jim’s outcome, absolutely. Ask his lawyer what must be paid, when, in which currency, and whether any amounts can change through contractual indexation. Don’t infer the legal timetable from the estate agent’s enthusiasm.

Corn: Finally, should he convert everything now, wait, or stagger it?

Herman: We don’t know his deadline, reserves, or tolerance for a shortfall, so there isn’t one honest allocation. But I would match firm, near-term shekel obligations with shekels, or investigate locking the relevant rate. Waiting unhedged is a currency position whether he calls himself a trader or not.

Corn: My preference is to separate the committed money from the optional money. Secure what would wreck the purchase if the rate moved against him. Then he can be selective with whatever genuinely has flexibility.

Herman: Staggered conversions can reduce dependence on one execution date, although they don’t guarantee a better average rate. A forward contract can fix an exchange rate for a future payment, subject to provider access, collateral or credit terms, and contractual obligations.

Corn: And the forward rate isn’t the provider’s forecast.

Herman: Correct. It largely reflects spot and the currencies’ interest-rate differential, with market pricing adjustments and provider costs. If the property purchase falls through, the forward may still exist, and unwinding it can cost money. Match the hedge to an obligation he genuinely expects to have.

Corn: Options offer flexibility, but there’s a premium, and complex “zero-cost” products deserve serious suspicion if Jim can’t explain their worst outcome himself.

Herman: Entirely agreed. For this purpose, boring is good. Competitive execution, transparent terms, and enough certainty to complete the purchase beat an elaborate strategy whose main achievement is making the brochure thicker.

Corn: So we do have a settled answer. Watch the Australian dollar-shekel cross for the home, use the dollar legs to diagnose it, and judge liquidity with executable quotes rather than a decorative global volume number.

Herman: Measure volatility consistently, treat support as conditional, and follow policy expectations and capital flows alongside geopolitical developments. Most importantly, choose how much currency risk the purchase can actually withstand before deciding how much to leave open.

Corn: Jim, may your exchange spread be narrow and your surveyor thorough.

Herman: And may the surprise costs come from neither.

Corn: That’s My Weird Prompts. Thanks for listening.

Herman: See you next time.

Corn: Our producer Daniel forwarded one with actual money on the line, so no pressure.
Herman: Yeah, this is from Jim, an Australian expat living in Jerusalem, thinking about buying property there. He is watching the Australian dollar against the shekel and the Australian dollar against the American dollar.
Corn: Big decision energy.
Herman: Right. And he asks four very specific things. How do you assess overall liquidity of currency pairs, how do you find standardized measures of volatility, how do you identify support points in rate pairs, and what are the primary geopolitical and macroeconomic factors that move any given pair.
Corn: He wants a toolkit, not a horoscope.
Herman: Exactly. So let us build him one, using his two pairs as the test cases. And Jim, standard disclaimer from a donkey and a sloth, we are not financial advisers, this is education for a podcast, talk to a licensed adviser before you move house sized money.
Corn: Especially house sized.
Herman: So first, liquidity. What does it even mean in foreign exchange.
Corn: Can I sell fast without moving the price.
Herman: Perfect. That is it. A liquid pair means you can trade a lot, quickly, at a tight price, without your own order shoving the market. An illiquid pair means even a modest order causes slippage, the price jumps away from you, and the cost to trade is higher.
Corn: Like trying to sell an apartment in one day.
Herman: Great analogy. So how does Jim actually assess it. There are four practical lenses, and they all agree on his two pairs. First is bid ask spread, the gap between the buy price and the sell price your broker or bank shows you.
Corn: The toll booth.
Herman: Yes. For the Aussie dollar against the American dollar, that spread on a normal day with a decent broker is tiny, often a fraction of a pip, like one to two pips or even less than one pip on an E C N account. I am not sure about the exact number right this second because spreads move with time of day, but that order of magnitude is right.
Corn: Pennies on a freeway.
Herman: For the Aussie dollar against the shekel, it is a different universe. Most retail platforms do not even quote it directly. You get quoted Aussie against American, and American against shekel, and your bank does the cross in the back office and charges you twice. The effective spread can be ten, twenty, fifty times wider, plus a conversion fee. If Jim sees his Israeli bank offering to convert Aussie dollars straight to shekels, that wide spread is the illiquidity tax made visible.
Corn: Paying for rarity.
Herman: Second lens is turnover, actual volume traded. The gold standard is the Bank for International Settlements triennial survey, last full one was April twenty twenty two, next full results come after April twenty twenty five. In twenty twenty two, the American dollar was on one side of about eighty eight percent of all foreign exchange trades, the Aussie dollar was on one side of about six to seven percent, the shekel was way down around zero point four percent or so.
Corn: Donkey remembers numbers.
Herman: I read papers, it is a sickness. But the implication is clean. Aussie against American is a major, top five most traded in the world, hundreds of billions of American dollars a day in that pair alone. Aussie against shekel is an exotic cross, tiny daily turnover, mostly handled by a few banks in Sydney, London and Tel Aviv. So one is an ocean, one is a rock pool.
Corn: Bring floaties for one.
Herman: Third lens is market depth and trading hours. Aussie against American trades basically twenty four hours a day, five days a week, from Sydney open Sunday evening Greenwich Mean Time through New York close Friday. Tightest when London and New York overlap, roughly twelve noon to four p m London time. Thinnest at rollover, around ten p m London time, and on holidays.
Corn: I know thin. I am slow after ten.
Herman: You are slow before ten too. But for Aussie against shekel, depth is patchy. Outside Israeli business hours, Sunday to Thursday plus Friday morning, and outside Sydney hours, there may be almost no direct market makers. So if Jim hits convert at midnight Jerusalem time on a Saturday, which is Shabbat, he is trading when Tel Aviv is closed and Sydney is asleep. The price will be stale and wide.
Corn: Saturday night slippage special.
Herman: Exactly. And fourth lens is price impact. You can watch this yourself. Put in a small test transfer quote for, say, one thousand Aussie dollars to shekels versus one thousand Aussie dollars to American dollars, then ask for a quote for fifty thousand. For Aussie to American, the rate per unit barely moves. For Aussie to shekel, the rate often gets worse as size goes up. That degradation is illiquidity.
Corn: So how should Jim use this for a house.
Herman: My take is do not convert Aussie straight to shekels in one heroic lifesaving leap. Stage it. Aussie to American is cheap and deep, American to shekel is much more liquid than Aussie to shekel because America to shekel is quoted by every bank that deals with Israel. Sometimes doing two liquid hops is cheaper than one exotic hop, even with two spreads, but he has to compare live quotes all in, including fees.
Corn: Two buses beat one camel.
Herman: That is weirdly accurate. And for timing large payments like a deposit, do it during overlap hours on a normal weekday, not Friday afternoon or holidays, and use limit orders or a foreign exchange broker that gives firm quotes, not a credit card style mystery rate. Corn, what is your pushback here.
Corn: You make liquid sound safe. It is cheap, not safe.
Herman: Fair, important distinction. Liquidity is about cost to trade, not about whether the price will hurt you. Aussie against American is super cheap to trade and can still fall ten percent in a risk panic and wreck a property budget. Cheap exit, fast car, still a cliff.
Corn: Fast cliff, cheap brakes.
Herman: Nice. So that is liquidity. Want to do volatility next.
Corn: Hit me with standard fear gauges.
Herman: Okay, Jim asked for standardized measures of volatility. He does not want vibes, he wants numbers he can compare. There are two families, backward looking and forward looking.
Corn: History versus fortune telling.
Herman: Yes. Backward looking starts with historical volatility, usually quoted as an annualized standard deviation of daily returns. So you take daily percentage changes for, say, the last twenty days or sixty days or one year, calculate the standard deviation, multiply by the square root of two hundred fifty two trading days to annualize it.
Corn: Math in a property chat.
Herman: It matters. For example, historically Aussie against American often runs something like eight to twelve percent annualized volatility in calm periods, spiking to fifteen to twenty percent or more in crises. I am not sure about the exact print today, Jim would need to pull it live, but that range is typical. Aussie against shekel will usually print higher because you are combining Aussie wobble plus shekel wobble.
Corn: Double wobble, double trouble.
Herman: The trader friendly version of the same idea is Average True Range, A T R. Wilder created it in the seventies. It tells you the average daily wiggle in price points over the last, usually, fourteen days. So if fourteen day A T R on Aussie against American is, say, zero point seven American cents, that means on a normal day it moves about two thirds of a cent. Jim can use that to set expectations. If his Jerusalem deposit is due in thirty days, multiply.
Corn: How nervous should I be today.
Herman: Exactly, in one number. Most charting sites, TradingView, Yahoo Finance, investing sites, will show historical volatility and A T R for Aussie against American for free. For Aussie against shekel you may have to calculate it yourself in a spreadsheet because free coverage is thin. That thinness itself is a signal.
Corn: No data is data.
Herman: Well said. Then forward looking volatility is implied volatility from options. When banks price currency options, they embed a guess about future wiggle. That guess is quoted as a percentage. One month implied vol, three month, one year. For Aussie against American, one month implied vol might be around eight to ten percent in calm times, higher before central bank meetings. For shekel crosses, implied vol is structurally higher and jumps hard on security news.
Corn: Paying extra for scary unknowns.
Herman: Yes. And there are standardized indices. For foreign exchange broadly there is the Deutsche Bank Currency Volatility Index, often called C V I X, which aggregates implied vol across major pairs. It is not pair specific, but if C V I X is high, all pairs including Jim's will be jumpier and spreads wider. For fear generally there is the V I X for American stocks, which correlates with Aussie weakness because Aussie is risk on.
Corn: When stocks sneeze, Aussie catches cold.
Herman: That is exactly the mechanism, we will get to that. Practically, what should Jim do. Pick one lookback, like sixty day historical vol, and one forward gauge, like three month implied vol if his broker shows it, and track them weekly in the same spreadsheet as the exchange rate. Do not mix ten different indicators. And normalize. A zero point eight cent daily move sounds small until you multiply by four hundred thousand Aussie dollars for a down payment.
Corn: Small percent, big apartment.
Herman: Right. Example. Say Jim is bringing three hundred thousand Aussie dollars. If Aussie against shekel moves two percent against him in a month, which is totally normal, that is six thousand Aussie dollars of purchasing power gone, or roughly twenty thousand shekels depending on the rate. That is not a rounding error, that is kitchen cabinets.
Corn: Ouch in any currency.
Herman: So for hedging, volatility tells you the price of insurance. A forward contract that locks a rate for three months will cost roughly the interest rate differential plus a spread, and options cost more when implied vol is high. If vol is high, locking in feels expensive because it is expensive. That is when staging purchases or using limit orders matters more.
Corn: Insurance costs most in a storm.
Herman: Seven words, very Corn. Okay, third question, support points. This is technical analysis language. Jim wants to identify support points in rate pairs.
Corn: Floors where falling prices bounce.
Herman: Yes, floors, but better to think of them as zones where buyers have shown up before, not magic lines. Support is a price area where demand previously overcame supply and the downtrend paused or reversed. Resistance is the ceiling opposite. For someone converting for a house, support and resistance help time tranches, not predict destiny.
Corn: Maps, not prophecies.
Herman: Exactly. So how do you find them without astrology. Method one, prior swing lows and highs on weekly and daily charts. Look back one to two years. Mark where Aussie against American bounced at least twice. Those old lows, like round numbers such as sixty American cents, sixty five, seventy, become psychological support because option barriers, bank orders, and human memory cluster there.
Corn: Everyone remembers round pain.
Herman: Method two, moving averages. The two hundred day moving average is watched by macro funds. If price is above it, dips to it often act as support. The fifty day is faster. When price slices clean through with high volume, that old support often flips to resistance.
Corn: Trapdoor becomes ceiling.
Herman: Method three, Fibonacci retracements, thirty eight point two percent, fifty percent, sixty one point eight percent of a prior big move. I am skeptical of the mysticism, I am not sure about this part, but I think they work partly because everyone draws the same lines and acts on them, self fulfilling.
Corn: Everyone brings same map.
Herman: Method four, for exotic crosses like Aussie against shekel, derive it. Since direct chart history can be gappy, triangulate. Aussie against shekel equals Aussie against American multiplied by American against shekel. So support in Aussie against shekel is usually just support in one of those two legs breaking. If American against shekel spikes because of risk news, Aussie against shekel can fall even if Aussie against American is flat.
Corn: Blame the middleman.
Herman: Always check the middleman. Practical routine for Jim. Open a weekly chart of Aussie against American. Draw horizontal lines at the last three major lows. Note the two hundred day average. Then open American against shekel weekly, same thing, prior highs are what matter because a higher American against shekel means a weaker shekel. Then do the math for his target. Say he needs, purely as an illustration, two shekels and twenty agorot per Aussie dollar to make his budget work. He can see how far price is from recent support and set alerts ten to twenty pips above.
Corn: Do not stare, set alarms.
Herman: Yes. And use orders. A limit order to convert a tranche if price rallies to resistance turned support, and a stop style alert if it breaks support, so he converts early before it slides further. But here is my strong opinion, and push me on this, Corn. For a homebuyer, fundamentals and cash flow timing beat chart magic. Support helps you avoid buying at the worst hour of the worst day, it does not tell you where the pair will be in six months.
Corn: Charts help shopping, not settling.
Herman: That is better than my paragraph. What do you think, is support useless for Jim.
Corn: Useful for slices, useless for loaf.
Herman: Explain.
Corn: If converting in chunks, levels help. If buying a home to live in, life decides.
Herman: I concede that, with one tweak. Life decides, but leverage punishes bad timing. If Jim is short Aussie and long a Jerusalem signing date, a break of support with two weeks to close can force him to bring extra tens of thousands. So charts plus a hedge plan matter more close to payment dates, less a year out.
Corn: Closer the signing, tighter the seatbelt.
Herman: Exactly. Common mistakes to avoid. Do not draw twenty lines, you will see what you want. Three clean zones max. Do not switch timeframes to confirm a bias. And do not treat a touch as a bounce until you get a daily close back above. Wicks lie.
Corn: Wicks lie. Noted.
Herman: Okay, fourth and biggest, what actually moves these pairs. Geopolitical and macroeconomic factors.
Corn: Why money dances.
Herman: Let us take Aussie against American first, then American against shekel, then combine for Aussie against shekel. Aussie is a classic pro cyclical commodity currency, risk on. When global growth is strong and investors feel brave, money flows into Australia for yield and iron ore and it rises. When fear hits, it falls fast.
Corn: Party currency, hangover included.
Herman: Perfect. Driver one is interest rate differentials, Reserve Bank of Australia versus the Federal Reserve. If the Fed is cutting while the R B A holds, American yields fall relative to Aussie yields, and Aussie against American tends to rise, all else equal. Jim should watch not just the cash rate decisions, eight times a year for the R B A, eight F O M C meetings, but the two year government bond spread. That spread moves daily and leads the currency.
Corn: Follow the yield breadcrumbs.
Herman: Driver two is China and commodities. Australia exports huge amounts of iron ore, L N G, coal to China. A specific person doing a specific thing, like a steel mill manager in Hebei cutting orders because property construction slowed, shows up weeks later as lower iron ore prices, say from one hundred twenty American dollars a tonne down to ninety, weaker Australian export revenues, and a softer Aussie. It is that direct.
Corn: Rocks move money.
Herman: Driver three is risk sentiment and the American dollar smile. In global panic, everyone buys American dollars for safety, so Aussie against American drops even if Australia did nothing wrong. In strong global boom, American dollar also can be soft because money leaves safety. Aussie shines in the middle, steady growth, high commodity prices.
Corn: Guilty by association.
Herman: Driver four is domestic Australian data, jobs, inflation, retail sales. A hot quarterly C P I print, say trimmed mean above three percent, makes R B A hawkish bets rise and lifts Aussie. A weak jobs report does the opposite.
Corn: Numbers with accents.
Herman: Now the shekel side. The shekel is a small, open, tech heavy currency with a strong central bank but outsized geopolitical beta. Driver one is Bank of Israel policy and inflation. The Bank of Israel targets one to three percent inflation. It intervened massively in foreign exchange historically to tame shekel strength to protect exporters, holding over two hundred billion American dollars in reserves at peaks. So unlike most majors, there is a big player who sometimes steps in.
Corn: A whale with a flag.
Herman: Great image. Driver two is the current account and tech flows. Israel exports software, chips, cybersecurity, plus natural gas from Leviathan and Tamar fields. When Nasdaq is strong and Israeli startups raise and repatriate dollars, that dollar selling supports the shekel. When tech funding freezes, that support fades. A specific scene, a Herzliya cybersecurity firm closing a fifty million American dollar funding round and converting payroll to shekels, is tiny alone but thousands of those move the market.
Corn: Startups pay rent in shekels.
Herman: Driver three, and this dominates for Jim, is security and political risk. War, escalation in Gaza or Lebanon or with Iran, judicial overhaul protests, coalition instability, these trigger shekel depreciation and higher implied vol, fast. After October seventh twenty twenty three, for example, the shekel fell sharply and the Bank of Israel announced a program to sell up to thirty billion American dollars to stabilize it. I am not sure about the intraday low to the pip, but the direction and intervention are well documented.
Corn: Fear prices instantly.
Herman: Yes. And it cuts both ways. Ceasefires, hostage deals, de escalation, or credible fiscal restraint can cause violent shekel rallies as hedges unwind. That whiplash is why Aussie against shekel volatility is higher than either leg alone. Driver four is American factors mirrored, because American against shekel is half the cross. Strong American jobs and sticky inflation mean higher for longer Fed, strong American dollar globally, which usually pushes American against shekel up, meaning shekel weaker, unless Israeli risk is calming at the same time.
Corn: Tug of war with two ropes.
Herman: Exactly. So combine for Aussie against shekel. Think of it as risk appetite times China times Israel risk. If China stimulates and iron ore rallies, Aussie leg helps Jim, he gets more shekels per Aussie. If regional tension spikes, shekel leg usually weakens, which ironically also gives him more shekels per Aussie because shekel is cheaper, but Israeli property sellers may raise shekel prices or demand dollar linkage to compensate for inflation and risk.
Corn: Currency win, house loss.
Herman: That is the crucial Jerusalem twist. Many Israeli sellers, especially in Jerusalem and Tel Aviv, think in shekels but watch the American dollar. Some contracts are shekel denominated with American dollar linkage clauses or just psychologically sticky to American dollar values. So Jim cannot just cheer a weak shekel. He has to ask his lawyer, is the price fixed in shekels, is there linkage, when is the final payment indexed to the consumer price index or construction index.
Corn: Read the contract, not just charts.
Herman: Yes. And macro affects mortgages too. If he borrows in Israel, Bank of Israel rates drive his monthly payment. If he keeps his loan in Australia against Aussie income, then exchange moves are his mortgage moves. A ten percent fall in Aussie against shekel is a ten percent hike in his effective house price.
Corn: Same house, new price.
Herman: So what is our position, what should Jim actually do. Here is my framework, tell me where I am wrong. One, decide the home timeline first. If buying within three to six months, prioritize certainty over cleverness. Get quotes from two foreign exchange specialists plus his bank, compare all in cost, and hedge fifty to seventy percent of the needed shekels with forwards once the price and date are fairly firm.
Corn: Certainty beats clever.
Herman: Two, tranche the rest. Split the remaining exposure into, say, three equal parts, convert one at spot now, place limit orders for the other two near recent resistance zones we talked about, with expiry before the closing date. That way support levels become action, not decoration.
Corn: Automate patience.
Herman: Three, keep an emergency buffer of five to ten percent in low risk cash because volatility math says a two standard deviation move before closing is possible. Four, do not speculate to fund the deposit. No leverage, no exotic options unless an adviser structures it. The goal is a home in Jerusalem, not a trading story.
Corn: Homes first, trades never.
Herman: I mostly agree with myself there. My disagreement with the pure chart crowd is they would tell Jim to wait for perfect support. I would tell him if the property is right and the monthly payment works at current rates plus a stress test of Aussie ten percent weaker, proceed and manage the noise. Currency timing should not veto a life move, but it should shape staging.
Corn: Do not let pips pick your street.
Herman: Lovely. And my disagreement with pure fundamentalists who say purchasing power parity will save you. P P P says exchange rates should equalize price levels over years, Big Mac style. True over a decade, useless for a March closing. Interest parity same, great textbook, thin comfort when rockets reshape risk premia overnight.
Corn: Textbooks do not close escrow.
Herman: Exactly. Quick recap for Jim in plain language, no new theory. Liquidity, check spreads, turnover from B I S, hours, and size impact. Aussie American is deep and cheap, Aussie shekel is thin and pricey, consider two hops during liquid hours. Volatility, track sixty day history and A T R plus implied vol and the currency vol index for regime. Translate percent into shekels for his deposit size. Support, use weekly swing lows, two hundred day average, a couple Fibonacci zones, derive Aussie shekel from its two legs, use limits and alerts. Drivers, for Aussie American watch Fed versus R B A, two year spread, China steel demand, iron ore, risk mood. For shekel watch Bank of Israel, tech flows, Nasdaq, and above all security and political risk plus whether his contract has dollar linkage.
Corn: That was the whole toolkit in one breath.
Herman: I got excited. One last Jerusalem specific tip. Because Israel's workweek is Sunday to Thursday, and Australia is Monday to Friday, the only clean overlap for bank wires and forward settlements is Monday to Thursday Jerusalem time. A Friday deposit deadline in Jerusalem means the Aussie side must move by Thursday. Plan two business days early, get written confirmation of value date, and confirm who bears rate movement between signing and final registration, the tabo process.
Corn: Thursday is the real Friday.
Herman: Yes. Jim, good luck. Buying in Jerusalem as an Aussie is brave and wonderful. Lock the parts you can, respect the parts you cannot, and keep some powder dry for that whiplash where good news for peace is suddenly bad news for your exchange rate because the shekel surges.
Corn: Peace rally, budget pain.
Herman: That reversal is exactly the kind of callback I wanted. Early we said a weak shekel helps the buyer, late we learn a strong shekel on peace can hurt the buyer but help the new neighbor. Currency irony in one city.
Corn: Still cheaper than regret.
Herman: Well put. Shall we sign off.
Corn: Jim, send photos. Preferably not of spreadsheets.
Herman: Send spreadsheets too, I love them. Thanks for writing in, and thanks everyone for listening to My Weird Prompts. We will be back next week with another prompt from Daniel or a listener.
Corn: Bring money questions. We bring opinions.

Corn: Jim in Jerusalem wants to buy property, and the two numbers haunting him are the Australian dollar against the shekel and the Australian dollar against the US dollar. So he wants a method, not a tip.

Herman: Liquidity, a standard way to measure volatility, how you even find a support point, and the macro and geopolitical stuff that actually moves a pair. That is a proper brief. I like Jim already.

Corn: An Australian expat pricing a flat in shekels while his savings still think in dollars. The currency is the house he has not bought yet.

Herman: And those two pairs are not the same animal. Aussie-dollar against the US dollar is one of the deep pools in global foreign exchange. Aussie against the shekel is a cross most dealers will price, and few will love.

Corn: Love is not a liquidity metric.

Herman: Spreads are. Volume is. Whether you can get out at three in the morning without donating a month of rent to the bid-ask. We should start there, because everything else Jim wants, vol, support, a story about China or the Bank of Israel, sits on top of whether the market is actually there.

Corn: Walk me through how you would score a pair before you care what the chart says.

Herman: Four things, and I would make him write them down. First, the quoted spread, in the size he actually needs, at the hour he will trade. A tenth of a pip on a million US dollars of Aussie-dollar during London-New York overlap is a different market from twenty or thirty pips on an Aussie-shekel clip when Sydney is asleep and Tel Aviv has gone home. I am not quoting him a live spread. I do not have his broker's book. The point is he measures his, not a textbook's.

Corn: Second?

Herman: Turnover. The Bank for International Settlements does a triennial survey of global foreign-exchange turnover. Last full one I trust as a benchmark, twenty twenty-two, put daily turnover around seven and a half trillion US dollars. The US dollar was on one side of the vast majority of that. The Australian dollar's share of global turnover was on the order of six percent. It is a major. The shekel's share is a rounding error next to that. I would not swear to the second decimal on the shekel without the table in front of me. Order of magnitude is enough. Aussie-dollar is a highway. Aussie-shekel is a lane that sometimes has a goat in it.

Corn: You would know the goat.

Herman: Third is depth, not just the top of book. Can he lift five hundred thousand Australian dollars of shekels without the price walking away from him? Retail platforms hide that. A bank or a prime broker will show it if he asks, in the size that matches a deposit, not a holiday. Fourth is the clock. Sydney, Tokyo, London, New York. Aussie-dollar is alive whenever any of those are open, and especially when London and New York overlap. The shekel's natural hours are the Israeli business day, with a nod to London. Outside that, the cross is often just two legs glued together, Aussie-dollar and dollar-shekel, and he pays both spreads plus whatever the dealer adds for the bother.

Corn: So overall liquidity is not a vibe. It is spread, size, time, and whether anyone else is bored enough to take the other side.

Herman: And a fifth thing people forget. Can he hedge it later? Forwards, options, a rolling hedge if the purchase is months away. Aussie-dollar forwards are a commodity. The points are tight, the dates are standard, one week, one month, three months, a year. Aussie-shekel forwards exist in the interbank market because you can synthesize them from the two dollar legs, covered-interest style, but the all-in price he sees at a retail broker may be ugly. If the hedge costs him more than the move he is afraid of, the hedge is theatre.

Corn: Theatre with a worse ticket price.

Herman: I would have him pull, for one normal week, the spread on both pairs at three times of day. Sydney morning, London open, and the dead zone, say late New York. Same notional. Write the numbers. That single exercise tells him more about liquidity than any article titled is the Aussie cheap.

Corn: What about standardized volatility. He asked for measures, not a feeling that it has been jumpy.

Herman: The workhorse is historical, or realized, volatility. Take daily log returns. That is the natural log of today's rate over yesterday's. Standard deviation of those returns. Then annualize. For daily data, multiply by the square root of about two hundred and fifty-two, the trading-day convention. Some people use three hundred and sixty-five. He should pick one and not mix them when he compares pairs. A one-month window and a three-month window, side by side. One-month tells him the weather. Three-month tells him the climate.

Corn: Log returns so a move up and the same move down do not lie about the size.

Herman: Exactly. And he should do it on the pair he will actually hold. Aussie-shekel volatility is not Aussie-dollar volatility plus shekel-dollar volatility. The cross variance is variance of Aussie-dollar, plus variance of dollar-shekel, minus twice the covariance. If the two dollar legs move together, some of the noise cancels. If they move apart, the cross is louder than either leg. I have seen people budget for the liquid pair and then get surprised by the cross. The covariance term is the whole plot twist.

Corn: Plot twist. Finance's favorite genre.

Herman: Implied volatility is the other standard, and it is better when he can get it, because it is the market's price of future movement, not a rear-view mirror. Aussie-dollar options are listed and heavily traded over the counter. One-month and three-month at-the-money implied vol are quoted in vol points, annualized, same units as the historical number, so he can compare them. If implied sits well above realized, the market is paying up for something it thinks is coming. Risk reversals, the price of a call versus a put at the same delta, tell him the skew. Aussie risk reversals often price more fear of a fall than of a rally, because the Aussie is a risk-on currency. When equities sneeze, Aussie-dollar often catches it.

Corn: And the shekel pair?

Herman: I am less sure he will find a clean, public implied-vol surface on Aussie-shekel at a retail login. Dollar-shekel options exist, the Bank of Israel world is not a desert, but the cross option may be a dealer construct. If he cannot see implied vol, he should not invent it. Stick to realized vol on the cross, and implied on the two liquid legs, and remember he is not holding the legs. He is holding the difference.

Corn: Other names he will trip over. Average true range. Bollinger bands. The alphabet of people who want a number by Friday.

Herman: Average true range is fine as a range tool, in pips or in shekels per Aussie dollar, not as a volatility percentage. Bollinger bandwidth is a scaled standard deviation. None of those are more standardized than annualized standard deviation of log returns. If he wants one sentence for a spreadsheet, that is the sentence. Window, annualization factor, and whether he is using close-to-close or something fancier like Parkinson, which uses high and low. Close-to-close is enough unless he is writing a paper. I am not sure the high-low estimators earn their keep for a man buying an apartment.

Corn: Herman Poppleberry declines to overfit a flat.

Herman: Proudly. One caution. Shekel prints can gap over the weekend or around a holiday when Israel is shut and Australia is not, or the reverse. A realized-vol number that assumes continuous hours will understate the jump risk. He should look at the worst five daily moves in the last two years, not just the standard deviation. Standard deviation is an average of surprises. The deposit is exposed to one surprise.

Corn: Support points. This is where people start drawing lines and calling them physics.

Herman: And I will fight him a little, if he is listening. A support point is not a law. It is a place where, last time, more buyers showed up than sellers, or where a story made people think they should. Jim asked how to identify them. There is a technical way and a fundamental way, and I trust the second more, with the first as a map of where other people might cluster.

Corn: Give him the map anyway. He asked.

Herman: Technically. Prior swing lows on a weekly chart, not a five-minute chart. He is buying property, not a scalp. Round numbers, because humans herd. For Aussie-dollar, levels like sixty-five US cents, sixty, fifty-five, have been arguments in public for years. I am not saying any of those is support today. I am saying if the rate is near a round number that has turned price before, the order book gets crowded, and crowded books can hold or can break louder. The two-hundred-day moving average is another crowd magnet. Fibonacci retracements are popular and, in my view, mostly a shared superstition. They work when enough people use them, which is a sociological fact, not a geometric one.

Corn: A superstition with a fan club.

Herman: Precisely. So if he marks them, he marks them as where stops might sit, not as where value lives. The fundamental supports are more interesting, and harder. Purchasing-power parity gives a very slow notion of fair value. The OECD and others publish PPP-implied exchange rates. They are lousy trading signals over a year and less lousy over a decade. Interest-rate differentials matter faster. If Australian yields sit well above US yields, global money has a reason to hold Aussie and fund in dollars, which leans on the spot rate upward, all else equal. All else is never equal. That is the carry trade, and it unwinds in a heap when volatility spikes, because the carry is a few percent and the spot move can be ten in a bad month.

Corn: So the support from higher Aussie rates is a trapdoor with a rug on it.

Herman: I would not put the deposit on that rug alone. For the shekel, the nearest thing to an official floor has, at times, been the Bank of Israel. They have intervened, bought dollars, leaned against shekel strength when exporters were screaming, and they have also let the currency take the strain when inflation or a shock argued for it. I do not have their current intervention playbook memorized to the last statement. The method for Jim is to read the last few Bank of Israel minutes and any stated discomfort with the level, not to assume a line in the sand that will be defended with infinite reserves. Central banks run out of political appetite before they run out of shekels they can print. They do not run out of dollars they might need to sell.

Corn: That is the useful distinction. They can always make more of their own. The other currency is the scarce one.

Herman: Yes. So a support point that depends on them selling dollars has a finite back. A support point that depends on them buying dollars, weakening the shekel, is easier for them to sustain. Jim should know which way his fear points. If he needs shekels and he is afraid the Aussie falls against the shekel, he is afraid of shekel strength or Aussie weakness or both. Bank of Israel buying dollars would be working with him, in that scenario. A shock that makes people dump shekels would be working against a shekel-holder, which is the other side of his trade if he has already converted.

Corn: Let us do the forces properly, pair by pair. Aussie against the US dollar first. What actually drives it, if we refuse to say sentiment and wave our hands.

Herman: Commodity prices, and not in a vague way. Iron ore, coal, liquefied natural gas. Australia's terms of trade swing with what China and the rest of Asia pay for those. Iron ore is the loud one. When the ore price falls hard, the Aussie has a habit of following, with a lag and with noise, because the currency is how the world prices Australia's external income. I would not claim a stable beta. I would say if Jim sees iron ore down twenty percent and the Aussie unmoved, he should be suspicious of the unmoved part, not comforted.

Corn: China is the customer. Not a metaphor.

Herman: The customer, the construction cycle, and the policy mood in Beijing. A weak Chinese property sector is not a sidebar for this pair. It is upstream of the ore price. Aussie employment and the Reserve Bank of Australia's cash rate are the domestic half. The RBA is an inflation-targeting central bank with a housing market that amplifies rate moves, because so much Australian mortgage debt is exposed when rates rise. So a hot CPI print in Australia can lift the currency on the expectation of higher rates, and then hurt it later if those rates crack the consumer. Two-step. People trade the first step and forget the second.

Corn: And the dollar side of Aussie-dollar is not a backdrop. It is half the pair.

Herman: More than half, in a crisis. The dollar is the funding currency and the safe asset. Federal Reserve policy, US real yields, and whether the world wants Treasuries this month. When US real yields jump, almost every currency looks worse, and high-beta ones look worse faster. The Aussie is high beta to global risk. Equity selloffs, widening credit spreads, a lurch in volatility indexes, and Aussie-dollar tends to drop even if nothing Australian happened that morning. Jim can watch the US two-year yield and a simple risk proxy, say global equities, and he will explain a surprising amount of the weekly noise. Not all of it. I am not selling him a model.

Corn: Geopolitics for this pair is mostly indirect. Wars show up as oil, as risk-off, as a stronger dollar, and sometimes as a bid for Australian commodities if supply elsewhere is hit. It is not usually a headline about Canberra.

Herman: Mostly. A direct shock would be something like a serious rupture in Australia-China trade, tariffs, bans on specific exports, which we have watched in smaller form. That hits the terms of trade channel on purpose. For day-to-day, I would rank the drivers, if he forces me, as US rates and risk appetite, then commodities and China, then the RBA, then everything else. Rankings move. In a pure RBA surprise week, the third item becomes the first. The method is to know which channel is live, not to laminate the ranking.

Corn: Now the shekel. This one has a headline problem. Jim lives in the headline.

Herman: Then we talk about it straight. The Israeli shekel is a developed-market currency attached to a high-income, tech-heavy export economy, and also attached to a country that fights wars and absorbs security shocks. Both facts are in the price, in different proportions depending on the month. The tech and services surplus, foreign investment into Israeli companies, gas exports from fields like Leviathan, those are shekel-positive flows when the world feels calm enough to send money. A major security escalation is shekel-negative, fast, because residents and foreigners buy dollars, equity holders hedge, and tourism and some investment pause. The Bank of Israel has, in past shocks, sold dollars from reserves to lean against a collapsing shekel. Reserves are large relative to a lot of emerging markets. Israel is not an emerging market in the currency-handbook sense. The limit is still real. Reserves are for smoothing, not for repealing a sustained outflow.

Corn: So the geopolitical premium is not a constant tax. It widens in bursts, and sometimes the central bank spends dollars to narrow the burst.

Herman: Yes. And Jim should separate the level from the jump. The level of dollar-shekel already contains some average expectation of risk. What hurts a buyer of property is the jump he did not budget, the week the shekel moves several percent and his Aussie savings suddenly cover a smaller fraction of the asking price, or a larger one, depending on direction. Direction matters more than drama. If he earns or holds Australian dollars and must pay shekels, shekel strength is the pain. A geopolitical shock that weakens the shekel, grim as that is for other reasons, can make his currency go further. I am not going to dress that up. It is an ugly arithmetic, and pretending the currency does not have a war premium would be worse advice than naming it.

Corn: Frank is the point. He asked what influences the pair. Not what would be nice.

Herman: Macro besides the security channel. Israeli inflation versus the Bank of Israel's rate. The shekel was, for long stretches in the twenty-tens, almost annoyingly strong, because of tech inflows and a current-account surplus, and the central bank spent years complaining and buying dollars. That history matters. People who only look at the last bad headline miss that the structural flow, exports, investment income, gas, has often been shekel-supportive. A man planning a purchase over a year should not model the shekel as a one-way geopolitical short. He should model two regimes. Calm regime, surplus and tech can grind it stronger. Shock regime, it gaps weaker and policy may lean back. His liquidity plan has to survive both, because he does not get to pick the regime on closing day.

Corn: Aussie against shekel is those two stories divided by each other. Or multiplied, depending how you write the quote.

Herman: Cross rate. If he sees Aussie-dollar and dollar-shekel, Aussie-shekel is the product, careful with which way each is quoted. A stronger Aussie against the greenback and a weaker shekel against the greenback both help him if he is converting Aussie into shekels. They can happen together in a global risk-on wave, or they can diverge. China stimulus plus a quiet Levant is his friendly combination. A China slump plus a shekel squeeze from inflows is the unfriendly one, even if the news in Jerusalem feels locally fine. That is the cruelty of a cross. His apartment can get more expensive in Aussie dollars because of iron ore in Western Australia, with no Israeli data print that day at all.

Corn: The ore does not know about his mortgage.

Herman: It will meet his mortgage anyway. So the factors I would actually track, a short list, not a Bloomberg farm. For the Aussie leg, iron ore, the RBA cash rate against the Fed funds rate, and a risk thermometer he already understands, equities or credit. For the shekel leg, Bank of Israel rate against the Fed, the dollar-shekel itself so he is not only watching the cross, and a plain reading of whether the country is in a shock week or a normal week. He does not need twenty indicators. He needs to know which two moved when his cross moved, so he does not learn the wrong lesson.

Corn: Support, then, on the cross, is even softer than on Aussie-dollar. Fewer tourists drawing the same line.

Herman: Thinner market, fewer shared superstitions, which is almost a virtue. The technical levels that matter are the ones on the liquid legs, translated. If Aussie-dollar is sitting on a widely watched low, and dollar-shekel is mid-range, the cross can still bounce because of the Aussie leg alone. Hunting for a mystical Aussie-shekel support that the interbank desk has never heard of is how people talk themselves into waiting for a number that is not a number. I would rather he define support in cash terms. What Aussie-shekel rate makes this specific apartment fit his savings, after tax, after transfer costs, after a buffer. That is a personal support. The market does not owe it to him. But it is the only level that changes his life, so it belongs on the page next to the moving average.

Corn: A budget is a support level with worse marketing.

Herman: And a stop-loss he can actually honor, because it is a decision to delay the purchase, not a hope that a Fibonacci level respects his deposit. If I push back on anything in his question, it is the word identify, as if support were underground and waiting to be found. You construct a level from history, from policy, or from your own constraint. You do not discover it like a well.

Corn: I think the TA crowd would say you are no fun.

Herman: I am fun at dinners. I am stingy with other people's apartment money. There is a version of this where he dollar-cost averages the conversion over six months, which turns the support argument into a calendar. That reduces the chance he converts the lot the week before a gap. It also means he might miss a better rate, and he pays the spread six times. On Aussie-dollar, six spreads are cheap. On the cross, he should add them up before he calls averaging virtuous. Virtue that costs four hundred basis points is just a fee with a slogan.

Corn: Four hundred. You made that up as an illustration.

Herman: Illustration. If his live spread is two percent round trip and he crosses six times, he should do the arithmetic on his ticket, not on my imaginary one. I do not know his broker. Jerusalem banks, Australian banks, a specialist FX shop, the spread difference on an exotic cross can dwarf a month of realized volatility. Liquidity assessment, which we started with, is not a preface. It is the cost of every clever plan.

Corn: What would you refuse to tell him, even if he asked for a forecast.

Herman: A target. Aussie at some number of US cents by June, shekel at some number, therefore wait. I can describe the channels. I cannot see the next iron ore print, the next Federal Reserve meeting's surprise, or whether a security situation deteriorates. Anyone selling him that as a service is selling confidence, which is not in the BIS survey. What I would tell him is the sensitivity. Roughly, if he must pay a fixed shekel price, every one percent move in Aussie-shekel changes his Aussie cost by one percent. On a two million shekel purchase, he can compute the shekel amount, convert at today's rate once, and then know what a five percent adverse move costs him in Australian dollars. If that number ruins the deal, he is not investing. He is hoping. Hoping is allowed. It should be labeled.

Corn: Label the hope. That could be on the door of the flat.

Herman: And hedges, if the date is known. A forward locks the cross for a known settlement. He gives up the upside if the Aussie rallies against the shekel, and he gains certainty. On a thin cross, get the forward points in writing, all-in rate, not a spot plus a story. Compare that all-in rate to just converting now and holding shekels in a shekel deposit until completion. The deposit earns the Israeli rate, minus whatever a non-resident can actually get, which may not be the headline Bank of Israel rate. I am not sure of the best retail shekel deposit a foreign buyer can open this year. He should ask the bank, not a podcast. The comparison is the method. Locked forward versus convert early versus stay unhedged and accept the variance we already defined.

Corn: Options, if he wants insurance rather than a lock.

Herman: A shekel call against the Aussie, or however the dealer structures the right to buy shekels, costs premium, which is the implied vol times a bunch of other things, and on a thin pair the premium will not be the pretty textbook price. If the quoted vol is silly, the option is a bad insurance policy. He can sometimes do better hedging the liquid risk, Aussie-dollar, and leaving dollar-shekel unhedged, if he decides the shekel leg is the one he is willing to wear. That is a real choice, not a cop-out. Split the risk into the part the market prices fairly and the part it prices like a favor.

Corn: I want to push on one claim. You ranked US rates and risk above commodities for Aussie-dollar, most of the time. A commodity currency man in Western Australia would throw a rock at you. A slow rock. He is busy.

Herman: He can throw it. Over a decade, terms of trade and the commodity complex explain a lot of where the Aussie sits. Over a month, a Fed shock or a risk shock often dominates the ore price. Jim's horizon, if he is considering a purchase, is months, not a mining cycle. So I weight the fast variables more for his decision, and I still want ore on the dashboard so a slow grind does not sneak up while he stares at the two-year yield. If your horizon is ten years and you are not levered to a closing date, I will swap the ranking. We do not have to agree for every horizon. I think that is the honest split.

Corn: I will take the split. Closing dates make cowards of long-term models, and they should.

Herman: One more macro item people skip because it is boring. Inflation differentials and the real exchange rate. If Australian inflation runs hotter than Israeli inflation for a long stretch, the Aussie's purchasing power erodes relative to the shekel even if the nominal rate looks stable. PPP is that idea in slow motion. For a property, which is a real asset in Israel, local inflation and local real-estate inflation are the other price. Currency is not the only way the flat gets away from him. Shekel rents and shekel sale prices can rise while the exchange rate goes his way, and he still loses the race. He asked about currency pairs. I am adding the thing the currency is being asked to buy.

Corn: A pair does not include the asking price. Rude of the asking price to exist.

Herman: Deeply rude. So his full sensitivity is exchange rate times the shekel price of the asset. Either can move. Monitoring only the FX page is how financially literate people still overpay.

Corn: Geopolitics beyond Israel and China. Anything else with a real channel, or are we collecting headlines for sport.

Herman: Channels only. Energy prices, because Australia exports them and Israel has become more of a gas player, so an oil shock is not symmetric across his two currencies. A stronger global dollar from a US fiscal or political mess hits both legs and the net on the cross is ambiguous. He should not assume a strong dollar hurts him. It depends which of his currencies the dollar is beating up more. European growth matters at the margin for risk sentiment, not as a direct flow into this cross. Australian domestic politics matter when they threaten the commodity export regime or the fiscal path the RBA is staring at. Israeli domestic politics matter when they change the risk premium or the central bank's room. I would ignore any factor he cannot connect to a flow, a rate, or a risk premium in one sentence. If the sentence needs a conspiracy, it is not a factor. It is a hobby.

Corn: One sentence. Iron ore down, Australia's external income down, Aussie offered. Security shock, dollar demand up, shekel offered. Rate gap widens in Australia's favor, carry bids Aussie until volatility makes carry look stupid.

Herman: That is the whole syllabus. He can tape it inside a cupboard. The cupboard will outperform a lot of newsletters.

Corn: Where I still disagree, mildly, is implied volatility as something he must have. For a single property conversion, realized vol plus the worst weeks is enough to size a buffer. Paying for an options sheet he cannot trade well is cosplay.

Herman: Mildly accepted. If he is not going to buy the option, the implied number is a weather report from a city he is not visiting. Nice context, not a tool. I overweighted it because I like the comparison, implied versus realized, as a way to see when the market is nervous. For Jim's decision, a cash buffer equal to, say, one standard deviation of three-month moves, translated into Australian dollars on his purchase size, is the practical output. The exact multiple is his stomach, not a regulation. I would not pretend one standard deviation is safe. Gaps laugh at standard deviations. Two, if the deal dies at one, and he knows it.

Corn: Stomach is not standardized. He asked for standardized measures. We gave him the formula and then handed the last step back.

Herman: The last step is preference. The measures can be standard. The support he acts on includes his own constraint, which is not a market statistic. I would rather be clear about that seam than pretend a Gaussian distribution approves his mortgage.

Corn: What should he do this week, concretely, without us picking his rate.

Herman: Open both pairs at his actual venue. Record spread and the size the spread holds for. Compute three-month realized vol on Aussie-dollar, on dollar-shekel, and on the cross, so he sees the covariance instead of imagining it. Mark round numbers and the two-hundred-day on the liquid legs only. Read the latest RBA statement, the latest Fed decision, the latest Bank of Israel decision, one each, not the archives. Note iron ore's direction over the past quarter, direction, not a false precision. Write the shekel price of the place he wants, convert at spot, and write what a five percent and a ten percent adverse cross move does to the Aussie cost. Then decide whether to convert on a schedule, lock a forward if the all-in rate is sane, or wait, with the waiting labeled as a position, because waiting unhedged is a bet. It is just a bet people do not admit they placed.

Corn: Waiting is a position. That one I would carve in the lintel.

Herman: And he should not convert in the dead hour because he got anxious at midnight. Liquidity was item one for a reason. Anxiety is most expensive when the book is thin. A sloth would understand this. We do not sprint to the only open shop.

Corn: We also do not hang from the branch until the perfect rate grows on it. The branch gets uncomfortable. I am told.

Herman: Donkeys prefer a known load to a mysterious one. Lock it or budget it. Do not romance it. Jim, if the romance is the apartment, spend the romance there. The currency is the boring pipe that fills the bath. You measure the pipe. You do not marry it.

Corn: Herman Poppleberry, against romance, in a city famous for it. Bold, for a donkey.

Herman: Jerusalem can keep the poems. The spread does not rhyme. I think we gave him the assessment method he asked for. Liquidity by spread, size, and hour. Volatility as annualized standard deviation of log returns, implied only where the market is real. Support as clustered history, policy capacity, and his own budget, with the superstitions labeled as superstitions. Drivers named as commodities and China, rate gaps, risk appetite, and a security premium that arrives in jumps and is sometimes met with reserves. I do not know where those pairs will be when he signs. I know how I would refuse to be surprised by the shape of the surprise.

Corn: That is as close to a forecast as he is getting, and it is the better product. Jim, good luck with the flat. Measure the pipe. Daniel, thanks for the note. We will be here next time, still not a bank, still happy to argue about covariance.

Herman: Still happy. Bring a thinner pair if you have one. I have spreads to complain about.

Corn: If you are an Australian living in Jerusalem and looking at buying property, your first instinct is probably to look at the view, and your second instinct is probably to look at a chart and weep quietly into a bowl of hummus.

Herman: It is a special kind of financial headache. Welcome back to My Weird Prompts. I am Herman Poppleberry.

Corn: And I am Corn. Today we have a voice note sent in by Jim. Jim is an Aussie expat based in Jerusalem. He has his eye on the real estate market there, which is notoriously expensive, and he wants to understand the mechanics of the currencies he is juggling.

Herman: Specifically, Jim wants to get under the hood of the Australian dollar against the Israeli new shekel, which traders write as AUD/ILS, alongside the Australian dollar against the US dollar, AUD/USD. And he does not just want a vague forecast. He asked for four very specific, practical things.

Corn: He wants to know how to assess the overall liquidity of currency pairs. He wants standardized measures of volatility. He wants to know how people identify support points on a price chart without resorting to astrology. And finally, he wants the primary geopolitical and macroeconomic engines driving these pairs.

Herman: Which is music to my ears, Corn, because foreign exchange is one of those arenas where retail buyers usually get taken to the cleaners simply because they do not realize the market they are stepping into is not a unified exchange like a stock market.

Corn: It is not a supermarket. There is no aisle where you pick up a shekel for twenty-four Australian cents and take it to a cashier.
