Herman: Exactly. So let us start where Jim started, with liquidity. Jim wants to know how to assess the overall liquidity of a pair. Corn, when someone asks how liquid a currency pair is, what are they actually trying to avoid?

Corn: Slippage, mostly. And the indignity of paying someone four percent just to move their own money across a border.

Herman: Right. Liquidity is the ability to trade an asset rapidly, in volume, without moving the market price, and with minimal transaction friction. Now, foreign exchange is the largest financial market on the planet. The Bank for International Settlements does a triennial central bank survey. The most recent one, from late twenty-twenty-two, clocked average daily turnover at around seven and a half trillion US dollars per day.

Corn: Seven point five trillion. Every twenty-four hours.

Herman: Every day. But here is the catch for Jim. That volume is concentrated in a tiny handful of pairs. The US dollar is on one side of almost eighty-eight percent of all trades. The Australian dollar is a major player. It is in about six point four percent of trades globally. AUD/USD is one of the ten most traded pairs in the world. It trades hundreds of billions of dollars every single day.

Corn: Which means if Jim wants to buy ten million US dollars with Aussie dollars, the market will barely notice he walked through the door.

Herman: He will get an institutional spread that is literally a fraction of a basis point. A pip or less. On retail brokerages, maybe half a pip to one pip. That is the gold standard of liquidity. Continuous two-way pricing twenty-four hours a day, five days a week, with thick order books in Sydney, Tokyo, London, and New York.

Corn: Now contrast that with AUD/ILS.

Herman: Night and day. The Israeli shekel accounts for something like zero point four percent of global foreign exchange turnover. And almost all of that turnover is executed against the US dollar, USD/ILS, or against the euro, EUR/ILS. There is effectively no deep, native interbank market where someone sits with an order book matching Australian dollars directly for Israeli shekels.

Corn: It is a synthetic cross.

Herman: Completely synthetic. If Jim calls an Israeli bank or an international transfer broker and says, convert half a million Australian dollars to shekels so I can put a deposit on an apartment in Rehavia, what the machine actually does behind the curtain is sell his Australian dollars for US dollars, and then immediately use those US dollars to buy Israeli shekels.

Corn: Two trades disguised as one. Which means two spreads.

Herman: Two bid-ask spreads, two sets of execution risk, and two market regimes. How does Jim actually assess this liquidity quantitatively? There are three standard proxies you can look at. The first and most accessible is the bid-ask spread relative to the mid-price. On AUD/USD, that spread might be zero point zero zero zero one, which is one hundredth of one percent. On AUD/ILS, if you look at a retail bank quote, that spread can easily be one and a half to three percent.

Corn: Three percent on a Jerusalem property deposit is a luxury car left on the table.

Herman: It is staggering. The second proxy Jim should look at is market depth, or order book volume, though that is harder for retail participants to see directly because forex is over the counter. But you can look at futures data on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange. Australian dollar futures have enormous open interest and deep order books. Shekel futures barely exist with any retail volume; institutional players use non-deliverable forwards or local Tel Aviv interbank forwards.

Corn: And the third proxy is trading hours overlap.

Herman: Yes. Temporal liquidity. Jerusalem is seven or eight hours behind Sydney, depending on daylight saving time. When Australian liquidity is at its peak during the Sydney and Asian session, Tel Aviv is asleep. When Tel Aviv is open and trading shekels against the dollar, the Australian banks have gone home for the night and their local interbank market is shut. Furthermore, the Israeli work week traditionally runs Sunday through Thursday, whereas global forex runs Monday through Friday.

Corn: So on Sunday in Jerusalem, local banks are trading shekels, but the global Australian dollar market is essentially dark until Wellington and Sydney open late in the day.

Herman: Precisely. If Jim tries to execute a conversion on a Sunday morning in Jerusalem, whatever provider he uses is going to slap an extra safety buffer onto the spread because they cannot hedge their Australian dollar leg in the primary wholesale market. They widen the spread to protect themselves against gap risk on the Monday morning open.

Corn: Lesson one for Jim: never convert money on a Sunday, even if the bank manager is smiling and handing you tea.

Herman: Absolutely. If you must execute AUD/ILS, you want to do it in the sweet spot of the day where London is open and overlapping with the Middle Eastern trading afternoon, because that is when European and American desks are quoting tight liquidity in both legs.

Corn: Let us move to Jim's second question: standardized measures of volatility. Because if you are timing a transfer, volatility is either your best friend or the reason you have to move into a smaller flat.

Herman: Volatility in foreign exchange is fascinating because it is divided cleanly into two camps: realized volatility and implied volatility. Jim asked for standardized measures, so let us break down what professionals actually track.

Corn: Start with realized volatility, because that is what actually happened in the real world.

Herman: Right. Realized, or historical, volatility is just the annualized standard deviation of daily log returns over a specific rolling window. Typically people look at twenty days, sixty days, or two hundred and fifty-two days, which is the trading year. If someone says AUD/USD has a thirty-day realized volatility of ten percent, that means if you project that daily variance across an entire year, you can expect the currency to trade within a plus or minus ten percent range roughly sixty-eight percent of the time, assuming a normal distribution.

Corn: Which it never is. Fat tails. Black swans. Central bankers making speeches on Wednesday afternoons.

Herman: Very fat tails. But it gives you a baseline yardstick. Another great, standardized measure of realized movement that retail traders use is ATR: the Average True Range, developed by J. Welles Wilder. Instead of standard deviations, ATR simply calculates the average daily range between the high and the low, accounting for any gaps between closes and opens, over fourteen days.

Corn: It gives it to you in pips. Cash in hand.

Herman: Yes. For example, right now AUD/USD might have a fourteen-day ATR of around fifty to sixty pips a day. So on an ordinary Tuesday, you should not be surprised if it swings half a cent up or down. If Jim wants to look at AUD/ILS, calculating an ATR or rolling historical volatility will immediately show him that the pair has dramatically larger daily swings in percentage terms than AUD/USD, especially during geopolitical shocks.

Corn: But realized volatility is looking in the rear-view mirror. What is the market pricing in for tomorrow?

Herman: That is implied volatility. And that is the standardized metric institutional investors live by. If you want to know what the smartest money thinks about the next month, you do not look at last month's chart; you look at the price of options. Specifically, the at-the-money forward implied volatility for one-month or three-month expiries.

Corn: Where does Jim find that without an institutional terminal that costs more than his rent?

Herman: There are public proxies. The Chicago Board Options Exchange actually tracks currency volatility indexes. There is the EUVIX for the euro, and there are standard implied volatility trackers for the Aussie dollar. For the shekel, it is trickier without a Bloomberg or Refinitiv terminal, but you can see implied volatility quoted in financial press reports from the Bank of Israel or major local brokerages.

Corn: What does implied volatility tell him that realized volatility misses?

Herman: It tells him the market's expectation of turbulence. But even better, in the options market, there is a metric called the risk reversal. I love risk reversals, Corn. They are the cleanest measure of directional bias you can find.

Corn: Explain the risk reversal without making everyone who is listening drive into a tree.

Herman: I will make it simple. An options dealer sells call options, which are bets the currency will rise, and put options, which are bets it will fall. In a perfectly balanced world where everyone thought the risks were equal on both sides, a twenty-five-delta call and a twenty-five-delta put would have the exact same implied volatility. They would cost the same.

Corn: But people are usually terrified of one specific direction.

Herman: Exactly. If the market is terrified that the Australian dollar is going to crash because of a slowdown in China, institutional investors rush to buy Aussie dollar puts. The price of puts spikes, while calls get dumped. The difference between the implied volatility of the call and the put is the risk reversal.

Corn: If the number is negative, people are paying through the nose to protect against a plunge.

Herman: Spot on. For AUD/USD, the risk reversal almost always trades at a put premium. The market structurally worries more about sudden drops in the Aussie dollar than sudden spikes. For the shekel, whenever conflict flares up or domestic political instability boils over in Israel, the risk reversal for USD/ILS blows out to a massive premium for dollar calls—meaning people are terrified of the shekel depreciating.

Corn: So if Jim sees the USD/ILS risk reversal spiking, he knows the smart money is aggressively hedging against a shekel drop. Which means his Australian dollars might soon buy more shekels, provided the Aussie is not collapsing at the exact same moment.

Herman: Which brings us directly to cross-pair dynamics. Remember, AUD/ILS is mathematically AUD/USD divided by USD/ILS. If you want to measure the volatility of a cross currency, the formula is not just adding the two volatilities together. You have to account for the correlation between them.

Corn: The covariance term.

Herman: The covariance. The formula for the variance of a cross rate is roughly the variance of the first pair, plus the variance of the second pair, minus two times the correlation between them multiplied by their standard deviations.

Corn: That minus sign is doing heavy lifting.

Herman: Huge lifting. If AUD/USD and USD/ILS move in opposite directions—say, the Aussie drops against the US dollar while the US dollar rises against the shekel—those moves reinforce each other, and the volatility of AUD/ILS explodes. If they move in the same direction, they can cancel each other out, dampening the volatility.

Corn: Math aside, let us tackle Jim's third question: identifying support points in rate pairs. Because everyone who has ever looked at a chart thinks they see a floor, until they step on it and fall through into the basement.

Herman: Identifying support is where technical analysis meets structural market mechanics. Jim needs to understand what support actually is. It is not an invisible line drawn by an ink pen. Support is a price level where the aggregate willingness to buy outweighs the aggregate willingness to sell, halting a decline.

Corn: The problem is that most retail traders look for lines. Institutional desks look for liquidity pools.

Herman: That is the crucial distinction. If Jim wants to identify credible support in AUD/USD or AUD/ILS, he should look for four concrete, observable structures. The first is horizontal structural support from swing lows on higher-timeframe charts. Not five-minute charts. Daily, weekly, monthly charts.

Corn: Show me a support line on a five-minute chart and I will show you a coin toss with a colorful background.

Herman: Exactly. When you look at a weekly chart of AUD/USD over ten years, you see glaring historical boundaries. For instance, the sixty-two to sixty-three US cent level has acted as a multi-year floor repeatedly. When the pair gets down there, central bank sentiment, institutional asset allocators, and sovereign wealth funds begin scaling into long positions because Australia's terms of trade rarely justify the currency trading much lower for sustained periods without a global catastrophe.

Corn: What is the second structure?

Herman: Round numbers. Psychological support and option strike density. You cannot dismiss human psychology in trading. On AUD/USD, zero point sixty-five, zero point seventy, zero point seventy-five. On USD/ILS, three point sixty, three point seventy, four point zero.

Corn: Why do round numbers matter? Is it just that humans have ten fingers?

Herman: Partially, yes, but mostly because that is where the options open interest sits. The Chicago Mercantile Exchange and the Depository Trust and Clearing Corporation process massive volumes of vanilla and barrier options that are struck at round psychological numbers. If millions of dollars in knock-out options sit at zero point sixty-four on AUD/USD, market makers who sold those options have to dynamically hedge their deltas as the price approaches that level.

Corn: Meaning they are forced to buy or sell the underlying spot currency to keep their books neutral.

Herman: Yes. That hedging activity physically creates support or resistance in the spot market. If market makers need to buy spot to defend their hedges as price approaches an option barrier, that buying creates an artificial cushion—a support level. But if that level breaks, and the option gets knocked out, the support evaporates instantly, and price tends to cascade through.

Corn: That is how people get trapped. They see a floor hold three times, they think it is concrete, they put their money down, and the moment it cracks, it drops like a stone.

Herman: Precisely. The third method is volume profile, or Volume at Price. Most retail charts show volume by time—how much traded at two in the afternoon. Volume profile shows how much volume was transacted at specific price levels over the past three months, six months, or year. Where you see high-volume nodes, that indicates fair value where buyers and sellers reached agreement. Below that node, you often find support because buyers who missed the boat previously see it as an attractive discount.

Corn: And the fourth structure?

Herman: Dynamic institutional levels: moving averages that macro funds actually track. Not exotic indicators, but the two-hundred-day simple moving average and the fifty-day simple moving average. When AUD/USD tests its two-hundred-day moving average from above, systematic trend-following algorithms—the CTAs, or Commodity Trading Advisors—frequently have automated rules to add to long positions or close shorts. That flow creates physical price support.

Corn: Now, Herman, how does any of that apply to AUD/ILS? Because AUD/ILS does not have its own autonomous options market with massive open interest.

Herman: It does not. And this is the trap Jim must avoid. If Jim draws support lines on an AUD/ILS chart, he is looking at an artifact. He is looking at a shadow cast by two other objects.

Corn: A derivative of two separate battles.

Herman: Exactly. If AUD/ILS hits a supposed support line, but that line is just an arbitrary mathematical consequence of where AUD/USD and USD/ILS happened to be on that day, it has zero predictive power on its own. To find genuine support on AUD/ILS, Jim has to find confluence between support on AUD/USD and resistance on USD/ILS.

Corn: Walk through that. If he wants AUD/ILS to bounce, what has to happen?

Herman: AUD/ILS goes up if the Australian dollar strengthens, or if the Israeli shekel strengthens against the US dollar—which means the USD/ILS rate falls. So a true structural floor for AUD/ILS happens when AUD/USD is hitting major long-term support—say, sixty-three cents—at the exact same time that USD/ILS is hitting massive technical resistance—say, three point eighty-five or four point zero shekels to the dollar.

Corn: Because at that moment, both underlying engines are poised to reverse in a way that pushes AUD/ILS up.

Herman: Exactly. If you only look at the cross chart, you are flying blind. You might see a beautiful double bottom on AUD/ILS, but if AUD/USD is about to slice through sixty-three cents like a hot knife through butter because iron ore prices just fell through the floor in Dalian, that AUD/ILS double bottom will disintegrate.

Corn: Let us move to the fourth and biggest question Jim asked: the primary geopolitical and macroeconomic factors influencing these pairs. This is the engine room. Let us take the Australian dollar first. What drives the Aussie?

Herman: The Aussie dollar is universally classified as a high-beta, risk-on, commodity-linked currency. It is tied to the hip of global economic growth.

Corn: If the global economy is booming, factories are running, and buildings are going up, people need rocks. And Australia has the best rocks.

Herman: Specifically iron ore, metallurgical coal, thermal coal, and liquefied natural gas. Australia runs a current account that has spent recent years in surplus, largely on the back of massive resource exports to East Asia, primarily China. China is Australia's largest trading partner by a country mile. If Chinese real estate construction slows down, Chinese blast furnaces buy less iron ore from the Pilbara region in Western Australia.

Corn: When iron ore drops from one hundred and thirty dollars a tonne to ninety dollars a tonne, Australia's terms of trade deteriorate, mining revenues fall, corporate tax receipts drop, and the Australian dollar softens.

Herman: Automatically. That is the commodity channel. The second major driver for the Aussie is global risk sentiment. Institutional traders treat the Aussie dollar as a liquid proxy for world trade optimism. When markets are panicking—whether it is a banking crisis, a pandemic, or fear of a global recession—capital flees high-beta currencies like the Aussie and runs into safe havens: the US dollar, the Swiss franc, the Japanese yen.

Corn: And the third driver is the interest rate differential. The Reserve Bank of Australia versus the Federal Reserve.

Herman: Absolutely. The carry trade. Historically, Australia had significantly higher interest rates than the United States, which made the Aussie a popular investment currency. People borrowed cheaply in yen or dollars to park cash in Australian bonds. But in the post-pandemic cycle, the Federal Reserve hiked interest rates faster and higher than the Reserve Bank of Australia. The Fed pushed above five percent, while the RBA peaked lower, around four point three five percent.

Corn: That gave the US dollar a yield advantage. Why buy Aussie paper when Uncle Sam pays you more for taking less risk?

Herman: It turned the historical carry trade on its head, keeping downward pressure on AUD/USD. Now, let us switch gears entirely to the other side of Jim's equation: the Israeli shekel. Corn, the shekel is an entirely different beast. What makes it tick?

Corn: It used to be a closed, high-inflation basket case back in the nineteen-eighties, and then it became an absolute juggernaut.

Herman: One of the strongest currencies in the world over the last fifteen years. And the engine behind that structural appreciation was two-fold: the Israeli high-tech sector, and the discovery of offshore natural gas.

Corn: The high-tech sector is critical to understand. It is not just that Israeli coders write good software. It is how that software gets paid for.

Herman: This is the financial mechanism Jim needs to visualize. Israeli tech startups raise capital in US dollars from venture capital firms in Silicon Valley, New York, and London. They sell their software to American and European enterprise clients in US dollars. But their expenses—the engineers' salaries in Tel Aviv, the office rents, the local taxes—must be paid in Israeli shekels.

Corn: So every month, Israeli tech companies take their bags of US dollars, dump them on the market, and buy shekels to pay payroll.

Herman: That created a massive, relentless structural bid for the shekel for over a decade. Trillions of shekels' worth of foreign direct investment flowed into Israel, far outstripping the current account outflows. Add to that the Tamar and Leviathan natural gas fields coming online, which turned Israel from an energy importer into an energy exporter, eliminating its energy deficit.

Corn: But that tech engine has a mirror image that governs daily volatility: Wall Street.

Herman: This is one of the most unique macroeconomic mechanisms in global macro. Israeli institutional investors—the pension funds, insurance companies, and provident funds that manage Israeli retirement money—hold massive allocations in US equities, primarily the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq.

Corn: Walk through what happens when the Nasdaq goes up.

Herman: It is brilliant. Israeli pension funds have target allocations for their foreign currency exposure. Suppose a fund wants no more than twenty percent of its total portfolio exposed to foreign currency risk. If the Nasdaq rallies twenty percent in a quarter, the value of their US equity holdings explodes. Suddenly, their portfolio is thirty percent exposed to the US dollar.

Corn: They are overweight dollars.

Herman: They are overweight dollars. So their mandate forces them to rebalance. How do they rebalance? They sell US dollar forward contracts to hedge the currency exposure. And selling dollars means buying shekels.

Corn: So when tech stocks rally in New York, the shekel gets stronger in Jerusalem.

Herman: The correlation between the S&P 500 and the shekel was near-perfect for years. If the Nasdaq crashed, Israeli institutional funds had their dollar equity value shrink, making them underweight dollar exposure. They had to close out their hedges by buying US dollars and selling shekels, driving the shekel down.

Corn: That was true right up until early twenty-twenty-three, when the domestic politics and geopolitical reality arrived with a sledgehammer.

Herman: Yes. The judicial reform proposals introduced in early twenty-twenty-three caused unprecedented domestic political protests, capital flight concerns, and questions about institutional stability. The historic correlation between the S&P five hundred and the shekel broke down completely. US tech stocks rallied, but the shekel tumbled.

Corn: And then came October seventh, twenty-twenty-three.

Herman: And the war. When war broke out, the immediate reaction was a violent sell-off in the shekel. USD/ILS spiked toward four point zero eight shekels per dollar. That is the geopolitical risk premium that now sits heavily on the currency.

Corn: But it did not stay at four point zero eight. The Bank of Israel stepped in.

Herman: And this is Jim's primary lesson in central bank intervention. The Bank of Israel is not like the Reserve Bank of Australia. The RBA almost never intervenes directly in the spot market to buy or sell Aussie dollars; they let the currency float freely, absorbing shocks like a shock absorber. The Bank of Israel, on the other hand, had spent fifteen years accumulating a colossal foreign exchange reserve precisely to prevent the shekel from getting too strong during the tech boom.

Corn: They had two hundred billion dollars sitting in the basement.

Herman: Just about two hundred billion US dollars, which is astronomical for an economy of Israel's size. Over a third of their entire gross domestic product. So when the war began and the shekel went into freefall, the Governor of the Bank of Israel, Amir Yaron, announced an emergency program: the central bank would sell up to thirty billion dollars directly from its reserves to stabilize the currency, and provide another fifteen billion in swap lines.

Corn: They drew a line in the sand.

Herman: They did. They sold around thirty billion dollars over the following months, soaked up the panic selling, and completely stabilized the exchange rate. The shekel rallied all the way back below three point sixty at one point.

Corn: That is the ultimate sovereign put. If you are betting against the shekel, you are not just betting against local market participants. You are betting against a central bank holding two hundred billion greenbacks that will happily burn through reserves to maintain financial stability.

Herman: Exactly. But the ongoing cost of that war creates fiscal drag. Israel's budget deficit expanded dramatically, reaching over seven and even eight percent of GDP during peak fighting. The sovereign credit rating was downgraded by Moody's, S&P, and Fitch. A higher fiscal deficit, higher borrowing costs, and potential for renewed escalation on northern or regional fronts mean the shekel carries a structural geopolitical risk discount that did not exist five years ago.

Corn: So let us put these two currencies together for Jim, because Jim is standing in Jerusalem holding Australian dollars, looking at real estate priced in shekels.

Herman: Property in Israel is priced almost exclusively in shekels. Years ago, landlords and sellers used to quote in US dollars, but the Bank of Israel clamped down on that decades ago. Jim's liability is one hundred percent in Israeli shekels.

Corn: And his capital, presumably, is sitting in Australian dollars.

Herman: Or US dollars. Let us look at what happens in different global macro regimes to Jim's purchasing power. Regime one: global peace, synchronized worldwide growth, booming trade.

Corn: China is buying iron ore, Wall Street is rallying, tech startups are raising money.

Herman: In that regime, the Australian dollar surges because commodity prices are high and risk appetite is strong. But the shekel also surges because tech inflows are massive and the Nasdaq is printing all-time highs. So AUD/ILS might actually stay relatively range-bound, because both currencies are running in the same direction.

Corn: Now take regime two: a global geopolitical shock or stagflation. Commodity prices soften because global demand tanks, but oil spikes, and a regional conflict expands in the Middle East.

Herman: That is pure chaos for the cross. If global growth falls, the Aussie dollar gets crushed against the US dollar. But if the conflict directly involves Israel, the shekel faces localized pressure against the US dollar. Which one falls faster? That depends on whether the Bank of Israel is intervening, and how dependent Australia is on immediate trade flows.

Corn: In late twenty-twenty-three, when the war started, AUD/ILS went from around two point four five down toward two point thirty-five, then bounced aggressively as the Australian dollar caught a bid and the shekel stabilized.

Herman: Exactly. And Jim also mentioned looking at AUD/USD. Why would an Aussie in Jerusalem care about AUD/USD if he is buying an apartment in shekels?

Corn: Because if he converts his Australian dollars into US dollars first, he might get a better rate, hold a more stable asset, and then convert to shekels only when he needs to close.

Herman: That is the classic two-step treasury management approach. But Jim has to be very careful here. If Jim converts his Aussie dollars into US dollars, he eliminates the Australian risk, but he now has a naked currency mismatch against his Jerusalem property purchase.

Corn: If he signs a contract to buy an apartment for four million shekels with completion in twelve months, and he holds US dollars, he is now an FX speculator.

Herman: An aggressive FX speculator. If USD/ILS goes from three point eighty to three point forty over that year—meaning the shekel strengthens—his US dollars will buy four hundred thousand fewer shekels when final payment is due. On a four million shekel contract, that is an unexpected sixty-thousand-dollar shortfall out of his pocket.

Corn: Unless he hedges.

Herman: Which brings us back to institutional mechanics. If Jim is buying property off-plan or with a delayed settlement, he cannot afford to leave his currency unhedged. What do multinational corporations do when they have a cross-border liability? They do not guess whether the Reserve Bank of Australia is going to cut rates or whether the Bank of Israel is going to sell reserves.

Corn: They use forward contracts.

Herman: Yes. An FX forward contract allows Jim to lock in an exchange rate today for a delivery date six months or twelve months in the future. Now, as an individual, Jim cannot walk into Goldman Sachs and open an ISDA master agreement. But there are specialized, regulated foreign exchange brokers—international payment firms—that offer retail and high-net-worth forward contracts.

Corn: How does the pricing of a forward contract actually work, Herman? Because people think the forward rate is a prediction of where the currency will be.

Herman: It is not a prediction at all. That is the number one misconception in finance. A forward rate is purely an interest rate parity calculation. Covered interest parity dictates that the difference between the spot exchange rate and the forward exchange rate must equal the interest rate differential between the two currencies over that period.

Corn: Covered Interest Parity. If the forward rate deviated from interest rates, someone could borrow in one currency, lend in the other, lock in the forward, and print free money until the universe collapsed.

Herman: Exactly. Arbitrage forces the forward rate to match the interest rate spread. So if Australian interest rates are four point three five percent, and Israeli interest rates—the Bank of Israel policy rate—are around four point five percent, the interest rate differential between Australia and Israel is very small.

Corn: Meaning the forward points are negligible.

Herman: Very small. Jim can lock in a one-year AUD/ILS forward at a rate that is remarkably close to the current spot rate. If he were locking in Aussie dollars against a currency with twenty percent interest rates, the forward rate would be wildly different from spot. But between AUD and ILS, or between AUD and USD where Australian rates are slightly below US rates, the forward points are manageable.

Corn: So if Jim finds a home he likes, agrees on a price in shekels, but his money is in Sydney in superannuation or savings, he can lock in the forward rate and sleep at night.

Herman: He eliminates the entire currency risk. If the Aussie dollar drops ten percent over the next six months because Chinese steel production collapses, Jim does not care. He locked in his rate. If the shekel rallies because a peace treaty is signed and tech valuations triple, Jim does not care. His property price in Australian dollars is fixed.

Corn: The only downside is if the currency moves in his favor, he does not get the windfall.

Herman: But you do not buy a home to play foreign exchange roulette. You buy a home to live in it, or to rent it out for a predictable yield.

Corn: Let us touch on the practical transaction side, because this is where ordinary people lose shocking amounts of money. Israeli banks.

Herman: Oh, boy. Israeli banking bureaucracy is legendary. It is an Olympic sport.

Corn: If you try to wire half a million Australian dollars from an account at Commonwealth Bank or Westpac directly into an account at Bank Hapoalim or Bank Leumi, what happens, Herman?

Herman: First, the compliance department at the Israeli bank will freeze the funds the second they hit the SWIFT network. Israel has extraordinarily strict anti-money laundering and know-your-customer laws, partly driven by international compliance requirements and partly by domestic tax enforcement. They will require Jim to provide absolute, watertight proof of the source of funds.

Corn: Tax returns, bank statements going back years, sale of previous property documentation, signed letters from an Australian accountant with an official stamp.

Herman: And if he does not have that ready, the money sits in escrow limbo, earning zero interest, while the transaction clock ticks down on his property contract. And worse: if he sends Australian dollars directly to an Israeli bank account without an explicit agreement on the conversion rate, the Israeli bank will convert the Australian dollars to shekels using their retail board rate.

Corn: The board rate. A polite term for highway robbery.

Herman: The spread between the buy and sell rate on an Israeli retail bank board for an exotic cross like AUD/ILS can easily be two, three, or four percent. On a five hundred thousand dollar transfer, a three percent spread is fifteen thousand dollars vanished into thin air.

Corn: Fifteen thousand dollars to press a button on a computer terminal that was installed in nineteen ninety-four.

Herman: Exactly. So Jim's operational playbook needs to look like this: Step one, do not use a standard commercial bank for the cross-currency conversion unless he has negotiated a private banking tier with fixed spread terms. Use an authorized, institutional foreign exchange specialist that has local clearing accounts in both Australia and Israel.

Corn: That way, the Australian dollars are deposited locally into an Australian account via the domestic payments network, the conversion happens at wholesale institutional spreads plus a known markup—say, twenty or thirty basis points—and the shekels are disbursed locally from an Israeli account via the local Zahav RTGS system.

Herman: Zahav is Israel's real-time gross settlement system. That avoids international intermediary wire fees, cuts execution time from days to minutes, and keeps the spread transparent.

Corn: And step two: clear the compliance hurdle before sending a single cent.

Herman: Get the pre-clearance from the Israeli receiving bank. Walk the compliance officers through the source of funds before initiating the transfer. If you do it after the wire is sent, you are sitting in a Jerusalem cafe biting your nails while the seller threatens to cancel the contract and pocket your deposit.

Corn: Let us circle back and answer the core prompt systematically for Jim, so he has a checklist to stick on his fridge.

Herman: First, assessing liquidity. For AUD/USD, look at spot bid-ask spreads—they should be under one pip—and track CME futures volume. For AUD/ILS, recognize it as a synthetic cross of AUD/USD and USD/ILS. Assess it by checking the spread offered by your provider against the synthetic mid-market price, avoid trading on Sundays, and execute during the London-Middle East afternoon overlap when both underlying pairs have maximum depth.

Corn: Second, standardized measures of volatility.

Herman: For historical, realized moves, track the twenty-day and sixty-day rolling annualized standard deviation, or use the fourteen-day Average True Range to get daily pip expectations. For forward-looking risk, monitor one-month and three-month implied volatility on AUD/USD options, and watch the twenty-five-delta risk reversal on USD/ILS. If the risk reversal on USD/ILS explodes, the market is pricing severe tail risk for the shekel.

Corn: Third, identifying support.

Herman: Ignore trendlines on short-term charts. Look for confluence on daily and weekly charts: multi-year horizontal swing lows, volume-by-price accumulation nodes, round numbers with high option open interest, and the two-hundred-day simple moving average. Most importantly, do not look for support on the AUD/ILS chart alone. Look for confluence where AUD/USD is hitting structural support at the exact moment USD/ILS is hitting structural resistance.

Corn: And fourth, macroeconomic and geopolitical engines.

Herman: For the Aussie dollar: Chinese industrial demand, bulk commodity export prices—iron ore and coal—global risk sentiment, and the RBA-Fed interest rate spread. For the Israeli shekel: foreign direct investment into the high-tech sector, institutional pension hedging tied to the performance of US equity markets, domestic fiscal deficits, geopolitical escalation risk, and direct foreign exchange intervention by the Bank of Israel backed by its two hundred billion dollars in foreign reserves.

Corn: That is the whole board. It is complicated, but none of it is magic. It is just plumbing, balance sheets, and human fear.

Herman: Which are the only three things that have ever moved financial markets.

Corn: Good luck with the flat hunting in Jerusalem, Jim. Watch out for stone floors in the winter; they are freezing.

Herman: And watch the spreads. Thank you for listening to My Weird Prompts. Send your questions, voice notes, and odd financial puzzles to Daniel, our producer.

Corn: Until next time, keep your hedges tight and your bank fees zero. Goodbye.

Corn: Jim is an Australian expat in Jerusalem, thinking about buying property, and wants to understand AUD against the shekel and AUD against the US dollar. He asks about liquidity, volatility, support levels, and the forces moving currencies. So: not “tell me where the exchange rate will be next Tuesday,” but “how do I avoid being surprised by the plumbing?”

Herman: A noble ambition. The plumbing is where the expensive surprises live.

Corn: Especially when the plumbing charges a spread.

Herman: Right. The first thing is to separate Jim’s question into two decisions. One is, “What will this property cost me in Australian dollars?” The other is, “When and how do I convert the money?” Those are related, but they’re not the same decision.

Corn: The apartment has a price. The exchange rate has opinions.

Herman: And occasionally it has very loud opinions. Let’s establish the quotation first, because a chart label can reverse your intuition. AUD/ILS means Israeli shekels per Australian dollar. If AUD/ILS is four-point-eight, one Australian dollar buys four-point-eight shekels. If that number rises, the Australian dollar has strengthened against the shekel, or the shekel has weakened against the Australian dollar. AUD/USD is US dollars per Australian dollar. If it’s zero-point-six-five, one Australian dollar buys sixty-five US cents.

Corn: So if AUD/ILS goes down, Jim gets fewer shekels for each Australian dollar.

Herman: Exactly. And if he needs a fixed number of shekels for a purchase, a falling AUD/ILS makes the Australian-dollar cost of that purchase rise. That can matter much more than whether a headline says the Australian dollar is “up.” The relevant question is up against what, over what period, and for how many shekels?

Corn: “The Aussie is up” is not a useful invoice.

Herman: It’s barely a useful sentence. And property transactions have practical details: deposit dates, completion dates, mortgage arrangements, fees, and possibly payment milestones. A rate that looks acceptable today may not be the rate available to him after bank spreads, transfer fees, and the timing of the actual settlement.

Corn: The advertised mid-market rate is the menu photograph.

Herman: Often, yes. It’s the reference rate between buyers and sellers, not necessarily the rate a customer receives. Jim should request a real quote for the amount he expects to transfer, in the direction he expects to transfer it. If he is turning Australian dollars into shekels, compare the final number of shekels delivered, after all charges. If he’s funding a purchase in stages, compare the cost of each stage.

Corn: Don’t compare one provider’s headline rate with another provider’s actual receipt. That’s how a fee puts on a tiny hat and pretends to be a currency move.

Herman: A nice image. The currency market itself is largely over the counter. It’s a network of banks, dealers, funds, businesses, and other participants, rather than one single central exchange where every trade in a pair is visible. So “the liquidity of AUD/ILS” isn’t one neat number that applies to every customer, every time, and every trade size.

Corn: The market is a network. The price on a phone is a suggestion.

Herman: A very useful suggestion, sometimes. But it doesn’t reveal the whole order book, and it may not reflect the cost of a large or time-sensitive transfer. Liquidity usually means how easily you can trade without moving the price much and without paying a large spread. You can assess it through several clues: the bid-ask spread, the depth of available quotes, how much prices jump around during normal trading, how many dealers will quote you, and what happens to the price when the market is stressed.

Corn: And the spread is the bit Jim can see without becoming a bank.

Herman: Usually. He can compare simultaneous buy and sell quotes from reputable providers. The difference between the rate at which he can buy one currency and the rate at which he can sell it is a practical measure of the spread. He should make sure the quotes are for the same amount, at roughly the same time, and include the same fee structure. A quote for a small test transfer may not tell him what he’ll get for a large property payment.

Corn: “Same time” matters because currencies don’t wait for your spreadsheet.

Herman: They really don’t. Also, AUD/ILS is not as deeply traded as AUD/USD. The Australian dollar is a major currency, and the US dollar is central to global foreign exchange. The shekel is a meaningful currency, but it’s a smaller market, and trading conditions can change sharply around local events or outside market hours. It’s reasonable to expect a wider spread and less depth in AUD/ILS than in AUD/USD, especially for a large transaction or at an inconvenient time.

Corn: The more exotic the route, the more the toll booth gets ideas.

Herman: Though I’d avoid calling AUD/ILS exotic in every context. It is a valid pair, and providers can quote it directly. But a lot of the underlying price relationship can be understood through the dollar. Roughly, AUD/ILS is connected to AUD/USD multiplied by USD/ILS. If an Australian dollar buys zero-point-six-five US dollars, and one US dollar buys, say, three-point-seven shekels, then the cross is approximately zero-point-six-five times three-point-seven, or about two-point-four shekels per Australian dollar.

Corn: That arithmetic is alarming.

Herman: The numbers were just a made-up example, not a current rate. I chose them to show the mechanism, and I should say that clearly because Jim is contemplating a real purchase.

Corn: Thank you. Finance fiction has a dangerously realistic costume.

Herman: The important point is that a provider may effectively route the conversion through the US dollar: Australian dollars to US dollars, then US dollars to shekels. Even when the customer sees one AUD/ILS quote, the provider may be pricing it from those two more liquid legs and adding a margin. That can be efficient, but it can also mean two spreads or a hidden markup. So Jim should ask for the final AUD-to-ILS rate and compare it with the indicative cross-rate calculated from AUD/USD and USD/ILS, taking account of fees.

Corn: If the path is indirect, ask what the detour costs.

Herman: Yes. And don’t assume that doing two separate trades yourself will be cheaper. It could mean two transaction charges, two opportunities for the market to move, and more complexity. The only useful answer is the all-in quote he can actually execute.

Corn: What about the big global statistics? Can those tell him whether a pair is liquid?

Herman: They give scale, not a personal execution guarantee. The Bank for International Settlements surveys global foreign-exchange markets periodically. In its two-thousand-and-twenty-two triennial survey, average daily turnover across FX instruments was around seven-point-five trillion US dollars. The dollar was on one side of roughly eighty-eight percent of trades, and the Australian dollar on roughly six percent. That survey shows how central the dollar is and that the Aussie is an important currency. It doesn’t tell Jim the spread he’ll get on AUD/ILS from his bank on a specific Tuesday.

Corn: Seven-point-five trillion dollars a day, and we still have to ask if somebody will give us a decent rate.

Herman: Global turnover is not the same thing as liquid depth in the exact pair, at the exact hour, for the exact amount. There may be more activity during the working hours of Sydney, Tokyo, London, and New York, but the liquidity profile changes as those markets open and close. The shekel’s trading activity is particularly tied to its local market and to the hours when major international dealers are active. If Jim is getting a quote while one side of a market is largely asleep, he might see a wider spread.

Corn: Currency markets are open nearly all week, not equally awake all week.

Herman: Exactly. And stress changes the plumbing. During a geopolitical shock, a central-bank announcement, a sudden change in risk appetite, or a market gap after a weekend, dealers may widen quotes or reduce the amount they’re willing to trade at a given price. A pair can have perfectly respectable average liquidity and still be awkward at the moment someone most urgently wants to transact.

Corn: Liquidity is easiest to praise in calm weather.

Herman: And this matters to Jim because his purpose is not to win a trading contest. He needs a reliable way to meet a shekel obligation. He might ask providers about transfer limits, settlement time, cut-off times, whether rates can be locked, and what happens if a payment is delayed. Those operational details are part of the risk, not an administrative footnote.

Corn: The wire can be delayed. The exchange rate can’t be asked to pause politely.

Herman: Now volatility. There is no single official standardized volatility number that says, “This is the volatility of AUD/ILS,” full stop. You need to specify the measure, the lookback period, and the frequency of the data. A common first measure is realized volatility: calculate the percentage return from one observation to the next, usually using logarithmic returns, then measure how much those returns vary over a chosen period.

Corn: In regular-person language?

Herman: How much the rate has actually moved around in the past. Suppose you have daily AUD/ILS closing rates for the past year. You calculate the daily percentage changes, take their standard deviation, and annualize it by multiplying by the square root of about two hundred and fifty-two trading days. That gives an annualized historical volatility estimate. The exact convention can vary, and currency markets don’t behave as if every calendar day is an interchangeable trading day, but it’s a widely used way to put scales on a chart.

Corn: It’s a ruler made from yesterday’s movements.

Herman: Yes, not a forecast. If a platform reports annualized volatility of, say, ten percent, that does not mean the currency is guaranteed to stay within ten percent of today’s rate over a year. It is a statistical description of recent variability under a particular calculation. Actual returns can be lopsided, clustered, and disrupted by events. The number won’t tell Jim the direction of the next move.

Corn: A speedometer for the past. Not a map.

Herman: Nicely put. He can compare realized volatility across AUD/ILS and AUD/USD if he uses consistent data, the same lookback, the same sampling interval, and the same calculation. He should also check different windows: perhaps one month, three months, one year, and several years. A one-month estimate captures current conditions but may be dominated by a brief shock. A long lookback can smooth away exactly the new regime he cares about.

Corn: One month is twitchy; five years may be asleep.

Herman: There’s also implied volatility from options markets. An option gives the buyer the right, but not the obligation, to exchange currencies at a specified rate and date. The option’s market price can be translated into an implied volatility. That tells you how much movement option traders are pricing for a particular future period, given the other inputs and conventions. For many currency pairs, dealers quote implied volatility for standard tenors such as one month, three months, or one year.

Corn: The future’s price, as inferred from people paying to insure against it.

Herman: That’s a useful intuition. But implied volatility is not pure consensus or a magic forecast. It reflects supply and demand for options, protection against particular outcomes, interest-rate relationships, and market conventions. For AUD/USD, there is a much deeper options market than for AUD/ILS. Jim may find a widely available implied-volatility series for AUD/USD, while an equivalent, reliable AUD/ILS series could be less accessible or less representative. He shouldn’t treat a thinly traded option quote as a precise measurement.

Corn: If nobody trades the ruler, the ruler is mostly decorative.

Herman: You can also look at an average true range, or ATR, on a chart. That’s a technical indicator that estimates the typical size of a price move over a chosen number of periods, including gaps. It’s often quoted in rate units, not as a clean annualized percentage. It can help visualize how much a pair tends to travel in a day or week, but it is not standardized across different price levels or chart settings. Two chart services may use different settings and give different ATR values.

Corn: The indicator has a ruler, but it chose the ruler itself.

Herman: Another useful tool is a rolling percentile or a z-score of recent returns. If today’s move is unusually large relative to the recent distribution, a z-score can flag that. But again, it depends on the chosen window and assumes a particular distribution more than currencies deserve. A currency return series can have fat tails: rare, severe moves happen more often than a tidy normal-distribution model suggests.

Corn: The tails are where the newspaper lives.

Herman: Exactly. For Jim’s decision, I would not make volatility a contest where he chooses the pair with the lower number. The exposure comes from the cost of the property in shekels and the number of Australian dollars he needs to deliver. He can build a simple scenario table. At today’s executable rate, how many Australian dollars does the required shekel amount cost? Then what if AUD/ILS moves five percent against him before payment? What if it moves ten percent? Include the provider’s spread and fees. The question becomes: could he still complete the purchase, and would the change be tolerable?

Corn: Volatility is easier to understand when it’s measured in apartments.

Herman: And the time horizon matters. If he has to pay a deposit next week, long-run averages may be less relevant than the calendar of his payment and today’s live market conditions. If he has payments spread over six months, he faces repeated exposure. He may choose to convert in stages, fix an exchange rate through a forward contract, or simply convert when he has the funds and the rate is acceptable. Each choice has trade-offs.

Corn: We have reached the part where “just wait for a better rate” becomes a plan.

Herman: A very common plan, and not really a plan unless he defines what “better” means and what he’ll do if the rate moves the other way. A forward contract can lock a rate for a future payment, but it isn’t free in the economic sense. The forward rate reflects the interest-rate difference between the currencies, along with the dealer’s margin and other costs. It may also require a deposit or collateral, and the customer must understand the obligation to settle. It removes some exchange-rate uncertainty but doesn’t make a poor purchase good.

Corn: The hedge does not turn the apartment into a bargain.

Herman: No. Staggering conversions spreads the timing risk: instead of converting the entire sum on one day, he converts portions at different dates. That reduces the chance of being completely unlucky on one particular day, but it doesn’t guarantee a better average rate. If the currency trends against him during that period, staggered conversion can still cost more than converting upfront.

Corn: Averaging is not a refund.

Herman: Exactly. And before using any product, Jim should check eligibility, fees, the provider’s terms, and local requirements. He is an Australian expat in Jerusalem, so the transfer may involve Australian banking rules, Israeli banking processes, property payment procedures, and identity or source-of-funds checks. He should get professional help for legal, tax, and property matters. That’s not because currency analysis is mysterious; it’s because a technically good rate doesn’t help if the money can’t reach the right account in time.

Corn: A bank compliance check is a terrible place to discover the completion deadline.

Herman: Now, support points. On a price chart, support is an area where a falling exchange rate has previously slowed or bounced. Traders may identify previous lows, price zones with lots of trading, round numbers, moving averages, or Fibonacci retracement levels. The theory is that buyers may appear at those levels, or sellers may hesitate. But support is not a wall, and it isn’t a fundamental property of the currency.

Corn: Support is a place a chart has visited, not a place it promised to defend.

Herman: That’s the crucial distinction. If AUD/ILS has bounced near a particular level several times, traders might pay attention to it. But a fresh geopolitical shock can push the rate straight through. Once it breaks, some traders who bought at support may sell to limit losses, adding pressure. So the old support area can become resistance, where a rising rate struggles to move higher. These are zones, not single magic digits.

Corn: The floor can become a ceiling. Very considerate of it.

Herman: Jim should be especially careful with exact support levels from a chart screenshot. The answer depends on the data source, the chart timeframe, and whether the rate is a bid, an ask, a midpoint, or an indicative feed. A daily chart may show a level that disappears on an hourly chart. A level that looks clear over two years may not be meaningful over ten years. For AUD/ILS, price data can also be less consistent across retail platforms than it is for a heavily traded pair.

Corn: A chart can be precise about a number that nobody can actually trade.

Herman: If he wants to use technical levels, he can decide in advance what role they play. For example, “If the rate reaches this zone, I will convert a planned portion,” rather than “This zone must hold, so I’ll wait.” The first is a decision rule. The second is a prediction wearing a hard hat.

Corn: The hard hat does not improve the forecast.

Herman: He could mark historical lows and highs, compare them across daily and weekly charts, and see whether the level has been tested more than once. But I would treat support as a way to organize timing, not as evidence that the exchange rate is cheap or expensive in an economic sense. A currency can remain “overbought” or “oversold” for a long time, and it can break every neat line on a chart.

Corn: Lines are very brave when the market is closed.

Herman: If the purpose is a property purchase, Jim also needs to be clear about which exchange rate is the one that matters. For the AUD/ILS payment, the direct cross is the relevant outcome. AUD/USD can help him understand one component of that cross, but it is not a substitute for checking USD/ILS. If AUD/USD rises while the shekel rises even more against the dollar, AUD/ILS could still fall. You need both legs.

Corn: Two currencies can both be right about the dollar and still make Jim’s life worse.

Herman: Let’s unpack the main forces. For AUD/USD, Australian and US interest-rate expectations matter a lot. Markets react not just to the current cash rate, but to expectations about future decisions by the Reserve Bank of Australia and the Federal Reserve. If traders think Australian rates will be relatively higher, that can support the Aussie, all else equal. If they expect the Fed to stay tighter while the RBA cuts, that can weigh on AUD/USD. But “all else equal” is doing heroic work there.

Corn: It’s the most employed phrase in economics.

Herman: Interest-rate expectations affect the returns on investments and the forward pricing of currencies, but exchange rates also reflect growth, inflation, and risk. Australia exports large amounts of commodities, including iron ore, coal, and liquefied natural gas. Commodity prices and demand from major trading partners, especially China, can influence Australia’s income and the Australian dollar’s outlook. A strong Chinese construction cycle can help support demand for Australian iron ore; a downturn or policy change can weaken it.

Corn: The Aussie often gets treated as a commodities report with a passport.

Herman: That’s an oversimplification, but there’s a reason it’s a popular shorthand. Australian employment, wages, inflation, household spending, and productivity affect the RBA’s assessment of the economy. Weather and supply disruptions can affect exports. The balance of trade and the current account matter in the broader background, though a monthly trade release does not mechanically dictate the exchange rate. Markets mostly move when data surprise expectations or change the outlook.

Corn: A number can be good and still make the currency fall if everyone expected better.

Herman: Exactly. On the US side, growth, inflation, jobs data, Treasury yields, and Federal Reserve policy all matter. The dollar often benefits when investors seek safety during global stress, although that is a tendency, not a law. The Australian dollar is often considered more sensitive to global growth and investor risk appetite. When markets are optimistic, investors may be more willing to hold currencies tied to growth and commodities. When there’s a rush for safety, the US dollar may strengthen and the Aussie may weaken.

Corn: “Risk-on” and “risk-off” sound like switches. They’re more like a badly labelled fuse box.

Herman: They are. A global shock can move the pair even if nothing important happened in Australia or the United States that day. The dollar’s role in global borrowing, trade invoicing, reserves, and financial markets makes its moves powerful. Changes in US yields can influence financial conditions around the world. So a rate decision in Washington may move AUD/USD more sharply than an Australian data release.

Corn: The US dollar gets a lot of attention for a currency that’s supposedly just one side of a pair.

Herman: Now add the shekel. The biggest structural forces include Israel’s economic outlook, inflation, interest rates set by the Bank of Israel, the state of public finances, foreign investment, and the performance of export sectors such as technology and services. Israel’s economy is unusually exposed to global technology markets, and flows into or out of Israeli assets can affect demand for shekels. Foreign investment, domestic institutions’ overseas investments, and hedging activity can all matter.

Corn: That’s a lot of different people trying to buy or sell shekels for reasons that have nothing to do with Jim’s apartment.

Herman: Precisely. Then there is the security and political environment. Conflict, escalation risk, changes in government policy, uncertainty around the budget, and concerns about institutions can affect investor confidence and the shekel. The response isn’t always a simple “bad news, weaker currency” calculation. A military or political shock can lead to intervention, changes in interest-rate expectations, flows into or out of assets, and shifts in the US dollar at the same time. The market is reacting to what people think the consequences will be, not assigning a fixed exchange-rate penalty to an event.

Corn: Headlines are not exchange-rate formulas.

Herman: And Israel’s central bank has tools. It can change interest rates, provide liquidity, and in certain circumstances intervene in the foreign-exchange market. Israel has previously used foreign-exchange reserves and intervention measures in periods of pressure. Whether an intervention is likely to work depends on the circumstances, the scale, credibility, and market conditions. Jim shouldn’t assume a central bank will keep the shekel within a particular range just because it has the capacity to act.

Corn: “Could intervene” is not the same as “will save my entry price.”

Herman: Exactly. The public finances matter too. Markets may pay attention to government spending, borrowing needs, debt outlook, and how geopolitical developments affect those. Changes in the perceived risk of investing in Israeli assets can influence capital flows and the currency. But there’s a timing problem: markets can react to speculation before a policy is announced, then reverse when the actual details are known.

Corn: The rumour can move first. The facts can arrive late and complain.

Herman: Australian and Israeli conditions then interact with US-dollar movements. Because AUD/ILS is approximately AUD/USD multiplied by USD/ILS, the pair can be pulled in opposite directions. A weaker Aussie against the dollar tends to push AUD/ILS down, all else equal. A weaker shekel against the dollar tends to push AUD/ILS up, all else equal. If both weaken against the dollar, the effect on the cross depends on how much each moves.

Corn: So “the dollar rose” still leaves two currencies to compare.

Herman: Right. Imagine a global risk-off episode. AUD/USD may fall because investors reduce exposure to growth-sensitive currencies. At the same time, USD/ILS may rise because investors seek dollars, because of local risk, or both. That second move tends to raise AUD/ILS, while the first tends to lower it. The net result depends on which effect is larger. Anyone claiming they know the cross just from one headline is skipping a whole leg of the table.

Corn: One leg is a theory. Two legs can at least stand up.

Herman: There can also be a local-market difference in how fast those movements appear. If a headline breaks while one market is thin, quotes may adjust unevenly, and a chart’s displayed cross may not be executable. That doesn’t necessarily mean there’s an arbitrage opportunity. It might mean the data are stale, the spread is wide, or the provider hasn’t refreshed its quote.

Corn: A stale price is not a gift from the universe.

Herman: A practical way for Jim to monitor this is to track three charts or rate series together: AUD/USD, USD/ILS, and the implied or quoted AUD/ILS cross. He can check whether the cross broadly matches the product of the two legs. If it doesn’t, he can ask whether the difference reflects timing, spreads, fees, or a quote that isn’t current. He should use a consistent source and timestamp.

Corn: Three charts. At least one can be blamed for ruining the day.

Herman: He should also build a short list of regular information sources, rather than refreshing every alarming headline. For Australia: RBA statements and minutes, inflation and employment releases, and key commodity and China-related news. For the United States: Federal Reserve communications, inflation and employment data, and Treasury yields. For Israel: Bank of Israel decisions and statements, inflation and growth releases, budget developments, and major political or security news. The point isn’t to become an amateur intelligence agency. It’s to identify which developments could affect his payment window.

Corn: The goal is informed, not permanently online.

Herman: Exactly. And be wary of stories that name a currency move but don’t distinguish cause from correlation. If AUD/USD drops after a Chinese economic release, that may be one factor, but US yields, global risk appetite, and positioning could have mattered too. If the shekel falls during a political crisis, there may also have been changes in the dollar, local rates, and capital flows. Currency attribution is messy.

Corn: The market does not attach a note saying, “I moved because of paragraph three.”

Herman: Now, what would I tell Jim to actually do? First, write down the shekel amount he needs and the dates on which he needs it. Include an allowance for transaction costs and any uncertainty in the purchase price. Then get executable quotes for that amount from more than one reputable provider, using the same timestamp where possible, and record the net shekels delivered. That establishes his real transaction cost.

Corn: Start with the number he must pay, not the number he hopes to admire.

Herman: Second, look at historical volatility using at least two or three windows, with consistent daily data. Add a few clear scenarios to show the Australian-dollar cost of the property if AUD/ILS moves against him by five or ten percent. Those percentages are examples for stress testing, not predictions. If the outcome would make the purchase unaffordable, the key issue isn’t whether a chart says support is nearby. It’s that he has a substantial currency exposure that needs a plan.

Corn: A support line cannot approve a mortgage.

Herman: Third, compare the market route and payment arrangements. Check whether his provider quotes AUD/ILS directly, what the all-in margin is, and whether a transfer through US dollars changes the final amount. Ask about settlement times and whether a rate can be fixed for the payment date. Get the terms in writing. If he considers a forward contract, understand the deposit, collateral, cancellation rules, and obligation to deliver.

Corn: “Locked rate” sounds relaxing until you read the word “obligation.”

Herman: Fourth, choose a rule he can stick to. If payments are due in stages, he might convert a defined portion on each date, or pre-convert when he has the funds, or hedge a known future obligation. He can decide what rate would make him comfortable, but he should understand that waiting for that rate may mean paying more later. A rule reduces impulsive decisions; it doesn’t guarantee a favourable outcome.

Corn: The best plan is the one that still exists after a bad headline.

Herman: I’d add one more: separate the property decision from the currency bet. If Jim wants the property because it suits his life and the price is acceptable in shekels, that’s a property judgment. If he delays the purchase because he expects AUD/ILS to improve, he is also making a currency forecast. He can make that choice, but he should name it honestly. Otherwise, the currency decision sneaks into the property decision and gets mistaken for prudence.

Corn: “I’m waiting for a better rate” can be a forecast with no expiry date.

Herman: And the reverse is true. Buying immediately removes the uncertainty of future exchange rates for that payment, but it doesn’t prove the rate was good. No one knows the perfect day in advance. For a person who needs a fixed amount of shekels, certainty can have real value. He may reasonably decide that a known cost is worth more than the possibility of a better rate.

Corn: Certainty is expensive. So is pretending it isn’t.

Herman: Where I’d be most cautious is using support and resistance to time a large transfer. The signals are subjective, especially in a cross with less transparent retail pricing, and they can fail during precisely the kind of event that matters in this region. They can help explain the chart and give a disciplined person a reference point. They shouldn’t be the foundation of the whole purchase plan.

Corn: The line on the chart should have a small job.

Herman: That’s it. Use the fundamentals to understand what might move the pair. Use volatility to understand the scale of past or option-priced movement. Use technical levels as context. Use executable quotes to measure the cost. And use a payment plan to control the exposure that is actually in front of him.

Corn: The quote is real. The support level is a suggestion. The property payment is a deadline.

Herman: That’s a pretty good hierarchy. And for the primary drivers, I’d keep the short version in mind: AUD/USD is heavily influenced by the relative outlook for Australian and US interest rates, Australian commodities and China-linked demand, US growth and yields, and global risk appetite. AUD/ILS adds the shekel’s interest-rate and economic outlook, Israeli investment flows, fiscal and political developments, and security risk. Through the cross, either currency’s movement against the US dollar can dominate.

Corn: And no single headline contains all of that, no matter how dramatic the headline sounds.

Herman: Right. The shekel’s risk environment deserves to be treated seriously, not reduced to a chart pattern. A property purchase is a large, illiquid commitment. Jim should understand both the currency exposure and the local rules around ownership and payment. If he needs tax, legal, or regulated financial advice, he should get it from qualified professionals who know his circumstances.

Corn: That’s not a disclaimer. It’s just a remarkably unglamorous part of buying a home.

Herman: The least glamorous parts often have the most expensive paperwork.

Corn: So, Jim: compare rates you can actually trade, measure volatility over more than one window, treat support as a zone rather than a promise, and track both legs of AUD/ILS through the dollar.

Herman: And decide how much uncertainty you can tolerate before you decide how to manage it. Don’t let a chart make that decision for you.

Corn: Or a cousin who says, “The Aussie always bounces here.”

Herman: Especially that cousin.

Corn: He has a support level for every bad idea.

Herman: Thanks for listening to My Weird Prompts. We hope Jim’s eventual exchange rate is kind, but we’d settle for his transfer arriving on time.

Corn: A modest forecast.

Herman: Goodbye.

Corn: Goodbye.

runs.prompt: The October 7th Hamas invasion of Israel was one of the most extraordinary military events in recent history. We've talked before about how Israel's defenses were actually overcome in practice looking at the mechanics of how a terrorist force was able to disable observation while simultaneously creating deception and infiltrating. What have we learned since the atrocity about how long the actual event was in planning and preparation? Not the immediate preparations that Israeli intelligence apparently missed, but from when the first seeds of the operation might have been planted how might an organization like Hamas, permanently wary of Israeli infiltration, have maintained compartmentalization up until the operation? Would ordinary Gazans have been taken by surprise by what they witnessed on that morning? Or have we seen evidence suggesting that awareness that the attack was eventual was more widely known than we might have expected?

entries.script:
Corn: How many people can know a secret before it stops being a secret?

Herman: Depends what they know. “Something big is coming” can circulate through a movement for years. “Be at this place at six thirty on Saturday” is a completely different secret.

Corn: One is a rumor. The other needs an alarm clock.

Herman: And that distinction is central to Daniel’s question today. How long was the October seventh attack in preparation, how did Hamas keep it compartmentalized, and how much did ordinary people in Gaza know beforehand?

Corn: Welcome to My Weird Prompts. I’m Corn.

Herman: And I’m Herman Poppleberry. We should put a date on what we’re discussing: the Hamas-led attack on Israel on October seventh, twenty twenty-three. About twelve hundred people were killed, most of them civilians, and two hundred fifty-one people were taken hostage.

Corn: Daniel says we’ve previously discussed how the border defenses were overcome. Today we’re moving upstream. Not the last few days of positioning people, but the years before that. When did an ambition become an operation? And who could see that happening?

Herman: My short answer is that the strongest public evidence supports serious planning over at least roughly two years, with important antecedents further back. Knowledge was layered. Senior planners knew far more than most fighters, and most fighters knew far more than ordinary residents. We have evidence of some wider anticipation, but not evidence that Gaza’s civilian population generally knew the date and nature of the attack.

Corn: Good. Now let’s make every word of that earn its keep. Especially “planning,” because people use it to mean anything from drawing an arrow on a map to putting fuel in a vehicle.

Herman: Exactly. I’d separate four clocks. The strategic aspiration: breach Israel’s defenses and attack communities or military positions. Capability development: training, intelligence collection, weapons, communications. Operational design: which forces do what. And authorization: this particular operation happens on this particular morning. Those clocks don’t all start together.

Corn: So if someone says, “They planned it for ten years,” the first question is, “Planned what?” An intention to attack Israel isn’t a ten-year appointment in a calendar.

Herman: Right. Hamas is an armed Islamist movement committed to fighting Israel, and it had pursued cross-border attacks, tunnels, and hostage-taking long before twenty twenty-three. Gilad Shalit was captured in a cross-border raid in two thousand six. That establishes a history of objectives and methods. It doesn’t establish that October seventh existed as a specific plan back then.

Corn: And the two thousand fourteen war exposed another element: tunnels intended to get armed men across the boundary. So the idea that the border could be penetrated wasn’t born in a meeting in twenty twenty-two.

Herman: No. But we need to resist retroactively treating every earlier capability as a component of a single master plan. Organizations acquire tools for several possible contingencies. Later they combine them. A tunnel, a drone unit, and a training compound can have histories that predate the operation eventually using them.

Corn: What’s the earliest firm foothold for the actual operation, rather than its family tree?

Herman: There are two particularly important public reporting tracks. One is the New York Times reporting in November twenty twenty-three on an approximately forty-page Hamas attack blueprint that Israeli officials called “Jericho Wall.” The Times reported that Israeli officials had obtained it more than a year before the attack.

Corn: That’s the document describing a remarkably similar sequence: rockets, attacks on surveillance, breaches, and armed men entering Israeli territory.

Herman: Yes. Crucially, it reportedly didn’t give a date. Its significance is that the broad operational concept existed well before the final preparations. Israeli officials had an outline of something close to the eventual attack and judged it beyond Hamas’s capabilities, or treated it as aspirational rather than executable.

Corn: A forty-page aspiration. Quite committed stationery.

Herman: And the second track is reporting, also by the Times, in October twenty twenty-four, based on minutes of secret Hamas leadership meetings seized by the Israeli military. The newspaper described ten meetings spanning January twenty twenty-two to August twenty twenty-three. Those records portrayed sustained planning for what leaders called the “big project.”

Corn: Before we give those minutes the weight of scripture, what’s the source problem?

Herman: They’re captured adversary documents supplied through an interested party. The Times said it assessed their authenticity, including by cross-checking details, but the public doesn’t have an independently accessible, complete Hamas archive. We should say “the documents reported by the Times indicate,” not pretend we personally audited every page in Gaza.

Corn: That’s not a reason to discard them. It’s a reason to keep the label on the jar.

Herman: Exactly. According to that reporting, Hamas initially contemplated launching in the autumn of twenty twenty-two, then postponed while seeking more support from Iran and Hezbollah. The meetings also described an effort to avoid a major confrontation in Gaza that might disrupt preparations. That gives us more than generic hostility. It gives us deliberation, scheduling, and postponement.

Corn: Which settles one thing rather cleanly. This wasn’t a spontaneous decision made after some incident in late September twenty twenty-three. Immediate events might have influenced timing or justification, but the machinery was already there.

Herman: Strongly agreed. Reuters also reported shortly after the attack, citing sources familiar with Hamas’s thinking, that it had carried out a roughly two-year deception campaign. That reporting emphasized cultivating an impression that Hamas wanted economic relief and wasn’t seeking another major war.

Corn: Does that mean we should put the beginning in twenty twenty-one?

Herman: As a cautious shorthand for intensive preparation, yes, approximately. But “twenty twenty-one” shouldn’t become a magic date. We have different sources describing different layers. The leadership minutes establish organized discussion by early twenty twenty-two; the blueprint establishes an advanced concept well before October twenty twenty-three; retrospective accounts push the preparation period back further.

Corn: I’d phrase it as: at least a couple of years for the identifiable operation, with a longer runway of capabilities and ambitions. Not one weekend, and not a confidently documented decade of this exact plan.

Herman: That’s my position too. There’s another subtlety: a plan can become more ambitious while it develops. We shouldn’t assume that the earliest version had exactly the scale, targets, or expected consequences of what happened. Nor should we assume that everything that happened that day was centrally scripted in advance.

Corn: Important distinction. Saying the attack was planned doesn’t tell you which individual crimes were ordered beforehand, which arose from broad instructions, and which were committed opportunistically. You need evidence for each claim. The overall operation and the conduct of every participant are different evidentiary questions.

Herman: Yes. And the documented advance identification of civilian communities and hostage-taking preparations matter enormously. This wasn’t simply a conventional assault that accidentally wandered into residential streets. But precision about individual responsibility still matters, especially when people use one captured paper to make claims about thousands of people.

Corn: Let’s turn to compartmentalization. Because the apparent paradox is real. You need lots of people to train for a large attack, but every additional person is another possible leak.

Herman: The paradox gets smaller once you stop imagining secrecy as a single locked box. Hamas didn’t need to conceal that it had armed units, trained for raids, or wanted to attack Israel. Those were public facts. The valuable secrets were the degree of readiness, the final scope, the coordination, and above all the timing.

Corn: So a fighter could practice attacking a mock Israeli position without knowing whether it was a standing drill, a contingency for a future war, or rehearsal for next Saturday.

Herman: Precisely. Public footage showed armed groups in Gaza conducting exercises involving mock Israeli positions, simulated incursions, and hostage-taking scenarios. Joint exercises by Palestinian factions had been held before the attack, including the “Strong Pillar” series beginning in twenty twenty. Those exercises demonstrated capabilities and intentions without publicly announcing an execution date.
