Corn: There’s a nasty intelligence problem there. If you watch someone rehearse something repeatedly, you can either become more alarmed or start filing it under “the thing they always rehearse.”

Herman: And both responses can be reasonable until other evidence distinguishes them. Repetition can normalize a warning signal. But we shouldn’t turn that into an excuse for ignoring it. The Times reported that a signals intelligence analyst warned in twenty twenty-three that a Hamas exercise resembled the Jericho Wall blueprint. Her concerns were dismissed by a superior.

Corn: That’s the point where “they hid everything” becomes misleading. Some of it was hidden. Some was visible and interpreted incorrectly.

Herman: Exactly. Concealment and misassessment worked together. An organization doesn’t have to make every clue disappear if its opponent has a framework that explains those clues away. Israeli assessments placed substantial weight on deterrence, Hamas’s governing responsibilities, and its apparent interest in economic concessions.

Corn: Governing Gaza was supposed to make Hamas cautious. Instead, people mistook a constraint for a guarantee.

Herman: Yes, although I’d push back slightly on making economic policy itself sound foolish. Permits and improved living conditions can affect incentives. The failure was treating those incentives as proof that leadership wouldn’t choose a catastrophic war. Leaders can value military or ideological objectives above the welfare of the population they govern.

Corn: I accept that distinction. “They have something to lose” is analysis. “Therefore they won’t do it” is a bet. And the people placing the bet weren’t the only people exposed to the loss.

Herman: On internal secrecy, the broad picture in reporting is a small leadership circle controlling the operation, with information distributed downward late. Yahya Sinwar and military commander Mohammed Deif were central figures. Marwan Issa is also widely identified as a key military leader. But a precise, verified list of everyone who knew the complete plan isn’t public.

Corn: Nor should we pretend “Hamas knew” is a useful answer by itself. Hamas has political officials, military commanders, local operatives, administrators, and people abroad. Membership doesn’t mean a shared view of the command room.

Herman: Quite. Reporting indicated that some political figures outside Gaza were not told the detailed plan in advance. And early reporting described fighters receiving their specific assignments only close to the operation. The exact accounts differ, so I wouldn’t build a minute-by-minute sequence from them. The consistent point is unequal access to information.

Corn: What about the reports of couriers and avoiding electronic communications? They’ve acquired an almost magical quality. As if a handwritten note defeats the entire Israeli intelligence apparatus.

Herman: It doesn’t. Reputable reporting has described reliance on face-to-face meetings, couriers, and less exposed communications. But the detailed internal communications history remains incomplete. The defensible conclusion is that Hamas was acutely aware of Israeli interception and penetration, not that we know every channel it used or that any channel was invulnerable.

Corn: Paper is not invisibility. It’s paper.

Herman: And some of the paper ended up in Israeli hands. Which rather proves the point. Hamas also has a long history of counterintelligence and pursuing suspected collaborators. That environment encourages restricted disclosure and distrust. But it carries costs: slower coordination, misunderstandings, and leadership receiving only what subordinates think is safe to say.

Corn: I’m glad you mentioned costs. These stories can accidentally make secrecy sound like an elegant management technique. In practice, a paranoid organization is full of frightened people and imperfect information. We’re explaining how something happened, not admiring an immaculate machine.

Herman: Absolutely. October seventh also involved chaos, communications failures, groups acting beyond a single tightly controlled sequence, and later entrants crossing through openings. Initial coordination and subsequent disorder can coexist. The scale of the disaster doesn’t mean every event was the product of flawless control.

Corn: Now the international circle. When people hear “Iran backed Hamas,” they often skip directly to “Iran knew the date.” What can we actually say?

Herman: Iranian funding, weapons assistance, and training support to Hamas are well established. Advance knowledge of this particular operation is a separate question. Early stories offered conflicting accounts. Public American assessments shortly afterward said there wasn’t evidence establishing that Iran directed the attack or knew its precise timing, and some intelligence reportedly suggested surprise among senior Iranian officials.

Corn: And those captured meeting records complicate “nobody outside knew anything.”

Herman: They do. The Times reported that Hamas sought Iranian and Hezbollah participation, including through contact with an Iranian official in twenty twenty-three. That supports awareness among some outsiders of a proposed major undertaking. It doesn’t by itself establish that Iran’s leadership or Hezbollah’s leadership received the final date and approved the actual operation as executed.

Corn: So “supported the organization,” “discussed an offensive,” and “had Saturday’s schedule” are three different claims. People keep stapling them together.

Herman: They do. There were also conflicting statements from participants afterward, each with reasons to exaggerate influence or deny responsibility. I’m not sure the complete external notification chain is publicly reconstructable. I would leave that uncertain rather than appoint a secret mastermind because the story feels tidier with one.

Corn: Let’s go to the part of Daniel’s question that could most easily get mangled: ordinary Gazans. Would they have been surprised?

Herman: Many plainly were, according to contemporaneous interviews and testimony. People described waking to rocket fire, hearing extraordinary reports, and learning through phones, broadcasts, and messages that armed men had entered Israel. But Gaza had more than two million residents. There’s no single emotional or informational experience we can assign to all of them.

Corn: Surprise also has several meanings. You can expect another war, support attacks on Israel, know a militant cousin is training, and still be completely blindsided by the morning, the scale, or what the attackers did.

Herman: Exactly. General anticipation of conflict is not foreknowledge of an operation. A resident who heard Hamas promise to attack Israel had heard something Hamas had said many times. Even a specific rumor about a coming offensive needs scrutiny: when was it recorded, how precise was it, and was it distinguishable beforehand from the rumors that went nowhere?

Corn: The winning lottery ticket always looks prophetic afterward.

Herman: And retrospective testimony is vulnerable to that effect. After a huge event, ambiguous remarks acquire new meanings. Someone remembers a relative saying, “Things will change soon.” Perhaps that relative knew something. Perhaps he was repeating factional bravado. Without a contemporaneous record or corroboration, we can’t confidently choose.

Corn: What about the footage of people crossing into Israel after the initial breach? That’s often presented as proof that this was widely known.

Herman: It proves that additional people crossed once the border had been opened and news was spreading. Some were armed; others appeared unarmed. There is evidence of participation in killings, abductions, and looting by people beyond the initial assault units. But conduct after the opening does not establish knowledge before it.

Corn: That isn’t splitting hairs. It’s the whole question. Joining something at nine doesn’t prove you knew about it at five.

Herman: Correct. And footage can identify acts or particular people when properly verified. It cannot establish the prior knowledge of a whole population. Equally, calling somebody a civilian because he lacks a uniform doesn’t tell you whether he’s participating in hostilities. Appearance, organizational affiliation, prior knowledge, and conduct are separate variables.

Corn: I want to linger there because there are two bad shortcuts. One says everyone seen without a uniform was an innocent bystander. The other says everyone in Gaza must have been in on it because some people joined in. Neither follows from the evidence.

Herman: Agreed. There’s another trap in videos of celebrations. Celebrating killings or hostage-taking is appalling. But even clearly verified celebration is evidence of someone’s reaction after the event, not automatically of advance notice. Moral revulsion doesn’t give us permission to change the tense of the evidence.

Corn: “Change the tense” is exactly it. The question is what people knew before. Not whether we like what some people did afterward.

Herman: And we have to consider what civilian surprise would actually look like in the record. Much of the early coverage focused on Israel, for obvious reasons, and then on the bombardment and humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza. We don’t have a representative, contemporaneous survey asking residents what they knew at six in the morning.

Corn: Nor would an opinion poll months later solve it. “Do you approve?” and “Were you told beforehand?” are not neighboring questions. They’re different rooms.

Herman: Yes. Surveys about support for the attack, or beliefs about what happened during it, tell us about attitudes and information environments. They can’t be repurposed as a measure of operational foreknowledge. That remains true even when a survey result is politically convenient for someone making the claim.

Corn: Is there credible evidence, though, that awareness extended beyond a tiny handful? I don’t want our answer to become “nothing can ever be known,” because the attack involved a lot of preparation.

Herman: There certainly had to be a broader circle with partial knowledge: trainers, intelligence collectors, unit commanders, people preparing equipment, fighters practicing tasks. Other armed factions ultimately participated as well. The question is what each person knew and when. A large support footprint is compatible with a small circle knowing the complete operation.

Corn: So Daniel’s alternative isn’t quite either-or. Ordinary residents could be surprised while hundreds or more people knew some relevant fragment. And a commander could know more than an equipment supplier without knowing the date himself.

Herman: Exactly. Think of knowledge as overlapping circles rather than a line between insiders and everyone else. We can infer some circles from the work required. We cannot infer their precise size or contents without evidence. I’d be wary of anyone producing a confident number for how many people knew the full plan.

Corn: Especially a very small, cinematic number. “Only five men knew” sounds wonderful in a documentary trailer. Five men cannot personally run every rehearsal, inspect every vehicle, and memorize every assignment. What they might uniquely possess is the authority and final schedule.

Herman: That’s the useful correction. Full knowledge can be concentrated while preparation is distributed. And “the date” itself may not have been fixed throughout the planning period. If leaders postponed an earlier launch, someone could genuinely have known about an intended operation in twenty twenty-two without knowing what would happen in October twenty twenty-three.

Corn: That makes a leaked warning tricky too. “They’re preparing a major attack” might be true for a long time. But it isn’t useless. It should alter what an intelligence service considers possible, even if it doesn’t let anyone circle a day.

Herman: Exactly. The absence of a date is not the absence of actionable warning. Israel’s own military and security investigations have acknowledged profound failures in understanding Hamas’s intentions and in responding to the attack. The public record supports criticism of assumptions and readiness without requiring us to believe that every tactical detail was available in advance.

Corn: I think that’s where I land on the apparent miracle of secrecy. It was partly secrecy and partly disbelief. Hamas hid the moment. Israel misread the capability and intent. Those failures multiplied each other.

Herman: I agree, with one reservation: “Israel” can flatten internal disagreement just as “Hamas” can. There were analysts and border observers who raised alarms. Institutions don’t simply know or fail to know. Information has to be heard, interpreted, escalated, and connected to decisions.

Corn: Fair correction. A warning sitting on someone’s desk is not the same as a government preparing for the thing it warns about. The paper has arrived. The belief hasn’t.

Herman: And that brings us back to the forty-page blueprint. The most unsettling part isn’t that every secret stayed secret. It’s that substantial knowledge could exist on the defending side without overturning the prevailing assessment. Intelligence failure can be a failure to believe your own evidence.

Corn: So let’s give Daniel a settled answer. The identifiable operation was prepared over years, with strong public evidence reaching back at least into twenty twenty-two and reporting pointing to intensive work around twenty twenty-one. Earlier attacks and capabilities supplied the groundwork, but don’t prove a decade-long fixed plan.

Herman: Hamas maintained secrecy primarily by separating general preparation from complete operational knowledge and final timing, while exploiting Israeli misjudgments. Some insiders and outside contacts knew pieces. The full distribution remains uncertain. And no, the available evidence does not support saying that ordinary Gazans generally knew what was coming that morning.

Corn: Nor does surprise mean every resident opposed it, or participation afterward mean everyone knew beforehand. Those are separate claims, and they stay separate even when collapsing them would make a more satisfying argument.

Herman: The extraordinary thing was not a secret perfectly hidden from every person. It was an operation whose crucial connections and timing remained concealed or unrecognized long enough to enable a catastrophe.

Corn: The clues existed. So did the wrong explanation.

Herman: Thanks to Daniel for the question, and thanks for listening to My Weird Prompts. I’m Herman Poppleberry.

Corn: And I’m Corn. See you next time.

Corn: Okay, today's prompt is a heavy one, but it's what Daniel sent, so let's get straight to it.
Herman: Yeah, Daniel wants us to go back to October seventh. Not the morning itself, we've done the mechanics of the fence and the cameras, but the before. How long was it in planning, how did they keep it secret, and did ordinary people in Gaza see it coming.
Corn: Planning, secrecy, surprise. The unholy trinity.
Herman: Exactly. And there's actually been a lot learned since, from captured documents, interrogations, Israeli inquiries, reporting by the Times and the Journal and others. It's still incomplete, but we can draw a much clearer timeline than we could in October twenty twenty three.
Corn: So when does the clock start?
Herman: The honest answer is there are two clocks. There's the dream clock and the plan clock. The dream of a mass incursion, take hostages, hold Israeli towns, that's old Hamas doctrine. Mohammed Deif has been talking about it in internal speeches since at least twenty fourteen, after the Gaza war that summer. He kept saying the next war would be on Israeli ground, not just rockets.
Corn: Ambitious for a guy in a wheelchair rumour.
Herman: Well, Deif survived multiple assassination attempts, he was badly injured, but he was still operational commander alongside Yahya Sinwar and Marwan Issa. And by twenty twenty one, that dream turns into paper. That's when Israeli intelligence later said the first detailed draft appears, what became known as the Jericho Wall document.
Corn: Jericho Wall. Subtle.
Herman: It's a forty page Hamas battle plan obtained by Israel in twenty twenty two, published by the New York Times in late twenty twenty three. It lays out in almost boring detail how to smash through the Gaza division. Which cameras to snipe, which bases to overrun, the order of operations, kibbutz by kibbutz. Re'im base, Nahal Oz, the Erez crossing.
Corn: And Israel read it and yawned.
Herman: Pretty much. Officers in the Gaza Division and in Unit eighty two hundred read it, and the assessment was, yeah, this is aspirational. Like Hamas wants to do this but lacks the capability. One officer reportedly called it a fantasy scenario. So it wasn't ignored exactly, it was filed as enemy ambition rather than enemy intention.
Corn: Famous last filing.
Herman: Right. But here's the key shift we've learned. After May twenty twenty one, after the eleven day war Israel called Operation Guardian of the Walls, Sinwar and Deif decide to actually build toward it. Israeli interrogations of captured Nukhba commanders and documents seized in Gaza in twenty twenty four point to summer twenty twenty one as the real start. That's two years and change before the attack.
Corn: Two years to plan a morning.
Herman: Two years to plan about six hours that changed everything. And they spent it very methodically. First, they created a general plan, then they broke it into compartmented pieces so almost nobody saw the whole thing.
Corn: So how small was the inner circle?
Herman: Tiny. This is one of the clearest findings. The full knowledge group appears to have been maybe five to seven people for most of that period. Sinwar in Gaza, Deif as military chief, Issa as his deputy, maybe Ayman Nofal, maybe a couple of battalion level planners for mapping. Even the Hamas political leadership outside Gaza, Ismail Haniyeh in Doha, Saleh al Arouri in Beirut, seem to have been kept in the dark until very late.
Corn: Your boss doesn't know you're invading.
Herman: I'm not sure about this part, but the evidence suggests Haniyeh was informed only days before, maybe hours. There are intercepted calls and Israeli assessments saying the outside leadership was surprised by the timing and scale. Which tells you how paranoid the Gaza leadership was, even of their own movement.
Corn: Trust no one, especially coworkers.
Herman: And especially because Israel had thoroughly penetrated Hamas communications in the past. Assassinations in the two thousands and twenty tens relied on informants and phone tracking. Sinwar in particular was obsessed with this. He'd spent twenty two years in Israeli prison, learned Hebrew, studied Israeli intelligence failures, studied how Israel recruits collaborators. He assumed every phone was tapped, every meeting could leak.
Corn: Reasonable assumption.
Herman: So they went radically low tech. According to captured operatives, top level discussions were face to face, no phones, no written minutes, often in tunnels. Orders went down on paper couriers. Units were trained on a need to know slice. One group trained only on drones, another only on paragliders, another only on breaching a replica fence, without being told when or how they'd combine.
Corn: Like rehearsing a play without the ending.
Herman: Perfect analogy. And they built at least six full scale mock Israeli bases in Gaza, full size, with the same guard towers, the same fences, the same communications rooms as Nahal Oz and others. Satellite imagery later showed these sites. Israeli analysts saw them being built in twenty twenty two and twenty twenty three and thought, oh, training propaganda.
Corn: Propaganda with live ammo.
Herman: They held at least four large scale public exercises, the Strong Pillar drills in twenty twenty two and twenty twenty three, where they practiced kidnapping soldiers, storming settlements, driving pickup trucks through breaches. They posted videos themselves. And Israel watched and concluded it was theater to impress the base.
Corn: Best camouflage is posting it.
Herman: That's the deception half, and it's brilliant in a dark way. Sinwar ran a parallel political deception. From late twenty twenty one onward, Hamas signaled it wanted calm. It stayed out of the August twenty twenty two fight between Israel and Islamic Jihad, and again in May twenty twenty three. Israel read that as deterrence working. Hamas is focused on governing, on salaries, on work permits.
Corn: Eighteen thousand work permits will mellow anyone.
Herman: That's the number, around eighteen thousand Gazans allowed to work in Israel by September twenty twenty three, bringing in millions of shekels a day. Israeli policy under successive governments was basically buy quiet with economics. Sinwar played along, sent messages through Qatar and Egypt and the UN that we want more permits, more aid, keep the money flowing. Meanwhile he's moving funds and explosives for the attack.
Corn: The long con with pay stubs.
Herman: And the Israelis bought it. The Gaza Division was thinned out. Troops moved to the West Bank to deal with unrest there around Huwara and Jenin. The border relied more on the smart fence, remote cameras, sensors, automated machine guns, with fewer soldiers actually watching. Hamas studied the shift patterns, knew that on Jewish holidays manning would be lowest.
Corn: Which is why October seventh.
Herman: Simchat Torah, a Saturday, early morning, fog in some sectors. A perfect storm. But back to compartmentalization, how do you train thousands without leaking. The answer is you tell the thousands almost nothing until the night before.
Corn: Thousands knew nothing?
Herman: The assault force was about three thousand Nukhba and other Hamas fighters in the first wave, plus later Islamic Jihad and others. Most of them, according to interrogations, were told they were going to another drill on October sixth. They were ordered to gather, hand in phones, sleep with gear. Only commanders opened sealed envelopes around three or four in the morning on October seventh with real targets and maps.
Corn: Surprise party, worst kind.
Herman: Some lower fighters said they only learned they were going into Israel when the bulldozers hit the fence at six thirty in the morning. They'd been told for months that breaching the fence was defensive training, to prevent an Israeli invasion. That level of discipline over two years in a place as leaky and desperate as Gaza is extraordinary.
Corn: Or terrifying.
Herman: Both. And they enforced it brutally. Hamas internal security, the General Security apparatus, executed suspected collaborators during that period, restricted movement near training sites, compartmented rocket and drone workshops. They even used deception within deception, letting rumors circulate about a tunnel invasion or a limited raid so if Israel heard chatter it would misjudge scale.
Corn: So did Israel hear chatter?
Herman: They heard a lot, and that's the tragedy we've learned more about since. Female spotters at Nahal Oz, the tatzpitaniyot, reported for months in twenty twenty three that they saw rehearsals, new holes in the fence being probed, drones testing camera blind spots, men on motorbikes timing response. They sent warnings up the chain in July, August, September.
Corn: Cassandras in headsets.
Herman: And there were Unit eighty two hundred warnings, including one analyst who flagged in the summer that Hamas's pattern matched Jericho Wall, and a warning in late September about a major drill that looked like preparation. The Nova festival extension, the decision to keep that party going near Re'im with thousands of young people despite security concerns, that's part of the Israeli inquiries too.
Corn: Hindsight is generously cruel.
Herman: It is, but the inquiries show it wasn't just hindsight. The system was primed to dismiss. The prevailing concept, the kontzeptzia, was Hamas is deterred, Hamas wants money, a big ground invasion is beyond them. So every signal got reinterpreted. Drones near the fence, oh they're testing us but won't act. Training videos, oh it's morale.
Corn: If all you have is deterrence, everything looks deterred.
Herman: Exactly. And Hamas actively fed that. In the weeks before, they staged violent protests at the fence then called them off, as if responding to Qatari pressure. They gave Israel the feeling it still had levers. Sinwar reportedly told mediators in September, we don't want escalation. Four days before the attack, Israel actually increased the work permit quota.
Corn: Ouch.
Herman: Yeah. Now your third question, what did ordinary Gazans know. This is where it gets complicated and where I think early coverage oversimplified.
Corn: Go on.
Herman: Were ordinary families told the date and hour? No. There's no evidence of that. Gaza has two point two million people, you can't tell them all and keep surprise. Most people woke up on October seventh to rockets and rumors, confused. Many learned what was happening from Telegram videos of fighters in Sderot and Ofakim.
Corn: So total surprise?
Herman: For most, yes in terms of timing. But did they know something big was eventual? That's different. And here the answer seems to be, many suspected Hamas was building toward a major confrontation, just not this form. You lived next to those mock bases. You saw paragliders training over the beach at dawn, which is weird because Gaza is tiny and paragliders are loud. You saw tunnels being dug, rockets moved at night. Fishermen, farmers near the border, they talked.
Corn: Hard to hide a paraglider.
Herman: Really hard when I'm on one, but Hamas managed by normalizing it as routine resistance training. And crucially, Hamas's own propaganda for years promised a liberation battle, incursion, prisoners to trade. Kids in summer camps did kidnapping roleplay. Imams preached about Al Aqsa being in danger. So the idea of an attack wasn't alien, but the scale, going house to house in twenty plus towns, taking two hundred fifty one hostages to Gaza, killing around twelve hundred people in a day, that was beyond what almost anyone imagined.
Corn: Expecting a skirmish, got a war.
Herman: And then there's the second wave, which tells us a lot. Around nine or ten in the morning, after the fence was breached in about thirty places along forty miles, ordinary Gazans, hundreds, maybe over a thousand, poured through on foot, on bikes, in cars. Some were organized Hamas auxiliaries, but many appear to have been civilians who saw an opening to loot, to steal tractors, TVs, to kidnap. Israeli video and later trials show unarmed men grabbing people at Be'eri and Nir Oz.
Corn: Opportunism at gunpoint.
Herman: That's the disturbing part. It suggests awareness spread incredibly fast that morning. By eight am WhatsApp and mosque loudspeakers in border areas like Shujaiya and Rafah were buzzing, the border is open, go in. So surprise lasted hours, not days. And that second wave committed many of the atrocities and kidnappings, which made the event even harder to control or reverse.
Corn: So compartmentalized at the top, porous at the bottom after go time.
Herman: Exactly. And we've learned from seized phones and interrogations that Hamas commanders anticipated this and in some cases encouraged it, to overwhelm Israeli response, to create chaos, to bring back more hostages to use as bargaining chips. Deif's recorded message that morning calling on everyone to join, Palestinians in the West Bank and beyond, was part of triggering that.
Corn: Did Iran know? Everyone asks.
Herman: I'm not sure about this part, but here's what reporting says so far. There were meetings in Beirut and Tehran in summer twenty twenty three with Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps officials and Hezbollah, where Hamas leaders discussed broad coordination. Wall Street Journal reported Iranian green light claims, but US and Israeli intelligence later said no direct evidence Iran knew the date or ordered it. More like Iran funded and trained generally, probably knew something was brewing, but didn't run the operation.
Corn: Funding without calendar access.
Herman: That's a good way to put it. Same with Hezbollah. They were surprised on October seventh and took days to decide to open limited fire on October eighth. If this was a coordinated regional plan with a start date, Hezbollah's response was oddly slow.
Corn: So Hamas went solo to keep the secret.
Herman: Solo is the point. Sinwar wanted Palestinian ownership, and secrecy required cutting out even allies. One captured document from early twenty twenty three, if authentic, talks explicitly about avoiding informing regional partners to prevent leaks to Israel. That fits the personality. Control everything, tell no one.
Corn: How did they pay for two years without noticing?
Herman: Another thing we've learned. Money moved through crypto, through Turkish and Lebanese exchanges, through Qatari cash for salaries that freed up other funds, through taxes on smuggling. Not huge sums by state standards, tens of millions, but enough for AKs, RPGs, drones bought commercially and modified, paragliders bought as sports gear, concrete for tunnels. Much of it dual use, invisible in a blockaded economy.
Corn: Sports gear with grenades.
Herman: And they disabled observation the morning of in a way that shows long study. At six thirty am, first a massive rocket barrage, over four thousand rockets in the first hours by Israeli counts, to force soldiers into shelters. Simultaneously, commercial drones dropped explosives on remote controlled machine gun towers and cameras. Snipers shot out the observation balloons and fiber nodes. Bulldozers and explosives opened the fence. It was straight from Jericho Wall, almost to the minute.
Corn: Practice makes massacre.
Herman: Yeah. That's blunt but accurate. They rehearsed that sequence for at least a year. Captured GoPro footage shows units calling out code words for each Israeli position. They knew the radio frequencies, the response time from Re'im base was supposed to be minutes, they planned to block the roads with burning tires to delay reinforcements.
Corn: They knew the commute.
Herman: They did. Former workers with permits had mapped towns. Interrogated fighters carried hand drawn maps of kibbutz dining halls, safe rooms, where the elderly lived. That mapping likely took the full two years, built slowly from open sources, drone footage, and human observation.
Corn: So back to Daniel's question. From first seeds to execution?
Herman: I'd answer it like this. Ideological seed, twenty fourteen to twenty eighteen, Deif and Sinwar talking about taking the fight across. Operational seed, May twenty twenty one war, decision to build. Detailed planning, late twenty twenty one through twenty twenty two, Jericho Wall drafted, mockups built, money moved. Intensive training and deception, twenty twenty two through September twenty twenty three. Final operational order, late September, with only a handful knowing the October seventh date until October sixth.
Corn: Two years of building, two days of telling.
Herman: And that ratio is why it worked. Israel was looking for a signature, tanks massing, phones lighting up. Hamas gave them the opposite, silence at the top, routine noise at the bottom.
Corn: So ordinary Gazans taken by surprise?
Herman: Overwhelmingly yes on timing, no on the general direction. People knew Hamas was preparing something violent, they just didn't know it would be a full scale invasion that would bring total war back on them. Many of the interviews since, with displaced families in Rafah and Deir al Balah, say the same thing. We woke up to celebration and by noon we were terrified of the response.
Corn: Celebration to terror by lunch.
Herman: And some knew more. Hamas families, tunnel workers, Nukhba relatives, people near training sites in Khan Younis, they surely knew their sons were doing something unusual in late September, disappearing for days, phones confiscated. But knowing your son is training is not knowing he's going to attack Sderot on Saturday.
Corn: There's a gap between unease and warning.
Herman: That's the gap Israel also lived in. Everyone felt unease, no one converted it to warning. Which raises the hardest lesson we've learned since. Compartmentalization doesn't require high tech. It requires patience and a willingness to let even your own people be surprised.
Corn: And to sacrifice them after.
Herman: That's the frank part we have to say. Sinwar and Deif knew Israel's response would devastate Gaza. Captured writings show they expected a major bombing campaign, displacement, thousands dead, and considered it a necessary cost to shatter the status quo and force a prisoner exchange and global attention. Whether ordinary Gazans would have consented if asked was never considered because they were never asked.
Corn: Consent wasn't in the envelope.
Herman: No. And that's why the surprise matters morally, not just operationally. This wasn't a national decision debated. It was a small cabal gambling with two million lives plus Israeli civilian lives, using secrecy not just against Israel but against their own population and even their own political leaders.
Corn: Small room, big fire.
Herman: I keep coming back to those female observers at Nahal Oz. Nineteen and twenty year olds, watching screens twelve hours a day, logging every training run, begging officers to listen. Some of them were killed in that first hour at their posts. They saw the preparation because they stared at it daily. The system above them couldn't imagine what they were seeing because it had decided Hamas thought differently.
Corn: They stared, the bosses blinked.
Herman: If there's a positive learning, it's that Israel and others now study this as a textbook case of strategic surprise despite tactical warning. Like Yom Kippur in nineteen seventy three, fifty years almost to the day before. Plenty of signals, correct enemy plan in hand, but a concept that filtered it out, plus an enemy that understood that concept and fed it.
Corn: Fifty years, same lesson, new drones.
Herman: And the deception keeps echoing. Even now, debates about who knew what when, whether the outside leadership approved, whether documents are complete, are clouded because Hamas wanted multiple stories. They wanted Israel to think they were deterred, Gazans to think they were governing, fighters to think they were drilling, allies to think they were coordinating, when in fact only three men held the full picture.
Corn: Three men, thirty breaches.
Herman: That's the arithmetic. So to answer Daniel directly, yes, planning was at least two years in the making with roots going back a decade. Yes, compartmentalization was extreme and deliberate, low tech, face to face, need to know training, sealed orders at the last night. And yes, ordinary Gazans were overwhelmingly surprised on the morning, even if many had sensed a storm coming and hundreds joined once the fence fell.
Corn: So they hid the when, flaunted the what, and let the why sort itself out.
Herman: Better than I could put it. They hid the when so well that even their own movement didn't know, they flaunted the what as propaganda so Israel dismissed it, and the why, Al Aqsa, prisoners, breaking the siege, was broadcast openly for anyone to hear but not to date.
Corn: Creepy competence.
Herman: Competence in execution, catastrophe in consequence. The operation succeeded tactically beyond their own expectations, they expected to get fewer hostages and be pushed back faster, and then it unleashed exactly what you'd expect from invading towns and livestreaming murder. No exit plan beyond hold hostages and negotiate from tunnels.
Corn: No envelope for day two.
Herman: None found so far. Captured plans detail hour one through hour six in obsessive detail, then get vague. Hold positions, take captives to Gaza, wait for Israel to mobilize, drag them into Gaza City. It's operational brilliance married to strategic nihilism.
Corn: Win the morning, lose the years.
Herman: Which is where we'll leave it for today. It's grim material, but Daniel asked what we've learned, and I think we've learned that surprise isn't about doing the invisible thing. It's about doing the visible thing for so long that no one believes you'll actually do it.
Corn: Familiarity breeds contempt, then breach.
Herman: Thanks for listening everyone. If you have a prompt, send it in, Daniel will pass it along. And we'll argue about it next time.
Corn: Even the heavy ones. Especially the heavy ones.

Corn: Herman, Daniel wants us back on October seventh, and not on the breach itself. He already heard that episode. He wants the years before the morning: when the first seeds were planted, how a group that assumes Israeli ears are everywhere kept the real plan in a very small box, and whether ordinary Gazans woke up as surprised as the rest of us.

Herman: That is the harder question, and the one the public record has actually filled in since the atrocity. The short version, which I want to complicate, is that the idea was old, the detailed concept was written down well before anyone in Tel Aviv took it seriously, and the date itself was held by a handful of men until the last hours. Ordinary people in Gaza had seen pieces. Very few of them had seen the whole thing.

Corn: Start with the seeds, then. Not the week of.

Herman: The military wing of Hamas had been chewing on a mass breach of the Gaza perimeter for years. This was not a mood that arrived in September of twenty twenty-three. Yahya Sinwar came out of Israeli prisons in the twenty eleven Shalit exchange already obsessed with a prisoner-release operation on a scale that would dwarf that deal. Mohammed Deif, who ran the Qassam Brigades and had survived more assassination attempts than most people have had dental appointments, had spent the better part of a decade treating the fence as a problem to be solved rather than a fact of life. I am not sure anyone outside their circle can date the first serious conversation. What we can date is the document.

Corn: Jericho Wall.

Herman: Jericho Wall. Israeli intelligence obtained a Hamas battle plan, roughly forty pages in some accounts, more than a year before the attack. The New York Times and others reported that it laid out a rocket barrage, drones against observation posts, breaches at multiple points, and a push into communities and bases. It was circulated inside the Israeli system in twenty twenty-two. A unit analyst flagged it as looking less like fantasy and closer to a real concept. Senior officers treated it as aspirational. Too big. Hamas did not have the capacity, or would not risk the response.

Corn: The plan was sitting in the inbox, labeled too ambitious to be a plan.

Herman: That is the cruel joke of the intelligence failure, and it matters for Daniel's question. The seeds were not hidden from Israel in the sense of never having been written down. They were misread. A long planning horizon actually helped the misreading. If you have watched an enemy drill the same stunt for years, the drill becomes weather.

Corn: How far back do the drills go, in what we can actually point to?

Herman: Visible training accelerated through twenty twenty-two and twenty twenty-three. Militants practiced on mock Israeli settlements inside Gaza. There is footage, some of it Hamas's own propaganda, of fighters breaching replica fences, clearing rooms, landing paragliders. Israeli lookouts and the media both saw versions of this. A widely discussed video from the autumn of twenty twenty-two showed something very close to the later method. The Israel Defense Forces noticed. The assessment, repeated in the inquiries afterward, was that Hamas was training for a limited raid or performing for its own public, not preparing to throw the whole military wing across the border on one morning.

Corn: So the organization was hiding the operation in plain sight by calling it practice.

Herman: Partly. And that is a classic compartment, though I want to be careful not to turn this into a manual. At the level of what investigators have pieced together, Hamas did not tell thousands of fighters, years out, "on this Saturday we erase the fence." They built skills in separate lanes. One group learns to fly a cheap quadcopter. Another rehearses a breach on a fake kibbutz that everyone in the neighborhood can see. A third stockpiles rockets. Each lane has an innocent-enough cover story inside a group that is already, openly, at war with Israel in its own telling. The thing that turns lanes into an operation is the date, the simultaneous order, and the knowledge that the other lanes exist and will move together. That last piece stayed upstairs.

Corn: Who was upstairs?

Herman: The names that keep coming back from Israeli assessments, Hamas statements, and the journalism since are Deif, Sinwar, and Marwan Issa, Deif's deputy, sometimes called the shadow man, killed later in the war. A small military council around them. Political figures in the Hamas leadership, including people in Doha, appear to have been cut out of the timing. Ismail Haniyeh's circle has been reported as surprised by the scale, even if nobody in that leadership can claim ignorance that the military wing wanted a huge operation someday. Sinwar ran Gaza. Deif ran the brigades. The useful split, for their purposes, was that the men with the political microphones were not the men with the clock.

Corn: Permanently wary of Israeli infiltration. That is Daniel's phrase, and it is not paranoia. Israel had spent years recruiting inside Gaza, running cyber collection, killing commanders with very specific intelligence. How do you plan something this large in that environment without the date leaking?

Herman: You assume every phone is a microphone, and you behave accordingly. What has come out, from IDF briefings, from captured documents described to reporters, and from interviews with officials who have seen the after-action material, is a few organizational habits rather than a clever gadget. One: the full concept lived on paper and in heads, not in a group chat. Two: the circle that knew the concept was not the circle that knew the day. Three: orders moved late, face to face or by courier, through commanders who themselves were only told what their sector needed. Four: the final briefing for a lot of the actual gunmen was measured in hours, not weeks.

Corn: Hours. That is the part I keep turning over. You cannot move that many people on hours of notice unless the muscle memory is already there.

Herman: Exactly. That is why the long runway and the short notice are the same plan, not two plans. Years to train the lanes and to make the training boring to the other side. Months to position rockets, weapons caches, civilian clothes, maps of specific communities. Then a very late expansion of who is allowed to know that this rehearsal is the one that leaves the mock fence and goes to the real one. Israeli and Western reporting after the attack converged on a picture in which many of the battalion-level fighters learned the full scope on the night of October sixth or the morning of the seventh. Some unit commanders knew earlier, on the order of days. The men at the top had known for much longer that a window was being chosen.

Corn: Do we have a harder date than "years" for when they committed, as opposed to when they daydreamed?

Herman: I am not sure about a single commit date, and anyone who offers one is probably smoothing the record. A few anchors are solid enough to say out loud. The Jericho Wall concept was in Israeli hands in twenty twenty-two, which means Hamas had written a detailed version by then, so the serious planning is at least into twenty twenty-one, and almost certainly earlier in outline. Prisoner exchanges and the failure of the twenty twenty-one war to produce a strategic result are part of the political weather Sinwar was reading. Through twenty twenty-three, Israel was consumed with the judicial overhaul fight, reservists were threatening not to show up, and the northern border with Hezbollah was the threat the General Staff preferred to brief. Hamas had also spent two years persuading Israel, with work permits, Qatari cash, and a relative quiet on the Gaza border, that the organization had been domesticated into a governing authority that liked its salary.

Corn: The quiet was the costume.

Herman: The quiet was the compartment that covered everything else. From roughly twenty twenty-one until the morning itself, the Gaza front was the one that did not blow up on schedule. Israeli policy, associated with the belief that Sinwar could be managed, treated economic relief as proof of deterrence. Hamas used the same relief as proof, internally and externally, that it was busy being a municipality. You maintain secrecy in a penetrated society less by magic and more by making the secret look like the thing the enemy already wants to believe.

Corn: What about the foot soldiers. If I am a platoon commander and I am only told the night before, what stops me from deciding this is insane and telling someone?

Herman: Some of them may have thought it was insane. The record we have does not show a leak that reached an Israeli decision-maker in time. A few points are worth holding apart from legend. These were not conscripts pulled off a beach. They were men already inside a clandestine military structure, vetted by years of tunnel work, rocket crews, and internal security that kills suspected collaborators. The late briefing is also a security device aimed at them. A man who knows on Tuesday can boast, or crack, or get arrested, by Friday. A man who is handed a sector, a time, and a rally point after dark has very little interval in which to be turned. Israeli officials have said they later found evidence of standing orders not to discuss the operation even inside the brigades, and of deliberate false stories about the scale, so that a captured fighter or a chatty cousin would describe a raid, not an invasion.

Corn: False stories inside your own force. That is a rough way to run an army.

Herman: It is how you run an army that expects to be riddled with informants. The cost is confusion, fratricide, and fighters who do not understand the political point of what they are doing. All of that showed up on the day. Some units had clear objectives, the military bases, the hostage-taking for a later trade. Others spilled into civilian communities and did what undisciplined men with late, thin orders do. The atrocity was not an accident of poor briefing. Killing civilians and taking hostages was part of the concept in the documents Israel had already seen. But the unevenness of the execution fits a force that was highly trained in pieces and poorly informed as a whole.

Corn: Daniel also asks whether ordinary Gazans were taken by surprise by what they saw that morning.

Herman: I think the honest answer is both, and the "both" is not a dodge. It depends which Gazans, and surprise about what.

Corn: Say it plainly, then.

Herman: Most civilians in Gaza were not in on the date, the hour, or the decision to start a war that would bring the Israeli army in behind the fighters. Journalists who got into the strip in the following weeks, and Gazans who spoke to Arab and Western outlets, repeatedly described the morning the way people describe an earthquake. The rocket barrage was the alarm clock. Neighbors came out because the volume was wrong for a normal exchange of fire. Parents pulled children off the street. A lot of people learned what was happening the same way Israelis did, from their phones, except their phones were showing gunmen in pickup trucks on Israeli roads and a leadership that had not asked them.

Corn: That is one half.

Herman: The other half is that "we had no idea they might do something like this" does not survive the visuals. Mock Israeli towns inside Gaza were not state secrets. Young men in Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad had been drilling in them. Neighbors of training sites knew training sites. The tunnel economy employs people. Families of Qassam fighters are not under the illusion that their sons are in the citrus business. There was a widely shared sense, especially among people close to the factions, that a big operation was a matter of when, and that the military wing talked about the fence as something that would fall. What they did not have, on the evidence we have seen, is a public countdown or a civilian evacuation plan, which tells you something ugly about how the leadership ranked Gazan lives against operational security.

Corn: No warning to their own population, because a warning is a leak.

Herman: And because the strategic point, as Sinwar had framed it for years, was to pull Israel into a war that would also pull in the region, and to do it faster than Israeli intelligence could cycle from disbelief to mobilization. Warning Gaza is warning Israel. So the first morning for a shopkeeper in Khan Younis and the first morning for a family in Nir Oz were both ambushes, of completely different moral kinds. One group was the target. The other was the cover and, as it turned out, the consequence.

Corn: Have we seen evidence that awareness was wider than the "handful of men" story?

Herman: Wider than the handful, narrower than the street. Let me separate layers, because the after-action argument gets sloppy here. Layer one: the authors. Sinwar, Deif, Issa, a military staff. They know the concept and, as the window approaches, the timing. Layer two: brigade and battalion commanders, brought in on a sloping schedule. Some Israeli reporting, including material briefed from interrogations of captured fighters, suggests selected commanders were read in during the final week, with instructions to prepare men without saying why the preparation had suddenly become specific. Layer three: the assault force itself, on the order of a couple of thousand fighters in the first wave. Estimates vary. Figures I trust enough to repeat sit around three thousand armed men crossing or attempting to cross in the opening attack, with more flowing in afterward, including opportunists who were not in the original order of battle. A large share of that first wave got the real order very late. Layer four: adjacent armed groups. Palestinian Islamic Jihad took part. There is decent evidence they were informed late and partially, enough to join, not enough to have shaped the plan. Layer five: everyone else in the strip, two million people, who saw training, heard boasts, lived next to rocket pits, and still did not know that Saturday was the day.

Corn: The boasts are the crack in the compartment, aren't they. Young men talk.

Herman: They do, and some talked. The New York Times, Haaretz, and Israeli television have all reported warnings in the months and even the days before. An Israeli noncommissioned officer in the border observation unit, the lookouts, had been saying for months that the drills looked like a real plan. Egyptian intelligence has said it passed a general warning that something big was coming out of Gaza. On the night of October sixth there were signs the Israeli system itself logged and underweighted: unusual movement, SIM cards lighting up, a briefing inside Gaza that one informant seems to have caught the edge of. None of that is the same as a Gazan public that knew. It is a border that was talkative at the edges, and a headquarters that had already decided the talk was noise.

Corn: I keep coming back to the lookouts, because they are the opposite of a secret. Women on a screen, watching a fence, saying the rehearsal has stopped looking like a rehearsal.

Herman: And being told, in effect, that Hamas was showing off. That misogyny-and-doctrine failure has been documented in the Israeli inquiries. It also answers part of Daniel's compartment question from the other direction. Hamas did not achieve perfect secrecy. They achieved secrecy relative to a threshold. The threshold was an Israeli decision to raise the alert, move a couple of battalions to the fence, and cancel leave on a holiday morning. They never cleared that threshold. A plan can leak in fragments for a year and still be operationally secret if the fragments are each deniable and the enemy has a story that explains them away.

Corn: The story was: they like the Qatari money, they fear the Egyptian-Israeli blockade tightening, Sinwar is a rational gangster.

Herman: And until six twenty-nine in the morning on the seventh, that story had not been falsified by a body count. Deterrence looks like a fact right up until it is a memory. I should plant the time properly. The assault is generally marked from about six thirty, with the rocket barrage a little before and the breaches in the same window. Simchat Torah morning. Holiday manning. A lot of the line units that should have been on the fence were elsewhere, including in the West Bank, because that was where the political temperature was.

Corn: So the compartment on the Hamas side and the preoccupation on the Israeli side were a matched pair.

Herman: Yes. And I do not think that is hindsight dressed up as insight. The inquiries, the IDF's own, the State Comptroller's work as it has emerged in pieces, the press investigations by Ronen Bergman and others, all land on a version of that. Collection was not the main failure. Integration and belief were. Which loops back to how an infiltrated organization plans. You do not need the enemy to know nothing. You need the enemy to know a version that flatters his theory.

Corn: What have we actually learned since, that we did not have in the first month?

Herman: A few things have hardened. First, the timeline. This was a multi-year project with a written operational concept in Israeli hands by twenty twenty-two, not a spasm planned in the summer of twenty twenty-three. The "immediate preparations" Daniel sets aside, the night-before movements, were the last layer, and Israeli intelligence did miss or dismiss some of those too. But the interesting miss is the earlier one.

Corn: Second?

Herman: The split between political and military knowledge looks real, not just a later alibi. Hamas's external leadership could celebrate a victory they had not scheduled. That is useful for them diplomatically and disastrous as a picture of command responsibility, but the compartment itself seems to have held. Third, interrogations and captured materials have supported the late-briefing account. Fighters describing being gathered, handed objectives, and sent, with a clarity that varies wildly by unit. Some knew they were supposed to seize hostages and bring them back into Gaza. The hostage-taking was not improvised by a mob, even if individual cruelties were. The documents Israel had from twenty twenty-two already included taking captives.

Corn: Fourth, the public in Gaza.

Herman: Fourth, and this is where I want to be more careful than the wartime argument usually is. There is evidence of broader ambient awareness that a major attack was imaginable and even expected in militant circles. There is not good evidence of a general public let in on the operation. There is evidence, strong evidence, that once the breaches opened, some civilians followed the fighters through, looted, and in documented cases took part in abuse and kidnapping. Israeli investigations and video from the kibbutzim and the Nova festival site show gunmen who were clearly Qassam or Islamic Jihad, and also people who do not fit a uniformed order of battle. That afternoon diffusion is not the same fact as a pre-dawn conspiracy of the whole strip. Conflating them has been politically convenient on every side.

Corn: Say what each side wants the conflation to do.

Herman: One telling wants every Gazan to have been a secret soldier, so that anything that happens to anyone in Gaza is retroactively precise. The other telling wants a spotless civilian population that had never seen a man with a rifle, so that the factions' strategy of locating the war inside a city does not have to be discussed. Both are false. The population was not the general staff. The general staff also did not ask the population.

Corn: Corn's short version, then. The neighbors knew the orchestra was rehearsing. They did not know the concert was Saturday, and they were not handed a program.

Herman: That is about right. And some of the neighbors were in the orchestra, and some wandered onstage after the curtain and did awful things, and most were in their apartments wondering why the rockets would not stop.

Corn: I want to sit with the security culture a moment longer, because Daniel asked how you maintain compartmentalization when you assume you are penetrated, and I do not want us to skip past the human mechanics.

Herman: The mechanics that have been described by people who have actually looked at the captured material are dull, which is why they worked. Paper maps. Oral orders. A bias against phones for anything that mattered. Commanders who had known each other since the second intifada, so the trust graph was old and small. A habit, built by Deif in particular, of disappearing. The man lived as if assassinated already. You cannot infiltrate a meeting that does not have a location. Issa was nicknamed for being hard to see, and the nickname was operational, not poetic.

Corn: And the training sites did the opposite. They were loud.

Herman: Loud on purpose, or at least tolerated as loud. If the enemy watches your training, and you keep training the same way for a year, his watchers become part of your deception without being recruited. They file the same report until the report is a template. "Subject conducted breach exercise, assessed as routine." The day it is not routine, the sentence is identical and the verb has changed tense.

Corn: There is a point in there about organizations, not just this one. Long preparation is invisible if it rhymes with what you already do.

Herman: Hamas's public identity was already armed struggle, already rockets, already tunnels, already a narrative about prisoners. An operation that is a larger instance of your brand does not look like a new object. Compare that to a group that has never picked up a rifle and suddenly needs a division. They would have had to invent the capability in secret, which is much noisier. Hamas had to hide a decision inside a capability everyone already conceded.

Corn: The decision being: we are willing to trade Gaza for this.

Herman: I think that is the decision Sinwar made, and I think a lot of the people who will live with it did not make it. He had written and spoken for years in a register that treated a huge war as potentially worth it if it broke the status quo, returned prisoners, and reattached the Palestinian issue to the regional agenda. Normalization between Israel and Arab states was moving. The two twenty-two Abraham Accords logic was creeping toward Saudi Arabia. From his chair, a managed quiet was a trap that ended in irrelevance. From a nurse's chair in Rafah, a managed quiet was the condition under which the hospital had power.

Corn: We should not psychologize him into a strategist and everyone else into a prop. Some number of commanders shared the wager.

Herman: They did. The wager was explicit in the concept papers. A shock that kills and captures enough Israelis to force a hostage negotiation, to humiliate the army, and to ignite other fronts. Hezbollah did open a front, the northern one, the next day, though not at the scale Hamas seems to have hoped. The West Bank flickered. Iran's other partners joined on their own calendars later. The regional chain-reaction was partial. The Israeli response was not partial. That is the part of the plan the compartment could not rehearse, because you cannot drill the other side's choices.

Corn: What about the stories that the operation was delayed, that they had wanted an earlier date, Passover or something similar.

Herman: Those circulate, and I would mark them as plausible but not nailed down. Holiday timing is obvious for a force that wants thin manning, and Passover twenty twenty-three has been mentioned in some Israeli media as a window that was considered. I have not seen a captured order that makes me willing to say "they slipped from April to October" as a fact. What I will say is that choosing a Jewish holiday was not an improvisation on the sixth of October. It was the sort of variable a staff writes into a plan that has been alive for years. Simchat Torah, fewer people in uniform, dawn coming up on a country that had been arguing with itself on television all year.

Corn: The judicial crisis as an input to their timing. Do we know they were watching that, or is that our narrative?

Herman: They were watching. Hamas media and Sinwar's own public comments tracked Israeli division. Whether it was decisive, or just comforting, I am less sure. A confident reading says they struck because they thought the army was rotten with protest and refusal. A more cautious reading, which I lean toward, says the crisis was one more reason the quiet would hold in Israeli minds, not the reason the operation existed. The operation existed because the fence was the problem they had set themselves, and twenty twenty-three was a year when the problem looked solvable.

Corn: Let me push on something you said earlier, about false stories told to their own men. If that is right, then some of the attackers were, in a grim sense, also surprised by the mission they were on.

Herman: Surprised by the scale, maybe. Not surprised to be attacking Israel. These were not people handed a fishing rod and told it was a rifle. But yes, interrogations summarized in the Israeli press include fighters who thought they were going after a base, or going to take a position and come home, and who found themselves in a civilian community with orders that expanded as the morning went well by their metrics. Success broke the plan as much as failure would have. When the army did not arrive for hours, men who had been given a sector kept going. That is how you get the long, sick wandering through Be'eri and Kfar Aza, the Nova site, Route two thirty-two, rather than a single sharp raid that snaps back at noon.

Corn: The compartment that protected the secret also guaranteed that, once it started, a lot of armed men would be under-commanded.

Herman: I think that is fair. Deif could not run a real-time campaign from a bunker with the radios off. He had to front-load intent into people and then accept what people do with intent. The intent, documented before the day, included slaughter and abduction. So I do not want "under-commanded" to launder what was commanded. I want it to explain why the day looked chaotic on top of being deliberate.

Corn: Ordinary Gazans watching that on a phone. What did they see, and when?

Herman: By midmorning, Arabic social media and Hamas channels were flooding with footage the attackers themselves were filming. That was a choice, not a leak. Part of the operation was the picture of the operation. Pickup trucks in Sderot, the police station, the fence lying open, bodies. For a Gazan audience the pictures were triumphalist and, for many people who have since spoken, frightening in the same breath. Anyone who could read a map knew the Israeli response would not be a weekend of airstrikes and a ceasefire, which had been the rhythm of twenty fourteen, twenty twenty-one, the smaller rounds. The open fence meant ground forces, and ground forces meant the neighborhoods around the launch sites.

Corn: Did anyone in Gaza try to say so, publicly, that morning?

Herman: A few local journalists and ordinary people posted variations of dread. It was not an organized protest, and it would have been suicidal to stage one in front of the factions on the day of their triumph. Over the following months, as the strips's death toll climbed into the tens of thousands, you do start to hear, in interviews with people who got out through Rafah or who spoke anonymously, a bitter version of Daniel's question. They ask it as an accusation against their own rulers. You knew what this would bring down on us, and you did not tell us, because telling us would have meant telling them.

Corn: That accusation is the civilian answer to the compartment question. The compartment worked. It worked on the people it claimed to represent.

Herman: Yes. And it is worth being exact about what "worked" means. It worked as surprise. It did not work as strategy, if strategy includes the survival of the political project that launched it. Sinwar was killed in twenty twenty-four. Deif was killed. Issa was killed. The brigades were shattered as a maneuver force. The hostages became the center of Israeli politics in a way that prolonged the war rather than ending it on Hamas's terms. Gaza was wrecked. None of that was hidden in a compartment. It was the predictable other half of the plan, and the authors either discounted it or decided it was acceptable.

Corn: I do not think "predictable" means they wanted the destruction. I think it means they rated it an acceptable price and were wrong about the exchange rate.

Herman: That is closer to my view than the cartoon of a death cult with no arithmetic. There was arithmetic. It was bad arithmetic. They looked at twenty fourteen, fifty days, and at Shalit, one soldier for more than a thousand prisoners, and they extrapolated. They did not price an Israeli society that experienced October seventh as a foundational massacre, about twelve hundred people killed, around two hundred and fifty taken, communities erased on the southern border. I am using round figures because the exact counts have been revised at the margins and I would rather be approximately right. The arithmetic assumed a hostage leverage that scaled. It did not scale. It locked.

Corn: Which is a lesson about long planning that I do not hear often enough. A plan refined for years can still be built on a stale model of the enemy.

Herman: The stale model was "Israel is strong against armies and weak against captured boys on television." October seventh produced captured children and old people and corpses, and the television effect ran the other way. A staff that has lived inside its own concept since twenty twenty-one will keep optimizing the concept. It will not volunteer to rerun the political premise. Compartmentalization makes that worse. If only five men can stress-test the idea, and all five already believe it, you do not get a red team. You get a refined mistake.

Corn: Would a wider circle inside Gaza have red-teamed it? I doubt the public gets a vote in that organization. But a wider military circle might have said, we can breach the fence and we cannot survive the month after.

Herman: Some of them may have said it and been ignored. We have hints, from reporting on internal Hamas arguments over the years, that there were factions more interested in governance and quiet, and a military wing that treated governance as camouflage. The camouflage won, because the camouflage was never the purpose. This is where I get uncertain, and I should flag it. I have not seen a clean document that says "commander so-and-so objected in August and was cut out." I have seen a pattern: objections, when they existed, lived in the political layer, and the political layer did not have the clock. So the red team was structurally outside the room.

Corn: Daniel's question about ordinary Gazans has a sharper edge if we ask it about the afternoon, not the dawn. Once the pictures were on every phone, awareness was total. What people did with it was not uniform.

Herman: Right. By noon, ignorance is no longer available as a description. You have families sheltering. You have people celebrating in some streets, which was filmed and is not seriously disputed. You have armed men still coming out of tunnels and through the gaps. You have civilians walking through the breached fence to loot kibbutzim, some of them later prosecuted in Israel, some killed in the return fire, some still unaccounted for in the chaos. Awareness did not produce a single public mood. It produced the moods a terrified, humiliated, tightly policed, heavily armed society produces when the lid comes off: fear, triumph, opportunism, paralysis.

Corn: I am wary of the triumph footage being used as a census.

Herman: So am I. A crowd outside a police station is not two million signatures. It is also not zero. The honest use of that footage is limited and still important. It shows that the operation was intelligible to a wider militant and semi-militant public as a victory worth cheering, which means the ambient story, "one day the fence falls," had been circulating for long enough to be ready. You do not get spontaneous crowds for a concept nobody has ever heard. You get them for a concept that has been sung, preached, and drilled in public until the day it happens is shocking in its reality and familiar in its script.

Corn: So the script was public. The performance date was not.

Herman: That is the cleanest way I have found to answer Daniel. If awareness means "knew there was a military vision of a mass breach, hostage-taking, and a regional war," then awareness ran well beyond the inner circle, into the factions, into families of fighters, into anyone who watched Hamas's own videos in twenty twenty-two. If awareness means "knew it would be this Saturday, at this hour, at this scale, and had a chance to leave the launch areas," then awareness was tiny, and the people who had it chose not to share it with the city they governed.

Corn: What still is not known? I do not want us inventing a neat archive.

Herman: The exact night the date was fixed. Whether there was a go, no-go meeting with a written record, or whether Deif and Sinwar simply stopped postponing. The degree of Iranian knowledge. This one has been fought over in public. American intelligence assessments reported in the press said Tehran was surprised by the timing, even if it had armed, funded, and trained the capability for years. Israeli political rhetoric often said the opposite. I think the capability-versus-timing split is the responsible reading until documents say otherwise. Iran helped build the orchestra. The Saturday downbeat looks locally chosen. Also unknown, in a way that matters: how many mid-level commanders refused, slipped the order, or warned someone. Silence in the record is not proof of universal enthusiasm. It is proof that dissent, if it happened, did not become an Israeli warning.

Corn: And on the Gazan civilian side, we are still working from interviews, not a poll. You cannot poll a war of that intensity and pretend you have a baseline of what people believed on October sixth.

Herman: No. Anyone who gives you a percentage is selling you a mood. What we have are repeated qualitative reports from reporters who do this carefully, plus the physical evidence of no evacuation, plus the propaganda choice to hide the date even from allied militias until late. Those point the same direction. Surprise at the event. No surprise that the men with guns had been preparing to use them.

Corn: I keep thinking about the mock kibbutz. A street of concrete houses in the sand, inside Gaza, built to be practiced on. Neighbors walking past it for months. That image does more work than any org chart.

Herman: It does, because it is the compartment made visible and therefore invisible. A secret that is a building. Children in the area knew the building. Israeli drones knew the building. The building was allowed to become boring. The morning it was copied, at real scale, with real families inside the original, the boredom ended in a way the neighbors could not stop and had not been invited to approve.

Corn: Herman. If we are settling Daniel's prompt rather than orbiting it.

Herman: We should settle it.

Corn: Planning and preparation, in the sense he means, run from at least the early twenty twenties, with roots in Sinwar's post-prison project and Deif's long war on the fence, and with a written plan in Israeli hands in twenty twenty-two. Not weeks. Years. The immediate preparations were the last skin of that fruit, and they were missed too, but they are not the story.

Herman: Compartmentalization was social and temporal more than technological. Small author group. Political leadership off the clock. Skills trained in separable, visible lanes. Cover of routine and of strategic quiet. Date withheld until days for some commanders and hours for many fighters. Internal deception about scale. A standing assumption that every digital channel was hostile. It held well enough. It did not hold perfectly. Fragments reached Egyptian intelligence, Israeli lookouts, and at least one night-before indication. The recipients did not believe the fragments could assemble.

Corn: And ordinary Gazans.

Herman: Taken by surprise by the morning, not by the existence of the ambition. Evidence of wider awareness is real and limited. It is awareness of a direction, not of an order. The order was kept from them on purpose. That is a finding about Hamas, not a consolation about anyone else.

Corn: I think that is the answer. I also think the mock fence is going to sit in my head longer than the org chart. A replica of your neighbor's house, used as a classroom, and the neighbor is the one who is not told when class ends and the real house begins.

Herman: The replica is the whole moral fact of the planning, compressed into concrete. They were willing to spend years teaching men the floor plan of places where families were sleeping, and unwilling to spend a sentence warning the city that would pay for the lesson.

Corn: Daniel asked what we have learned since the atrocity. We have learned that the atrocity had a syllabus. The syllabus was old, partly public, and still deniable, because everyone who could have closed the school had decided the class was theater.

Herman: And the students were told the performance date last, which is the detail that will keep mattering when people try to turn the whole strip into either a conspiracy or an alibi. The syllabus was visible. The call time was not. Both of those can be true, and on the record as it stands, both are.

Corn: That is as far as I am willing to go without pretending we have Sinwar's diary. If a document shows up that moves the commit date or the Iranian timing, we should come back and move with it. Until then, years, a small room, a late order, a surprised city, a surprised country, and a plan that treated both surprises as features.

Herman: Agreed. And the feature was the crime. The planning explains the surprise. It does not dilute what the surprise was for.

Corn: Herman Poppleberry, thank you for not rounding this into a fable.

Herman: Corn, thank you for making me say the layers out loud instead of hiding in "it's complicated." Listeners, if you have a prompt that needs the same treatment, send it to Daniel. We will argue with the record, not with a slogan.

Corn: Until next time.

Herman: Until next time.

Corn: Daniel sent a voice note that sounds like he recorded it while pacing around his basement in the dark.

Herman: He does that when he gets hooked on military doctrine. It is an intense one today. He wants us to look at October seventh, but specifically the timeline behind it. Not the tactical breach at the fence, which we looked at months ago, but the deep clock. When did the idea actually get put on paper, how did a group operating under total digital surveillance keep a secret that big for years, and did anyone on the street in Gaza see the shape of it coming before that Saturday morning?

Corn: The logistical miracle of keeping a mouth shut.

Herman: That really is the core paradox of it. You are talking about the Gaza Strip, forty-one kilometers long, roughly ten kilometers wide. It is arguably the most intensively monitored rectangle of dirt on the planet. Unit eight-two-hundred listening to every phone call, Shin Bet running human informant networks built over decades, overhead drones, thermal imaging, automated sensor towers. And yet, an operation involving thousands of people was planned right under that nose.

Corn: So where does the timeline actually start? Because after the attack, the immediate take was that this was cooked up after the May twenty-twenty-one clashes.

Herman: Right, Operation Guardian of the Walls. That was the eleven-day conflict where Hamas fired thousands of rockets and Israel hit back hard from the air. A lot of early analysis said, look, Hamas felt emboldened by their performance there, Yahya Sinwar realised long-range rocketry had diminishing returns, and they pivoted to a ground invasion. But the documents recovered by the Israel Defense Forces inside Gaza over the last year, especially from the tunnels under Khan Younis, push that date back significantly.

Corn: How far back?

Herman: The minutes of Hamas military council meetings recovered by the IDF point to late twenty-nineteen, or at the very least early twenty-twenty. There is a memo from Sinwar and Mohammed Deif outlining what they called the Big Project. That was their literal internal codename for it.

Corn: The Big Project. Modest.

Herman: Very bureaucratic, actually. The documents show that by twenty-twenty, the conceptual leap had already occurred. For years, Hamas doctrine was defensive deterrence mixed with asymmetric harassment. You dig cross-border tunnels, you pop up, you grab a soldier like Gilad Shalit in two thousand and six, and you trade him for a thousand prisoners. Or you fire rockets to force concessions on border crossings and work permits. The Big Project abandoned that logic entirely. It was not designed to kidnap one soldier to bargain with. It was designed as a combined-arms systemic collapse of the IDF Southern Command.

Corn: That is an enormous doctrinal shift for an irregular militia. You do not just wake up on a Tuesday and decide you are the Wehrmacht sweeping through Sedan.

Herman: Exactly. And the captured records reveal that Sinwar was actively lobbying the leadership in Qatar and Iranian officials in Beirut and Tehran as early as twenty-twenty-one, saying, we are preparing an event that will change the regional architecture. Now, Iran and Hezbollah seem to have kept their distance from the operational specifics, which we can get into, but the seed was planted five years ago. Think about that. That means while Israel was congratulating itself on finishing the underground sensory barrier in late twenty-twenty-one, that massive concrete wall meant to kill the cross-border tunnel threat, Hamas had already moved on. They looked at the wall and said, fine, we will go over and through it instead.

Corn: Which brings us to the second part of Daniel's prompt. Compartmentalization. If you start planning an army-level offensive in twenty-twenty, you have a five-year window for someone to get chatty on WhatsApp.

Herman: Or just get loose with a cousin. The human intelligence fabric Shin Bet ran in Gaza was notoriously dense. If you had cancer and needed an exit permit to get treated in Jerusalem, Shin Bet talked to you. If you were a merchant bringing in goods, they talked to you. If you were an unhappy mid-level Hamas fighter with gambling debts or family rivalries, they found you. So how did Hamas stop the leak?

Corn: By going completely sixteenth century.
