Herman: Literally sixteenth century. The operational core was restricted to a microscopic cabal. We are talking about maybe five or six men. Yahya Sinwar, his brother Mohammed Sinwar, Mohammed Deif, Marwan Issa, and possibly Rawhi Mushtaha. Even Ismail Haniyeh and the political bureau sitting in air-conditioned suites in Doha were largely kept in the dark about the timing and the scale.

Corn: Imagine being the political leader of an organization and finding out your military wing started a regional war by watching Al Jazeera over breakfast.

Herman: That appears to be pretty close to what happened. The political leadership knew an operation was being planned in the abstract, because they were being asked to secure funding and diplomatic cover. But the date, the targets, the operational details? Zero. The internal documents show that Sinwar treated his own political bureau as an operational security hazard. Why? Because political figures travel. They go to Istanbul, they go to Cairo, they use cellphones, their aides carry iPhones. Any one of those phones could be infected with Pegasus or monitored by regional intelligence agencies that share data with Israel.

Corn: If your phone is a microphone, the only secure device is no device.

Herman: And that was the iron rule. The operational orders inside the tunnel complexes were delivered by hand. Handwritten notes, folded, sealed, carried by trusted family couriers or deeply vetted personal guards who had no idea what was written on the paper. In the deep tunnels under Khan Younis and Gaza City, Hamas installed hardwired, closed-circuit telephone lines. Analogue lines. No connection to the wider Palestinian telecommunications grid, no internet protocol, no cellular signals leaking into the air for Israeli listening posts on Mount Hermon or the blimps over the border to suck up.

Corn: Very low tech. Very slow. Very effective.

Herman: It turns Israel's greatest strength into a completely useless paperweight. Israel spends billions on signals intelligence. Unit eight-two-hundred is celebrated worldwide as a tech incubator disguised as a spy agency. They can intercept a whisper from an antenna ten miles away. But if two men sit in a concrete room sixty feet underground and write on a yellow legal pad, the billions of dollars do nothing.

Corn: A five-cent pencil beats an algorithmic signal interceptor.

Herman: Every single day of the week, if you have the discipline to stick to it. And the discipline was enforced brutally. Anyone suspected of leaking was not just interrogated; they were executed and their families disgraced. But compartmentalization was not just about hiding the plan from Israeli ears. It was about hiding the plan from the very soldiers who were going to carry it out.

Corn: This is the part that always fascinates me. You need thousands of fighters to storm twenty-two military bases and kibbutzim. You cannot give them a handwritten note five minutes before the fence blows up and say, by the way, go capture a tank. They had to practice.

Herman: They did practice. In broad daylight. That is the crazy brilliance of the deception plan. They built mock Israeli kibbutzim, complete with watchtowers, fake gates, and replica Merkava tanks made of wood and sheet metal. And they ran assault drills on them for eighteen months right in front of the Israeli border towers.

Corn: The ultimate hiding spot. The open field.

Herman: Exactly! The young female spotters, the tatzpitaniyot of the IDF border units, saw this every single week. They wrote urgent reports up the chain of command saying, the Nukhba forces, Hamas's elite commandos, are practicing storming guard towers, they are practicing taking hostages, they are practicing neutralizing automated machine-gun nests. And what did Israeli military intelligence, Aman, say?

Corn: Boys will be boys. They are just putting on a show for the donors.

Herman: Literally that. They dismissed it as bluster, what they called mufalsim, theatrics. The intelligence consensus in Tel Aviv was that Hamas was deterred. The doctrine was that Hamas wanted economic stability, that the twenty thousand work permits Israel was issuing for Gazans to work inside Israel were keeping the peace, and that these military exercises were just psychological posturing to keep their own domestic base happy. Hamas knew that was the Israeli mindset, so they leaned into it. They used the Israeli arrogance as their primary camouflage.

Corn: It is the purloined letter principle. If you want to train three thousand men to breach a border, do not hide them in a basement. Put them in the sun, film them, put it on TikTok, and let the other guy convince himself it is just content.

Herman: And keep the fighters themselves stupid about the actual objective. The captured Nukhba fighters who were interrogated after October seventh gave remarkably consistent testimonies on this point. They knew they were training for a large-scale raid. They had been practicing breaching fences, riding motorbikes in tight formations, and clearing rooms. But they were told these were generic contingency drills.

Corn: When did they actually get told it was real?

Herman: Most of them were told less than twelve hours before the zero hour. On Friday evening, October sixth, local commanders called their units to their local mosques or designated assembly points for evening prayers. No phones allowed. Then they were moved into the staging areas and tunnel exits near the border. It was only around three or four in the morning on October seventh that the company commanders opened sealed envelopes and read out the specific assignments. You, team A, your job is the Re'im military base. You, team B, your job is Kibbutz Be'eri. Here are your maps. Here are your aerial photographs of the layout. Go.

Corn: Imagine sitting in a tunnel at four in the morning, finding out you have two hours before you are expected to assault a fortified military headquarters with an AK-forty-seven and an RPG.

Herman: The panic and the adrenaline must have been off the charts. But because the training was modular, it worked. They did not need to know the master strategy. Team B did not need to know what Team F was doing twenty miles north. They just had to execute the specific drill they had practiced fifty times on the wooden mock-up: blow the gate, suppress the guard post, enter the living quarters. The modularity was the security. If one guy got captured on Friday night because he wandered off or had an attack of conscience, he could only betray his immediate cell's assembly point. He did not know the invasion plan because he had never seen it.

Corn: That answers the mechanics for the militants. But what about Daniel's other question? The ordinary people in Gaza. Did the street know?

Herman: That is a much more complicated and uncomfortable question, Corn. There is no simple yes or no, because Gaza is not a monolith, but it is also not a place where major movements can occur in total isolation from the population.

Corn: You cannot move thousands of armed men toward a border without someone noticing the traffic.

Herman: Well, look at the timing. Six-thirty on a Saturday morning. Most people are asleep, or just finishing morning prayers. But in the weeks and months leading up to October, there were distinct ripples through the economy and society that, in hindsight, look like blaring sirens. Let us take the economic indicators first. In the summer of twenty-twenty-three, there were rare, public street protests across Gaza. The Want to Live movement, Bidna Na'eesh.

Corn: People protesting against Hamas's heavy taxes, power cuts, and dire living conditions.

Herman: Right. Thousands of Gazans took to the streets in July and August twenty-twenty-three. And Hamas cracked down on them viciously. Beating protesters, arresting organizers, raiding homes. Now, why does that matter for the timeline? Because several analysts, including some Palestinian commentators who have since spoken out from abroad, argue that the internal pressure on Hamas was reaching a critical boiling point. Sinwar was losing his grip on the domestic narrative. The misery was palpable. If you ask ordinary Gazans today about the mood that summer, they talk about a sense of unbearable claustrophobia and economic despair. Did they know an invasion was planned? No. But did they feel that Hamas was preparing some kind of dramatic eruption to break the domestic deadlock? Many say yes.

Corn: A collective sense of the air pressure dropping before a hurricane.

Herman: Exactly. But there were physical signs, too. Consider the border riots that Hamas staged along the security fence in August and September twenty-twenty-three. Ostensibly, these were protests about the treatment of Palestinian prisoners in Israeli jails and visits by Jewish activists to the Temple Mount. Every Friday, hundreds of young men, the so-called Revolutionary Youth, went to the fence under Hamas direction, burning tires, throwing pipe bombs, and trying to pull down pieces of the perimeter.

Corn: And Israel treated it as routine border management. Tear gas, rubber bullets, occasional sniper fire.

Herman: Routine nuisance. But what were those young men actually doing? They were mapping Israeli response times. They were seeing how quickly the IDF surveillance blimps pivoted, where the snipers set up their firing positions, and crucially, they were planting explosive charges against the base of the fence under the cover of thick black tire smoke. Many of the young men participating were just angry, unemployed kids who were paid a small stipend by Hamas front groups to go cause trouble at the fence. They did not know they were setting the stage for an invasion. But they knew the border was suddenly the center of gravity again.

Corn: They were operational stagehands who thought they were just rioting.

Herman: That is a great way to put it. They were stagehands. But then you have the secondary wave on the morning of October seventh itself, which is where the question of ordinary Gazans' awareness becomes really painful and historically fraught. When the fence was blown wide open by bulldozers at sunrise, the first wave through was the Nukhba commandos. Highly trained, uniformed, carrying specific target folders. But the second and third waves, which poured through an hour or two later? That was not just Hamas.

Corn: That was Palestinian Islamic Jihad, other smaller factions, and then hundreds of unaffiliated civilians and looters.

Herman: Thousands, according to Israeli estimates. People riding farm tractors, bicycles, running on foot through the massive gaps in the fence. How did they know the fence was down? Because once the rockets started firing at six-thirty, thousands of rockets in twenty minutes, a barrage unlike anything seen before, and once the news spread on local Telegram channels that the border had collapsed, the dam broke.

Corn: Telegram is the digital town square there.

Herman: It moved at internet speed. Channels like Gaza Now were posting videos within minutes. Look, our boys are inside the bases, the soldiers are running, the fence is open. If you live two kilometers from the border, and you have been trapped inside a walled enclave your entire life, and suddenly the wall ceases to exist, what happens? A chaotic, predatory free-for-all. People rushed in. Some out of sheer, wild curiosity, some to loot appliances and agricultural equipment from the kibbutzim, and many, tragically, participated in the abductions and killings of civilians.

Corn: Which complicates the idea of an innocent bystander population entirely disconnected from the event.

Herman: It makes the moral and operational landscape incredibly messy. You have accounts from survivors at Kibbutz Nir Oz, for example, who describe waves of looters who were clearly not military. Men in flip-flops, teenagers, grabbing televisions, motorcycles, and then grabbing Israeli civilians to drag back to Gaza to sell or trade to militant factions. There is documented evidence of ordinary Gazans holding hostages in private family homes for months. That does not mean every Gazan supported it or knew about it. Thousands of Gazans were horrified that morning, knowing full well what the Israeli military response would look like.

Corn: Anyone with half a brain knew what was coming down the pipe from the Israeli Air Force.

Herman: Absolutely. There are reports of families packing their bags at seven in the morning on October seventh, before the first Israeli jet even took off, because they knew the sky was going to fall on them. They saw the footage from the border and said, our leaders have signed our death warrants. So the awareness was not advance operational knowledge. It was an instant, intuitive understanding of the catastrophe that had just been unleashed.

Corn: But let us push on this. What about the work permit holders? Daniel mentioned whether awareness was more widely known. There were eighteen to twenty thousand Gazan laborers crossing into southern Israel every week to work in construction, agriculture, and inside those exact kibbutzim. Did they feed the intelligence machine?

Herman: That was the immediate suspicion in Israel. People in Kibbutz Be'eri and Kfar Aza said, how did the attackers know where the security coordinator lived? How did they know which houses had dogs? How did they know the code to the automated security gate? The immediate emotional conclusion was: the workers we employed, the guys who ate lunch on our porches, sold us out.

Corn: Did they?

Herman: The investigative reporting on this, particularly by Israeli journalists and military debriefs, shows a much more nuanced picture. Shin Bet investigated thousands of those workers who were detained in Israel after the attack. They found very little evidence of a widespread, conscious spy ring among the ordinary laborers. Most of those men were desperately protective of their work permits; an Israeli permit was worth five to ten times an average Gaza wage. It was their family's lifeline. If they got caught doing surveillance, they lost everything.

Corn: So where did the detailed floor plans come from?

Herman: Hamas did not need the workers to be spies. They had much better sources. First, open-source intelligence. We live in an era where people post everything on social media. Kibbutz Facebook pages, real estate listings showing internal layouts of homes, community newsletters that published maps of the grounds, holiday schedules, guard duty rosters.

Corn: The local community newsletter. The ultimate intelligence vulnerability.

Herman: It sounds absurd, but it is true! Kibbutz newsletters would literally publish things like, Moshe is on gate duty this weekend, but he is swapping with David because his daughter has a bat mitzvah. That was public on the internet. Second, Hamas used small commercial drones, bought off Alibaba or smuggled through Egypt, flying along the perimeter for years, taking high-resolution video of the patrol patterns. And third, they did interrogate or debrief workers when they returned to Gaza, often under coercion. A worker comes back through the Erez crossing, Hamas security pulls him into an office, and asks casual-sounding questions: Where are they building the new road? How many soldiers did you see at the checkpoint? Did they check your truck? The worker answers because he has to, without realizing he is filling in a grid map for an assault unit.

Corn: You do not need a spy if you have five hundred oblivious guys giving you one pixel each.

Herman: That is the phrase! Mosaic intelligence. Hamas's intelligence division, led by Mohammed Khamis Dababish, was remarkably proficient at assembling that mosaic. They took thousands of tiny, legal, innocuous data points and built a photorealistic targeting package. When the fighters hit the bases, they knew the location of the communications servers. That is not something a farmhand working in an avocado grove knows. That came from deep operational analysis, satellite imagery, and probably technical surveillance of IDF radio chatter.

Corn: So if the workers were mostly clean of direct complicity, what about the money? You cannot build a subterranean army and feed thousands of fighters for five years without a financial footprint that people notice.

Herman: This is where the story gets deeply international and where the complicity extends far beyond the borders of Gaza. The money trail is insane, Corn. We are talking about an operational budget estimated by Western intelligence to be hundreds of millions of dollars. Where did it come from?

Corn: The suitcase of cash from Qatar is the famous one.

Herman: Right, the suitcases of hundred-dollar bills, thirty million dollars a month, carried through Ben Gurion Airport with Israeli approval and driven straight into Gaza. The logic of the Netanyahu government at the time was to keep Hamas funded enough to govern Gaza and prevent a humanitarian collapse, while keeping the Palestinian leadership divided between Gaza and the West Bank. But that cash was officially earmarked for civil servants' salaries and impoverished families. Hamas just used that to offset its budget, while diverting tax revenues directly to the military wing.

Corn: Money is fungible. Who knew?

Herman: Everyone knew! But beyond the Qatari cash, Hamas built a global investment portfolio. The United States Treasury Department issued sanctions documents in twenty-twenty-two and twenty-twenty-three that detailed a secret investment network worth over five hundred million dollars. Real estate companies in Turkey, mining firms in Sudan, financial services in Algeria, shell companies registered in the United Arab Emirates. Controlled by an operative named Zaher Jabarin, who essentially ran Hamas's offshore merchant bank.

Corn: Real estate in Istanbul funding shock troops in Rafah.

Herman: Precisely. And then you have cryptocurrency. Hamas was an early and sophisticated adopter of crypto. Between twenty-twenty and twenty-twenty-three, crypto wallets linked to Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad received tens of millions of dollars in Bitcoin and Tether. They used virtual asset service providers based in Moscow, like the Garantex exchange, which was sanctioned for laundering illicit Russian funds. So you have a pipeline that runs from illicit Russian crypto brokers through Turkish banks, turning into cash carried through tunnels under the Egyptian border at Rafah, or smuggled via maritime routes on fishing boats.

Corn: And none of this flagged an immediate alert that an invasion was imminent?

Herman: It flagged financial crime alerts, but intelligence agencies suffer from a terrible disease called mirror-imaging. Israeli and American analysts looked at this massive financial network and said, look, Hamas has become a regional corporate empire. They have real estate, they have construction companies, they have government payrolls. Why would they risk all this wealth and administrative power by starting a catastrophic war they cannot win? The assumption was that money brings conservatism.

Corn: It works on suburban accountants. Why not religious fanatics?

Herman: Exactly! They assumed Sinwar wanted to be the mayor of Gaza, when Sinwar saw being the mayor of Gaza merely as an administrative chore on the way to an apocalyptic showdown. The money was not an end; it was fuel for the Big Project. The captured documents showed that Sinwar was willing to see the entire Gaza Strip flattened, all that infrastructure destroyed, because in his strategic calculus, the destruction of Gaza was a necessary price to shatter the status quo, derail the Saudi-Israeli normalization talks, and drag Iran and Hezbollah into a regional war of attrition that would destroy Israel over decades.

Corn: It is the ultimate ideological blind spot. You assume your enemy wants what you want: peace, quiet, economic growth, a nice patio.

Herman: That is the fatal flaw in the concept, the infamous conceptzia that the Israeli security establishment is now tearing itself apart over. They believed their own economic deterrence theory so thoroughly that any evidence contradicting it was simply discarded or reinterpreted to fit the model.

Corn: Which brings us back to Daniel's core question. How long was the preparation? We have the seed planted in twenty-nineteen. The mock kibbutzim built in twenty-twenty-one. The financial pipes laid over years. But what about the tactical training? Who taught an irregular militia to execute combined-arms drone warfare? Because the drone drops on the Israeli sensor towers were remarkably modern. That is straight out of the Ukraine playbook.

Herman: That was the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps, specifically the Quds Force. The timeline of tactical upgrades shows a dramatic shift after twenty-twenty. Iran brought key Hamas engineers and tactical planners out of Gaza, through the tunnels into Sinai, up through Lebanon, and into training facilities in Iran. General Esmail Qaani, who took over the Quds Force after Qasem Soleimani was assassinated in twenty-twenty, oversaw specialized programs for Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad fighters.

Corn: What were they teaching them?

Herman: Paragliding, for one. You do not learn how to fly a powered paraglider by reading a manual in a basement in Khan Younis. You need open airspace, wind currents, and instructors. Iranian commandos trained Hamas paragliders in specialized camps near Isfahan. They taught them drone-dropped munitions: how to take an off-the-shelf commercial quadcopter, wire a three-D-printed drop mechanism to the landing gear, load it with a modified PG-seven warhead, and hover precisely over the blind spot of an automated machine-gun turret.

Corn: A three-hundred-dollar drone killing a million-dollar remote weapon system.

Herman: And disabling the fiber-optic relay cables running along the fence. That was not improvised. That required exact technical knowledge of where the sensor cables were laid and how the Israeli border surveillance architecture communicated with the command posts at Re'im. The Iranians helped them map those vulnerabilities. But notice the timeline: that training was completed by late twenty-twenty-two. That means Hamas sat on that capability for nearly a year without using it.

Corn: That requires unbelievable self-control. Most insurgent groups get a cool new toy and want to use it immediately.

Herman: That is what makes this so atypical. Usually, a terrorist cell builds a bomb, they get paranoid they are about to be caught, and they blow it up as soon as possible. The longer you hold a plan, the higher the mathematical probability that an informant slips, a courier gets arrested, or an electronic intercept catches a stray word. Holding an operation of this scale for over two years, while continuing to stage small-scale provocations that make you look weak and undisciplined, is a masterclass in strategic patience.

Corn: They played dead.

Herman: They played dumb, which is even better. They let the Israelis think they were incompetent, corrupt bureaucrats who cared more about collecting import taxes on cement than fighting a jihad. There is a story told by Israeli intelligence officers now, looking back at intercepts from twenty-twenty-two. They heard Hamas commanders complaining about the cost of living, complaining about fuel shortages, arguing over low-level municipal garbage collection. It sounded like an organization that had aged out of revolutionary fervor and settled into boring, middle-aged municipal management. And it was all deliberate background noise.

Corn: Or those specific commanders really were just worried about the garbage, because they were kept out of the loop by Sinwar.

Herman: That too! If ninety-five percent of your organization genuinely thinks the priority is garbage collection and municipal budgets, then the Israeli listening posts will accurately hear ninety-five percent of the organization talking about garbage. The sincerity of the ignorant is the best deception tool you have.

Corn: So to Daniel's final query: was awareness of an eventual attack widely known among the Gazan public? How would you settle that?

Herman: I would settle it this way: the concept of an eventual, catastrophic confrontation was universally assumed; the reality of October seventh was an absolute shock.

Corn: Explain that distinction.

Herman: If you asked any person living in Gaza in September twenty-twenty-three, do you think this situation can last another five years? Every single person would have said no. The blockade, the lack of clean water, the unemployment rate over forty percent, the periodic bombardments, the internal tyranny of Hamas. Everyone knew the pressure cooker was going to blow. Sermons in the mosques talked constantly about liberating Al-Aqsa, about the final battle, about the return to the villages of nineteen-forty-eight. It was the ideological oxygen of the enclave. So the idea that war was coming was not a secret. It was the weather forecast.

Corn: But nobody had October seventh on their calendar.

Herman: Nobody had that on their calendar. Not the grocer in Gaza City, not the student at the Islamic University, not the mid-level civil servant, and certainly not the political leadership of Hamas sitting in Doha. When people woke up on that Saturday morning to the roar of thousands of rockets and saw the images of bulldozers pushing down the fence without a single Israeli helicopter appearing in the sky for hours, the initial reaction on the street was pure, dizzying disbelief. Some celebrated in the streets, handing out sweets, caught in a wave of nationalist euphoria; others immediately ran to the bakeries to stockpile flour and fuel, knowing with absolute certainty that Gaza was about to be pulverized into dust.

Corn: Euphoria on one corner, existential terror on the other.

Herman: Often in the same person within the span of ten minutes. Because everyone understood what the Israeli reaction would be. Israel's entire security doctrine since nineteen-forty-eight has been built on deterrence through overwhelming, disproportionate retaliation. If you kill a dozen soldiers, they flatten a neighborhood. If you kill twelve hundred people and take two hundred and fifty hostages? There was not a single adult in Gaza who did not realize, within three hours of that border breach, that the world they had inhabited for the last twenty years had just come to an end.

Corn: What strikes me most in all this is the inversion of technology. We spend trillions on autonomous platforms, algorithmic intelligence, artificial intelligence, face recognition, persistent satellite coverage. And a small group of men with clipboards, paper notebooks, and five years of silence dismantled the entire system in about forty-five minutes.

Herman: It is a profound lesson in the limits of technocratic security. The technology works, but only if the mind interpreting the data is willing to accept what the data says. The Israelis had the Jericho Wall document. We should mention that.

Corn: That forty-page battle plan the IDF had sitting in a drawer for over a year.

Herman: Yes! An intelligence analyst in the Southern Command, a non-commissioned officer, looked at the drills Hamas was running and compared them to that captured document. She said, they are practicing the exact steps outlined in Jericho Wall. Point for point. And her superior officer dismissed her warning, calling it an imaginary scenario. The technology collected the plan. The human beings just refused to believe Hamas had the audacity to execute it.

Corn: It turns out, if you want to know what someone is going to do, you do not need to hack their phone. You just have to listen when they tell you what they are going to do.

Herman: And believe them. That was the five-year plan. It was written down, it was practiced in broad daylight, it was funded through international shell games, and it relied entirely on the arrogance of the opponent to keep it hidden.

Corn: A terrifyingly simple blueprint.

Herman: Terrifying in every conceivable dimension.

Corn: That is the show. Send your questions, prompts, and basement voice notes to Daniel. We will look at them, or Herman will read fifty intelligence dossiers about them while pacing around his paddock.

Herman: I do not pace. I browse thoughtfully.

Corn: You pace. Goodnight, everyone.

Herman: Goodnight.

Corn: Daniel’s question is about the years before the morning: how long was this being prepared, who knew, and what did ordinary people in Gaza understand? The uncomfortable answer is that we can see a long-running plan and a tightly held operational secret. Those are not the same thing.

Herman: Right. And that distinction matters, because “Hamas planned this for years” can sound as if the whole of Gaza had been briefed, or as if every detail was settled years in advance. Neither follows. What we’ve learned points to a leadership project developed over a long period, then converted into a specific operation through years of intelligence gathering, training, and rehearsal. The people who knew the exact date and full plan appear to have been a much smaller circle.

Corn: A long plan, a short invitation list.

Herman: Extremely short, by all accounts. But let’s separate what is well supported from what is inference. We have Hamas statements, reporting based on Israeli intelligence documents and interrogations, captured material, and later analysis of the attack itself. They don’t all answer the same question. Hamas has an interest in presenting the attack as a historic triumph. Israeli authorities have an interest in explaining how the warning failed. Journalists and investigators are piecing together fragments after a catastrophe. So we can make a strong account, but not pretend we have the meeting minutes.

Corn: The meeting minutes would presumably be hard to retrieve.

Herman: Yes. The filing system is not ideal.

Corn: “Operation October Seventh: snacks, agenda, invasion.”

Herman: What we can say is that the attack did not spring from a sudden decision in the last few weeks. Hamas had been studying the communities and military positions near Gaza for a long time. Israeli investigations and reporting have described Hamas obtaining detailed information about border locations, roads, kibbutzim, military bases, security arrangements, and the routines of people who lived and worked near the fence. That kind of intelligence is not assembled overnight.

Corn: It is the unglamorous part of a military plan. The map before the motorbike.

Herman: Exactly. The attack’s first hours relied on knowing where to go and what to do once they got there. The attackers didn’t just breach the border and improvise. Their target lists and movements showed preparation for specific communities and installations. They knew routes, entrances, and in some cases the layout of homes and public buildings. That suggests sustained observation, information gathering, and rehearsing different tasks.

Corn: And the task list was horrifyingly practical.

Herman: Yes. Military posts, roads, the border barrier, nearby towns and kibbutzim, the festival site at Re’im. The attackers were divided into groups with assignments. Some were meant to hit military facilities, some to enter civilian communities, some to secure routes or widen the breach. There were also signs of plans to seize hostages and take them back into Gaza. The exact intended scale and sequence remain matters of investigation, but the organization and breadth are plain.

Corn: When a force arrives with maps and assignments, “spontaneous outbreak” is not a serious description.

Herman: No. And it’s worth clarifying the word “invasion.” Hamas’s armed wing, the Izz ad-Din al-Qassam Brigades, led the assault, with other armed groups and individuals joining the cross-border violence. It was not a conventional army moving in a neat line. But it was a coordinated attack across multiple points, designed to overwhelm the defenses and exploit the openings. Calling it improvised would be wrong.

Corn: How far back do we go, then? Is there a known seed moment?

Herman: There isn’t a single confirmed date that historians can point to and say, “There: that was the first seed.” Hamas leaders have described the operation as years in the making. Some reporting based on documents seized by Israel has suggested that the idea and planning were developed over several years, with a more detailed blueprint emerging well before the attack. The New York Times, in reporting published after October seventh, described a Hamas plan for a broad assault that had been in the organization’s possession for years. Israeli officials said they had obtained or seen material that resembled the plan but did not treat it as an imminent operational blueprint.

Corn: The distinction between “we know this is a possible plan” and “they are doing it tomorrow” is where intelligence earns its salary.

Herman: And where it can fail very badly. There had been warnings and indications that Hamas was training for raids and looking at how to breach the barrier. Israeli forces had also seen exercises that included attacking mock Israeli positions. There was a replica training site in Gaza, described in reporting as a mock-up of an Israeli community or military installation, where fighters practiced assaulting buildings and moving through them. Israeli observers could see at least some of that activity. But it was interpreted within a broader assumption that Hamas was deterred, focused on governing Gaza, and not prepared to risk a full-scale war.

Corn: A training village is a fairly unsubtle clue.

Herman: It is. But an intelligence service can observe a clue and still misread what it means. Israeli security officials had become accustomed to thinking of Hamas as a group that wanted to keep its rule in Gaza and avoid the costs of a major conflict. There was also a belief that the barrier, surveillance network, and rapid military response would contain a limited incursion. The idea that Hamas could coordinate a large assault and hold Israeli forces back long enough to cause a mass-casualty disaster was discounted.

Corn: A fortified wall can become a very expensive blind spot.

Herman: That’s one of the brutal ironies. The barrier was built and monitored to prevent infiltration. Hamas treated it as a system to study and defeat. The assault did not just attack concrete and fencing. It targeted the sensors and observation posts, cut communications in places, used explosives and vehicles to open breaches, and exploited the time it took for Israeli command and forces to understand the scale of what was happening. The surprise was not only that there were holes. It was that the defenders did not respond as if the whole system had been penetrated.

Corn: So when did the general concept become the October seventh operation?

Herman: We don’t know precisely. There are several layers: the strategic decision to mount an attack; the development of a plan; intelligence collection; training and preparation; and the final timing decision. Those can span different periods and involve different groups. Hamas leaders have said the operation was planned over years. Israeli assessments reported in the press have described a planning process involving Yahya Sinwar, the leader of Hamas in Gaza, and Mohammed Deif, the commander of the Qassam Brigades. Deif was widely described as a key operational architect. But the full internal chronology has not been publicly established.

Corn: “Planned for years” doesn’t mean somebody circled October seventh on a calendar in 2019.

Herman: Precisely. It may mean the organization had a strategic concept, then developed and refined a plan, then selected the date later. The immediate preparations were probably more compressed: final orders, assembly, moving fighters and equipment, and making sure the units were ready. Those are the preparations the prompt explicitly wants to set aside. But the deeper preparation—studying targets, practicing, building the capability, deciding what kind of attack to attempt—was a long process.

Corn: A recipe can exist for years before anyone turns on the oven.

Herman: I’m going to gently object to the oven, because this is a grim recipe.

Corn: I said it was a bad recipe.

Herman: Fair. One of the more informative pieces of evidence is the training. The attackers had practiced using explosives against obstacles, moving in groups, attacking buildings, and handling particular objectives. Their equipment and tactics were not all sophisticated, but the operation was designed around the strengths they had: surprise, numbers, motorcycles and pickup trucks, paragliders, locally produced rockets, and rapid movement through breached points. They didn’t need a conventional army’s logistical tail. They needed enough preparation to move quickly and create confusion before Israeli forces could regroup.

Corn: The sophistication was in the plan, not necessarily in the hardware.

Herman: Exactly. And the plan took advantage of habits. Israeli forces had become reliant on remote surveillance and technology at the border. The attackers knew where observation systems were and how to suppress them. They used rockets to draw attention and complicate response, then breached the fence at numerous locations. Some fighters crossed by air on motorized paragliders; others came through the ground breaches. Once inside, the groups dispersed toward targets. This is one reason the attack looks like a cascade of separate scenes, even though it was coordinated.

Corn: A single operation experienced as dozens of emergencies.

Herman: Yes. And the planning also had to account for what Hamas could not know. They could not control how fast the Israeli response would arrive, how civilians and soldiers would react, or how long they could hold ground. So the operational plan needed to be robust enough to produce chaos quickly, without depending on a long occupation of Israeli territory. Taking hostages and returning with them was, in part, a way to carry the impact back into Gaza even if the attackers could not remain across the border.

Corn: That is a cold piece of strategic reasoning.

Herman: It is. There were also claims about coordination with Iran or Hezbollah. Hamas has had long-standing relationships with Iran, and there has been military, financial, and political support over time. But public reporting after the attack, including reporting based on intelligence officials, did not establish that Iran or Hezbollah knew the exact date or approved the specific operation in advance. Hamas officials themselves offered varying accounts of how much allies knew. So we should distinguish the larger history of support from proof of direct advance knowledge of October seventh.

Corn: “They have a relationship” is not the same sentence as “they received the launch time.”

Herman: Right. And Hamas had reason to keep the final plan from allies as well as adversaries. A larger circle means more opportunities for surveillance, interception, accidental disclosure, or a political decision to stop the operation. Keeping the plan narrow could protect it from Israeli intelligence, but also from leaks through Hamas’s own network and the people around it.

Corn: Let’s get to the part Daniel is really asking about: how do you keep something that large secret inside a crowded, politically controlled place?

Herman: First, you don’t necessarily tell the whole organization the whole plan. You divide work. A fighter can train for a specific task without knowing the overall date or destination. One group can collect information about a border site; another can prepare equipment; another can rehearse entry techniques. They need enough information to do their job, not enough to reconstruct the full operation.

Corn: The classic compartment. Give a person a room and a key, not the blueprint to the whole building.

Herman: Yes. And Hamas is not just a guerrilla organization; it has military, political, security, administrative, social, and governing structures. Those structures overlap in ways that make it difficult for outsiders to know where one ends and another begins, but it would be a mistake to assume every employee or supporter knows military plans. A small command group can control operational information while the broader organization continues ordinary activities. A government still has to run services, manage salaries, negotiate over crossings, and deal with local disputes. Those routines can provide cover for the fact that selected people are preparing for something else.

Corn: The normal business of government is a very effective disguise for not looking like a normal government.

Herman: There is also the value of mundane explanations. People moving around for training, security, political meetings, or military exercises may not attract attention if those activities are already part of life in Gaza. A unit can rehearse one component under the cover of a familiar activity. Equipment can be moved in quantities that don’t look unusual to the people who see it. And if everyone involved thinks a major operation is possible in principle, they still may not know when it will happen.

Corn: A thousand people can know the weather is dangerous. That doesn’t mean a thousand people know the storm’s exact path.

Herman: That’s a good way to put it. We should be careful, though, because we don’t have a verified organizational chart of who knew what. The strongest inference is that the final operational details were tightly compartmentalized, and that commanders relied on trust, direct control, and secrecy. Some reporting has described a small inner circle around Sinwar and Deif. We can say the exact plan and timing appear to have been restricted. We cannot confidently assign a precise number of people who knew.

Corn: So not “three people knew,” unless somebody has a source better than a dramatic headline.

Herman: Exactly. Hamas’s security culture is shaped by the danger of Israeli intelligence penetration. Israeli services have had sources and surveillance capabilities inside Palestinian groups, and Hamas has spent years trying to identify and prevent infiltration. That doesn’t mean it can make itself impermeable. No organization can. But fear of informants encourages compartmentalization, vetting, internal counterintelligence, and a habit of discussing sensitive matters face to face or through trusted channels.

Corn: There’s a grim irony in a group that fears infiltration using such a visible, complicated plan.

Herman: Visible pieces, hidden whole. A training exercise can be observed without revealing the date. A mock-up can be seen without making the purpose obvious to the observer. And if Israeli analysts already believe Hamas is deterred, they may file the evidence under “capability development” rather than “imminent attack.” Secrecy is not only hiding facts. It’s also exploiting the other side’s expectations about what those facts mean.

Corn: Which is more effective than hiding a full-scale training ground under a bedsheet.

Herman: Probably. The operational security may also have involved giving fighters their instructions late. Some accounts of the assault suggest that at least some participants may not have known the full destination or exact objective until shortly before they crossed. That would reduce the number of people who could leak the plan in advance. But reports based on interviews and captured documents vary, and I would not turn that into a universal statement about every attacker.

Corn: “The fighters knew nothing” is as implausible as “everyone knew everything.”

Herman: Yes. The attackers knew enough to carry out their tasks. The more important question is what they knew about the scale and consequences. A person told to attack a particular military post knows they are participating in an attack. They may not know the whole multi-pronged plan. A person told to join a training exercise may know even less. There are degrees of awareness.

Corn: And the civilian population is not one large room with one shared mind.

Herman: That’s crucial. “Would ordinary Gazans have been taken by surprise?” could mean, did they know Hamas intended some kind of major attack? Did they know it would happen that morning? Did they expect fighters to cross into Israel? Did they understand what would happen once they entered homes and communities? Those have different answers.

Corn: The date and the scale are the things most likely to have been secret. The general possibility of violence was not secret.

Herman: Right. Gaza had lived with repeated conflict, rocket fire, Israeli airstrikes, border confrontations, and Hamas military activity for years. Many people would have known that Hamas and other armed groups maintained forces and weapons. Residents near training areas might have heard or seen exercises. Some people would have known individuals in the armed wing. That does not mean they knew a cross-border assault was being planned for October seventh.

Corn: Knowing that someone owns a weapon is not knowing they’re leaving at dawn.

Herman: And even people with a broad awareness of preparations may have expected a different kind of escalation: rocket fire, a border protest, a limited raid, or another round of fighting. The specific operation was exceptionally large. It involved fighters crossing in multiple ways and reaching several communities and military sites. The evidence we have does not show that ordinary Gazans, as a population, were told about that plan in advance.

Corn: What evidence would we expect to see if it were widely known?

Herman: That’s complicated. We might expect pre-attack conversations, unusual movement, people warning relatives not to travel, or substantial anticipatory preparations. But a clandestine operation can leave little public trace, and people may not report what they know. The absence of widespread public evidence is not proof no one knew. It does, however, limit the claim that the population broadly had advance notice. We have not seen credible evidence that large numbers of ordinary residents knew the date and details before the attack.

Corn: There were people who crossed after the breaches opened, though.

Herman: Yes, and that is one of the clearest reasons not to overcorrect into a comforting story that everyone in Gaza was shocked and uninvolved. Videos from October seventh show armed fighters and, in some cases, civilians crossing into Israel after the barrier had been breached. There was looting, and some people took part in violence or entered homes. Human rights organizations and journalists have documented those scenes. They are real. They matter. But they are evidence about what some people did after the assault began, not proof that Gaza’s general population had advance knowledge of the plan.

Corn: The first person through a broken gate may be an accomplice, a looter, or a person following the crowd. The video doesn’t automatically tell us which.

Herman: Exactly. It also doesn’t tell us what that person knew beforehand. The assault created an extraordinary opening. People may have crossed because they knew fighters were entering, because they were swept along in a chaotic moment, or because the breach offered an opportunity to loot. Some may have been affiliated with armed groups; some may not. It is impossible to classify every individual from a clip. But we can say the presence of civilian participants in some acts is not speculative.

Corn: And we can say that the existence of civilian participants doesn’t make them representatives of every family in Gaza.

Herman: Correct. We should neither erase those individuals nor generalize from them to millions of people. Gaza’s population includes children, people who wanted nothing to do with Hamas, people who supported Hamas, people who opposed it, people who feared it, and people whose views changed over time. Hamas’s control over the territory did not mean every resident had access to its military plans. It did mean that the organization operated in a dense civilian environment, where military preparations and civilian life could be adjacent in ways that make clean distinctions difficult.

Corn: The government can be dominant without being omniscient.

Herman: And residents can be familiar with a military presence without being read into its operations. Imagine you live near a group that runs the local authorities, controls armed units, and conducts regular exercises. You may know the broad pattern of activity. You might recognize a training session. You might have a cousin who belongs to a unit. None of that tells you that an operation has been authorized, that it will happen on a particular morning, or that its targets include civilian communities.

Corn: The difference between “something is coming” and “this is what is coming” can be enormous.

Herman: It can. There’s another distinction: ideological or political support is not foreknowledge. Polling after the attack found significant support for the October seventh assault among Palestinians, though the results varied by location and wording, and support shifted as the war unfolded. Those polls can tell us something about political attitudes at the time respondents were surveyed. They cannot tell us who knew about the operation before it happened. Approval after the event is not evidence of advance knowledge.

Corn: A reaction is not a rehearsal.

Herman: Exactly. And polling in wartime is a difficult instrument. People may answer under pressure, may be grieving or angry, may interpret the question differently, or may see the attack through the immediate lens of retaliation and suffering. None of that means the findings should be ignored. It means they answer a different question from Daniel’s.

Corn: Did anyone in Gaza publicly signal that it was coming?

Herman: There were rumors and warnings after the fact, and there have been claims about people discussing the operation in advance. But public claims of foreknowledge need careful handling. Some stories have been based on secondhand accounts or anonymous sources; some have been disputed. There have also been allegations that particular people must have known because they behaved strangely, or because they posted something ambiguous. Those are not enough to establish broad advance awareness. So far, the strongest public evidence is about the attackers, the command structure, and preparations visible to Israeli intelligence—not a reliable trail showing general civilian foreknowledge.

Corn: If a rumor becomes a fact every time someone repeats it, intelligence analysis gets very easy.

Herman: Too easy. There were also journalists and activists who, after the attack, asked how such a large operation could have happened without ordinary residents noticing. That is a reasonable question, but “noticing activity” and “understanding the plan” are separate. People may have seen training, unusual movements, or heightened security measures without knowing what those signs meant. A resident could have thought, “There’s another military exercise,” or “Hamas is preparing for a possible clash.” That is not the same as knowing that fighters would enter communities across the border.

Corn: The signal may be visible while the message remains unreadable.

Herman: Yes. The same goes for people who may have helped with logistical details. A driver might transport a person without knowing the destination’s significance. Someone might supply food or equipment under an ordinary explanation. An employee could carry out a task without knowing it was part of a larger assault. That’s a common feature of compartmentalized conspiracies and clandestine operations: people can contribute to a process without seeing the whole design.

Corn: Which makes the question “How many people knew?” almost impossible without defining “knew.”

Herman: Exactly. There might be a small group that knew the date, scope, and objectives. A larger group could know the broad strategic goal. More people could know that units were preparing for a serious operation without knowing which one. Still more could observe fragments and never connect them. And then there are people who learned what was happening only when the attack was underway, through their phones, the sounds of fighting, or seeing people cross back into Gaza.

Corn: That last category would not have needed a briefing. The morning delivered its own.

Herman: Tragically. For civilians in Gaza, many would have learned of the attack as it unfolded or through the images and rumors that spread rapidly. Some residents reportedly celebrated; others were alarmed. Some may have feared immediate Israeli retaliation. It’s difficult to reconstruct individual reactions, and there was no safe, neutral survey of people asking what they knew at each hour. We should resist turning the lack of a comprehensive record into a sweeping conclusion.

Corn: There is a temptation to make a whole population either innocent witnesses or one giant conspirator.

Herman: And both are inaccurate. The actual picture is less emotionally convenient: a small armed organization made the plan; a wider set of fighters and facilitators had varying levels of knowledge; some civilians joined violence or looting once the breach opened; many others likely had no advance knowledge; and some may have suspected that something serious was being prepared without knowing its timing or shape.

Corn: That’s less tidy than a headline.

Herman: Much more useful than a headline. We should talk about why Hamas might have chosen to keep the plan hidden even from people who supported its goals. The operation was so consequential that disclosure would create risk. Israel had human sources and signals intelligence. Hamas had reason to assume that communications were monitored. A date could be exposed through a single intercepted message, a careless phone call, or a person under interrogation. So limiting the circle was not just a security preference. It was essential to the design.

Corn: They were trying to make an attack visible only after it was too late to stop.

Herman: That’s right. And they also had an incentive to preserve the appearance of routine. If Israeli analysts expected Hamas to avoid a major war, Hamas could continue to appear focused on governing, negotiations, economic arrangements, or localized military activity. That might have helped sustain the Israeli belief that the group was contained. It’s possible Hamas deliberately cultivated that impression. Israeli investigations and press accounts have described signals of restraint and a pattern of avoiding escalation at certain moments. But we have to distinguish a deliberate deception campaign from an opponent’s own mistaken assumptions. They can reinforce each other.

Corn: If the other side wants to believe you’re quiet, you don’t have to whisper.

Herman: Yes. There’s also an organizational advantage in having the political leadership and military leadership manage different kinds of communication. Public statements could be conciliatory or focused on immediate political issues while the armed wing prepared. But we shouldn’t picture two perfectly separate worlds. Hamas’s political and military leadership are connected; they share strategic aims and authority. The question is who had access to which operational detail, not whether the organization’s public and military sides had no relationship.

Corn: A compartmentalized organization still needs someone who knows where the compartments are.

Herman: Exactly. And that person becomes an enormous point of failure. But a very small command circle can accept that risk if it believes operational secrecy is more important than broad participation. There’s a trade-off: narrow planning improves security, but it can reduce flexibility and increase the consequences if commanders are killed or communications fail. The attack’s early chaos suggests that Hamas had enough decentralized structure for groups to keep moving once the plan began, but it also appears that the assault exceeded what many participants—and perhaps some commanders—could control.

Corn: The operation’s success at getting through the barrier did not mean it remained controlled after that.

Herman: Right. The attackers killed civilians and soldiers, took hostages, and committed acts of extreme violence. Those acts were not accidental side effects to be softened with technical language. The scale and targets matter. The plan’s preparation doesn’t make the violence less barbaric; it tells us it was not a spontaneous riot. And the fact that some people may have joined in after the breach doesn’t make the assault a mass movement with advance public authorization.

Corn: Planning and participation are separate questions. So are explanation and excuse.

Herman: Absolutely. Understanding the preparation is not an attempt to justify it. It matters because it shows how an organization can exploit a security system, how a long-term project can be concealed, and how warning signs can be present without producing an accurate forecast. It also matters for understanding the human toll: the victims were not killed by a random accident at the border. The operation included intentional attacks on civilian communities.

Corn: The word “surprise” can be misleading, too. Israel was surprised strategically. Individual fighters may not have been. Civilians may have learned at different moments.

Herman: That’s a useful breakdown. The Israeli security establishment was surprised by the scale and timing, despite warnings and observable preparation. The Hamas commanders who set the operation in motion were not surprised. The fighters who had their assignments may have known an attack was coming, though not necessarily every part of the plan. Ordinary Gazans, as a whole, appear not to have had advance knowledge of the exact operation. Some individuals likely knew more; some may have recognized signs; some joined once it was underway.

Corn: And “appears” is doing honest work there.

Herman: It is. We cannot inspect the private knowledge of a population. We can assess the evidence available. We have strong evidence of long-term Hamas planning and preparation. We have substantial evidence of a tight operational circle and deliberate compartmentalization. We have evidence that some people beyond the military participants may have witnessed or joined aspects of the attack once it began. We do not have solid public evidence that ordinary Gazans broadly knew the date, targets, or full scale in advance.

Corn: So, if Daniel wants a clean verdict: the operation was years in the making, but the launch details were probably held by a relatively small circle.

Herman: Yes, with one refinement: “years in the making” describes the development of the capability and strategic plan, not necessarily a fully fixed, unchanged plan waiting for a date. There was likely evolution. Hamas had to gather intelligence, build units, train, test tactics, and wait for conditions it considered suitable. A plan can be conceived years earlier and revised as the military and political context changes.

Corn: The plan was old. The calendar page was not.

Herman: Nicely put. And on ordinary Gazans: many probably were surprised by the specific event and its scale. Some were not surprised that violence was possible; some knew something about Hamas’s military activity; some individuals may have had advance knowledge; and some participated after the attack began. The evidence does not justify saying that the population as a whole knew the operation was coming.

Corn: It also doesn’t justify saying no one outside the command structure had any idea.

Herman: Right. The honest position is between those absolutes, but not because we’re trying to be diplomatically neutral. It’s because the evidence supports a narrower conclusion. We can make a clear judgment without pretending to know what no one has established.

Corn: That’s the whole answer, really: long preparation, narrow secret, uneven awareness.

Herman: And the terrible lesson for intelligence is that a group can show you pieces of a plan without showing you the moment they intend to use it. Hamas had practiced. It had studied the border. It had built the units and rehearsed attacks. Israeli intelligence had seen some of that, but the assumptions used to interpret it were wrong. The barriers and sensors created confidence, and confidence made the warnings easier to discount.

Corn: The surveillance system saw the rehearsal. The institution saw a rehearsal for something less dangerous.

Herman: Exactly. That gap between observation and interpretation is where the surprise lived. It wasn’t that every warning was invisible. It’s that the warnings were assigned a meaning that fit the prevailing theory: Hamas was deterred, Hamas wanted to preserve its rule, Hamas would not risk a major war. The attack showed that a group can be rationally interested in maintaining its governing position and still choose an operation that risks destroying it, because its leaders value other goals more highly.

Corn: You can’t infer that someone won’t act because the consequences look bad to you.

Herman: Especially when you don’t know what they believe they can gain. That doesn’t mean the attack was inevitable or that Israeli failure was unavoidable. It means the analysis had to consider that Hamas might accept costs that seemed irrational from the outside. And once the attack began, the local communities and military positions were exposed to a plan built to exploit precisely the response delays and assumptions that had accumulated.

Corn: Which leaves us with a bad morning that had a long shadow behind it.

Herman: Yes. It was not planned in one night, and it was not known to everyone. The evidence points to years of preparation, an inner circle that guarded the operational details, and a much wider population in which awareness ranged from ordinary familiarity with armed activity to actual participation after the border was breached. For the exact date and the full design, we do not have evidence of broad public foreknowledge.

Corn: Daniel, that’s our best answer: long project, narrow circle, no credible case for mass advance awareness.

Herman: And no reason to flatten the people who did take part into a statistic about everyone else. The distinction is important, even when it is uncomfortable.

Corn: It’s uncomfortable either way. The facts don’t become kinder if we blur them.

Herman: No. They just become less accurate.

Corn: That’s My Weird Prompts. We’ll see you next time.

Herman: Take care, and keep your categories separate. They’re doing a lot of work.

runs.prompt:
Hey, Herman and Coron. Here's one of those prompts that I'm sending in that I'm setting a reminder to listen back to at some point and say, 'Daniel, did you really need to send that in? You sound like a crazy person.' Maybe it's not the first one. But here is a topic that is going to sound a little out there, but in the spirit of this podcast, let's just run with it.

I'll tell you what I'm doing today. I'm almost finished getting our place ready for the move, decluttering. We've gone from a cluttered apartment to zero clutter. Everything that we didn't need is thrown out. Everything is labeled.

I did some prompts last week asking about industrial paint markers. I never knew that these things exist — actually, I take that back. I never had good results with them, so I just assumed they were all rubbish. I picked up and asked ChatGPT for what's a decent one and learned, more importantly, about the chemistry. If you need to get them to stick on wood, what are you buying? What does an oil-based marker do that an alcohol-based marker doesn't? How long do they cure for, all the rest of it? Not the most scintillating topic under the planet, but I'll tell you why I'm in an elevated mood today, a good mood. I don't think it's due to the markers, because these are xylene-free and scentless, but they really do a nice job at bedding down.

You guys know that I have ADHD. I'm very open about that fact, and we've done many episodes about ADHD. I mentioned before that I thought buying a headtorch was one of those weird hacks that I hit upon for finding things. We did a super episode yesterday, and I think it was probably something you might need a neuroscience degree for. The subject matter was when people have — and this is something I have personally — a hard time filtering out conversations or music or sounds in the background. We talked about how what might present as the same system, I might say it's like a sensory filtering disorder, can actually have three very distinctive inherent neurological causes, seen in autism, ADHD, the rest of it.

Because I'm marking stuff for the move, I'm finding it just to do the things I need. But I'm also marking things that I'm always mislaying around the house. I have a notebook. I love the process of writing notes — something I kind of fell out of, and now I'm discovering again. I'm talking about just bullet journaling, opening up a notebook. If you asked me where my ADHD brain drives me crazy, it's mislaying the same few things around the house. One of them is my keys and my wallet. This is the classic one, so I have a key-wallet thing. This notebook is always vanishing on me. There are a few things like it — it might sound like a flippant thing, but this notebook is where I jot down client ideas, life plans. So when I can't find my notebook, it drives me nuts.

Now, here is what I am doing. I have in my hand the Sakura Pen-Touch 2mm, a beautiful pen, medium point. It is AP-rated. It's a white paint pen from Sakura, a Japanese manufacturer, alongside Edding, probably the biggest one in the space. I'm writing on my notebook, this big label with paint that says 'notebook' underline. I'm looking around my office now and I notice that it catches me. I can see, oh, there's where my notebook is. So I feel like I'm landing onto something. This might seem to some people crazy. It might seem like visual clutter. Do you really want to have these big labels all over your workspace? But for a few things that I really want to call my attention to, I'm finding this to be helpful.

I'm trying to find another example. What have I done today? The step ladder that's constantly going missing — wrote 'office' because we found one that looks almost the same and is for the patio. Again, these are things that to neurotypical people might sound stupid, obsessive, ridiculous. I've definitely self-censored about this kind of stuff before, and I felt I should probably not tell anyone about this because they're going to think I'm totally crazy. But it's one of those things that if you're wasting time every day and it's annoying you, whatever works works, and I'm happy to run with it.

So anyway, Herman and Coron, now that I've told you about this organizational method, I'd love to get your take on arranging your space if you have a home office or living space and you have ADHD or some other form of neurodivergence, and like me, you're highly prone to just putting things down without even registering it for a second. I'm not suggesting that writing gigantic signs on everything is the be-all and end-all approach, but I would like to discuss — and this is why the prompt is, I'm trying to ask something a little bit deeper here — I'd like to discuss how our visual processing might differ in ways that make mislaying things particularly prevalent, and why simply putting out big callouts on things or maybe simple home organization strategies that we can implement.

Decluttering is number one — that reduces your visual clutter. And sometimes it is just having these big signs or, you know, saying 'in stationary drawer' or something like that. There's a reason that I've kind of discovered the world of labeling and sensed for a long time that there's something really to this. I always feel at the time this was a complete waste of time. Why did I spend three hours writing labels around the house? And then for the next year, I'm like, oh, thank goodness I did that, because now I know where it is and I can find it. That was a really good use of time. So it's one of those things that at the time it feels a bit crazy, later you see the benefits.

Herman and Coron, I hope that lays the groundwork for a wider discussion for those of us with neurodivergence who are very prone to mislaying things. I've been losing things and putting things down in places that I couldn't remember since I was probably a teenager. So this isn't a new phenomenon, but today I have a new ally: the paint pen. Herman and Coron, let's talk about visual processing in ADHD and other forms of neurodivergence in today's episode of My Weird Prompts. Today, really putting the 'weird' in 'weird prompt.'

entries.script:
Corn: Daniel has written “notebook” on his notebook, and he would like to know whether this is neuroscience or a cry for help.

Herman: I vote for useful environmental design. Although writing “notebook” on a sandwich would give us a more interesting diagnostic problem.

Corn: Welcome to My Weird Prompts. I’m Corn, here with my brother, Herman Poppleberry. Today, our producer Daniel has discovered the industrial paint pen, and several household objects have acquired subtitles.

Herman: And his actual question is excellent. Why do some people, particularly people with ADHD, keep putting things down without registering where they went? Why might a big white label make an object easier to find? And how do you arrange a home so that finding your notebook doesn’t become the first project you write in it?

Corn: First, a ruling. Labeling things that you repeatedly lose is not ridiculous. It’s a reasonable response to a recurring problem. You don’t owe your desk an understated aesthetic.

Herman: Absolutely. But I want to separate three things that can feel identical: not noticing where you put something, not remembering where you put it, and looking right at it without recognizing that it’s the thing you need.

Corn: The notebook can disappear at three different departments.

Herman: Precisely. And the intervention depends on which department is losing the paperwork.

Corn: Let’s use his actual scene. Daniel has a client idea. He writes it down, gets up to check something for the move, puts the notebook on a stack of packing materials, and returns twenty minutes later. Gone. Except it hasn’t moved.

Herman: At the moment he put it down, his attention may have been on the next task. The placement wasn’t strongly encoded into memory. Later, he experiences that as forgetting, but there may never have been a clear memory of the placement to retrieve.

Corn: So “try harder to remember” is arriving after the incident.

Herman: Often, yes. We can remember incidental things without deliberately attending to them, so it isn’t an absolute rule. But attention strongly influences what gets encoded. If you’re mentally composing an email while your hand deposits the notebook, the email may get the processing resources and the deposit may not.

Corn: I dislike that the email gets custody.

Herman: Then there’s working memory: keeping a goal or location active while doing something else. You think, “Notebook on chair, move this box, answer that question,” and the little thread connecting you to the chair gets displaced.

Corn: And the third department is visual search.

Herman: Yes. The notebook is physically visible, but you have to select it from competing objects. Its cover may blend into the desk. It may be partly covered. You may be searching for its usual orientation, and today it’s edge-on beside a laptop.

Corn: That last one feels important. We don’t search for a philosophical notebook. We search for the dark rectangle we expect to see.

Herman: Exactly. Search is guided by features and expectations: color, shape, size, likely location. Your brain isn’t identifying every object in the room with equal thoroughness. That would be exhausting.

Corn: You’ve seen me enter a hardware shop.

Herman: An impressive demonstration of serial processing.

Corn: Now put ADHD into that picture without telling everyone their visual cortex is broken.

Herman: ADHD is associated, on average, with difficulties regulating attention and executive functions. That can affect maintaining the search goal, resisting distraction, organizing possessions, and consistently carrying out a put-it-away routine. But people vary enormously. We shouldn’t take Daniel’s missing notebook and infer one specific visual-processing abnormality.

Corn: That’s my concern with the framing. “Visual processing differences” sounds satisfyingly deep. Sometimes the explanation is that you put your notebook beneath a shipping label while thinking about lunch.

Herman: I agree, with a qualification. There is research into visual attention, distractor suppression, eye movements, and sensory processing in ADHD. Those are legitimate areas. But findings from a laboratory task don’t give us a neat explanation for one person’s house. Losing objects can emerge from several ordinary processes interacting badly.

Corn: Ordinary mechanisms, unusually expensive outcome.

Herman: Exactly. And “ordinary” doesn’t mean trivial. Repeatedly interrupting your work to search for essentials can be genuinely disabling.

Corn: Daniel also connected this to difficulty filtering conversations and background sounds. Can we connect those, or are we just putting everything in the same neurological drawer?

Herman: We can connect them at a broad level: selecting relevant information while competing information is present. But auditory filtering and finding a notebook aren’t the same task. And sensory experiences in ADHD, autism, and other conditions overlap without necessarily sharing one mechanism.

Corn: So no universal filter switch.

Herman: No. Nor a clean rule that autistic people have one kind of filter and people with ADHD have another. Within either group, profiles vary. Someone may find sound overwhelming but be excellent at locating objects. Someone else may tolerate a noisy café and lose their wallet twice before leaving it.

Corn: Versatility.

Herman: Daniel’s observation is still valuable. He changed a feature of his environment, and a frequently lost object became easier to notice. We can take that seriously without claiming the paint pen revealed his neural circuitry.

Corn: Let’s examine the pen, then. White lettering, large enough to catch his attention, on the cover of a notebook. Is the word doing the work, or is it basically a white flag?

Herman: Probably some combination, and we can’t tell from his report. High contrast can make a region more visually distinctive. Large lettering can be legible at a distance. A familiar word can confirm identity once he looks toward it. And because he just made the label, it may have novelty and personal relevance.

Corn: Which is a polite way of saying he might notice it because he spent the morning being delighted with his pen.

Herman: That’s a real possibility. Novelty can temporarily help. But that doesn’t make the intervention fake. A label can remain useful after it stops being exciting, especially if it gives the notebook a stable, distinctive appearance.

Corn: Would you have written “notebook,” though? I think I’d choose one broad white stripe. You don’t need to read your keys.

Herman: For finding an object at a glance, a simple distinctive feature may be better than a word. A bright spine, a contrasting patch, a distinctive key fob. But the word has advantages if several objects look similar or if the label communicates a destination or purpose.

Corn: Which brings us to his ladders. One belongs in the office, one on the patio, and they look almost identical. “Office” isn’t identifying the species. It’s identifying the assignment.

Herman: Exactly. That label answers “Which one is this?” and “Where does it belong?” The notebook label mainly answers “Is that the thing I’m looking for?” Same technology, different job.

Corn: And a drawer label answers a third question: “Where should I look before I dismantle the apartment?”

Herman: Yes. I’d distinguish object identification, storage location, and action cues. “Notebook.” “Stationery.” “Take these keys.” You can use labels for all three, but knowing which problem you’re solving helps you write a useful one.

Corn: “Important things” fails all three.

Herman: It’s a category designed to become a sedimentary layer.

Corn: Here’s where I push back on Daniel’s “whatever works works.” Mostly, yes. But if everything gets a giant label, you’ve rebuilt the clutter in typography.

Herman: Completely. Salience is relative. If every surface shouts, no surface is particularly informative. I’d reserve high-contrast callouts for the few objects or locations that repeatedly cause friction.

Corn: Not a house that looks like it’s evacuating itself.

Herman: And not necessarily the brightest possible colors. For someone who finds visual intensity uncomfortable, a consistent, restrained system may work better. High contrast doesn’t have to mean fluorescent orange. A plain white label on a dark drawer can be both calm and readable.

Corn: Daniel has also just decluttered the apartment. That is a gigantic confounder in his pen experiment.

Herman: It is. He changed the object and the background. Fewer competing items could explain some of the improvement. The label may add more. We don’t have to identify the exact percentage to keep both useful changes.

Corn: But we should avoid crediting the marker with clearing the room.

Herman: Sakura’s marketing department will survive.

Corn: There’s a little chemistry claim in his message worth catching. He says the pen is xylene-free, scentless, and AP-rated, so his elevated mood probably isn’t the markers.

Herman: The Art and Creative Materials Institute’s AP seal indicates evaluation for toxicity under intended use. It doesn’t mean a product is edible, suitable for skin, or safe to inhale deliberately. And lack of smell isn’t proof of lack of vapor.

Corn: Your nose is not a safety data sheet.

Herman: Exactly. Use the product according to its label, with the recommended ventilation. Xylene-free means it doesn’t contain that particular solvent, not that every ingredient is water. And paint markers aren’t all chemically interchangeable: surface preparation and curing depend on the actual formulation.

Corn: Also test the label somewhere discreet before turning a favorite notebook into a solvent compatibility study.

Herman: Especially flexible covers, coated plastics, or things you’ll handle constantly. Dry to the touch isn’t always the same as fully cured. But we needn’t become a coatings podcast.

Corn: Not until the paint dries.

Herman: You’ve been holding that.

Corn: Now, the headtorch. Daniel previously discovered that wearing one helps him find things. What might that be doing?

Herman: Several practical things. More illumination can make detail easier to see. Light coming from close to your line of sight puts illumination where you’re looking. As you move, shadows and reflections can reveal edges or an object tucked into a gap.

Corn: And it turns searching into a specific activity. Not wandering around thinking, “I’m a person who has lost something.” You put on equipment.
